lead: Both readings turn on one small Greek word, kairos, the appointed time. Paul tells the Romans, “you know what time it is”: the night is nearly over, so get up and dress for the day. Gabriel tells Zechariah that his words “will be fulfilled in their time”, and the old priest, who cannot yet believe it, must wait for that time in silence. One reading wakes us and the other quiets us, and a fast needs both.

r.h: The night is far gone
set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome, probably from Corinth around AD 57, before he had ever visited them. After eleven chapters on what God has done in Christ, chapters 12–15 turn to how believers are to live. Just before this passage he has said, “Pay to all what is due them” (13:7), speaking of taxes and honour. Today’s reading picks up that word: there is one debt that can never be paid off.
str: vv. 8–10: love is the one debt that remains, and it fulfils the law.
vv. 11–12a: the hour: the night is ending and salvation is near.
vv. 12b–14: the change of clothes: put off the works of darkness and put on Christ.
kw: The same root as “what is due” in v. 7. Taxes can be paid in full and the account closed. Love is an account that stays open, because the one who loves never reaches the point of having loved enough.
Greek has two common words for time. Chronos is time that passes; kairos is time as a decisive moment, the right hour. Paul does not mean the hour on the clock but the hour in God’s plan.

The verb for putting on clothes. Paul uses it of baptism: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27). What was given once in baptism must be put on again each morning.
vv: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.

Paul lists the commandments about the neighbour (v. 9) and says they are summed up in Leviticus 19:18. Love does not cancel the commandments. A person who truly loves will not steal from a neighbour or betray him.
Besides this, you know what time it is, how it is now the moment for you to wake from sleep.
Paul speaks to baptised people. Believers too can sleep: not by rejecting the faith, but by living as if nothing were about to happen.
the night is far gone, the day is near.
This is the language of the last hour before dawn. The Christian lives between Easter, when the light has already broken, and the Lord’s return, when it will be full day.
Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.
“Flesh” in Paul does not mean the body as something bad. It means human life closed in on itself and turned away from God. “Make no provision” is practical: do not plan ahead for your own falls.
ch: These verses have a famous place in Christian history. St Augustine tells in his Confessions (8.12) how, in a garden in Milan, he heard a child’s voice saying “take and read”, opened Paul’s letters, and came upon Romans 13:13–14; at the end of the sentence, he says, the darkness of doubt went away. The Catechism reads vv. 8–10 as Paul’s summary of the commandments of love (CCC 2196).

r.h: Because you did not believe
set: Zechariah is a priest serving in the Temple, chosen by lot to offer the incense, and Luke calls him and Elizabeth righteous (1:6). The angel has just told him that his prayer is heard and that Elizabeth will bear a son (1:13). These three verses are his reply and the angel’s answer. The scene is the first of the matching pair that opens Luke’s Gospel: here an old priest in the sanctuary, and soon a young woman in an unknown town (1:26–38).
str: v. 18: Zechariah asks for proof and gives his reason: he and his wife are old.
v. 19: the angel gives his name and his credentials.
v. 20: the sign: silence until the promise is fulfilled.
kw: A Hebrew name usually explained as “God is my strength”. In the Old Testament he appears only in Daniel, who sees him “at the time of the evening sacrifice” (Daniel 9:21). Luke’s readers would hear that the time of which Daniel spoke is drawing near, and at the same hour of worship.

This is the first time Luke uses the verb, which will run through his Gospel and Acts. The first person in the Gospel to “evangelise” is an angel, and the first person to receive the good news fails to believe it.
The same word as in Romans 13:11. God’s words have their own hour, and they are not cancelled because a good man cannot believe them.
vv: How will I know that this is so? For I am an old man, and my wife is getting on in years.

In the Greek Old Testament these are almost the words of Abraham: “how am I to know” (Genesis 15:8). Zechariah stands in a long line of people who found God’s promise too large. His difficulty is real, and his faults are those of a faithful man who has prayed for a long time and stopped expecting an answer.
I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news.
Zechariah has just entered the holy place to stand before God in the name of the people. The angel answers that he stands before God always. Whoever is sent from there does not need further proof.
But now, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time, you will become mute, unable to speak, until the day these things occur.

Zechariah asked for a sign and receives one, though not one he would have chosen. The people are waiting outside (1:21–22), and he cannot speak to them. Yet the promise stands. His unbelief delays his voice but does not delay God’s work.
ch: The Church sees in John the Lord’s immediate precursor (CCC 523). St Augustine, preaching on John’s birth, contrasts John the voice with Christ the Word (in substance); the priest’s silence comes before the birth of the one who will be “a voice”. Christian readers have always set this scene beside the Annunciation: both Zechariah and Mary ask a question, and the angel’s different answers show that God reads what lies under the words.

qa: Why was Zechariah punished for his question, when Mary also asked a question and was not?

The two questions sound alike but ask different things. Zechariah asks how he can be sure, and the angel himself names the problem: “you did not believe”. Mary does not ask for proof. She asks how it will happen, given that she is a virgin (1:34), and she ends by consenting (1:38). Zechariah’s silence is also more than a penalty. It is the sign he asked for, and it ends in praise when his son is named (1:64).
rite: The Twenty-five Day Fast traditionally begins today. These readings show what such a fast is for. It is not hunger for its own sake. It is getting up before dawn, taking off what belongs to the night, and learning a little of Zechariah’s silence so that we may have something to sing at Christmas.
study: Where in my life am I asleep, not by rejecting the faith but by living as if nothing were about to happen?
Is there a promise of God I have stopped expecting? What would it mean to wait for it in silence during this fast?

lead: Today’s readings are about faithfulness that holds from both sides. Paul reminds a quarrelling Church that “God is faithful” and will strengthen them to the end. In John, Jesus says that the Father has not left him alone, and that the proof of who he is will come at the very moment he seems most abandoned, when he is lifted up. The Son who is held by the Father calls us into his own fellowship.

r.h: God is faithful
set: Paul founded the Church at Corinth and wrote this letter from Ephesus (16:8), probably around AD 54–55. He has heard of factions, lawsuits, disorder at the Lord’s Supper and rivalry over spiritual gifts. Yet he opens, as he usually does, with a thanksgiving. It is striking that he thanks God for the same speech, knowledge and gifts that the Corinthians will soon be told they are misusing (chapters 12–14).
str: vv. 4–5: thanks for the grace given and the riches received.
vv. 6–7: the testimony was strengthened; no gift is lacking as they wait.
vv. 8–9: Christ will strengthen them to the end, because God is faithful.
kw: From charis, grace: a particular form that grace takes in someone. The word already tells the Corinthians that a gift is a gift, and not an achievement to be proud of.
The Corinthians are gifted but not finished. Paul places all their riches inside a time of waiting for the Lord to be revealed.

A sharing in something together. Paul will use the same word for the cup and the bread of the Holy Qurbana, a “sharing” in the blood and body of Christ (10:16). The vocation of a Christian is to share the life of the Son.
vv: so that you are not lacking in any spiritual gift as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The verb for waiting implies eagerness. A Church with every gift still lives by what it does not yet see.
He will also strengthen you to the end, so that you may be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The Old Testament’s “day of the Lord” now has a name: it is the day of Jesus Christ. Paul’s confidence does not rest on the Corinthians, as the rest of the letter will show.
God is faithful; by him you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

This is the sentence the whole passage leads to. In just these six verses the name of Christ is repeated again and again, before Paul says a word about their problems. He wants the Church to look at Christ first.
ch: The Catechism teaches that charisms are graces of the Holy Spirit which serve the building up of the Church, and that they are to be received with thanksgiving and tested by the pastors (CCC 799–801; Lumen Gentium 12). It also calls God’s faithfulness the ground of our trust (CCC 214), and describes the Church’s life as a communion with Jesus, into which he drew his disciples from the beginning (CCC 787).

r.h: He has not left me alone
set: Jesus is in the Temple at Jerusalem, in the debates that follow the Feast of Tabernacles (John 7–8), speaking near the treasury (8:20). His hearers have just asked, “Who are you?” (8:25). In this chapter “the Jews” stands for those in the debate who oppose him, above all the authorities. It does not mean the Jewish people as a whole: Jesus and his disciples are Jews too, and this reading ends with many believing in him. The Church rejects any blame laid on the Jewish people as such (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
str: vv. 26–27: the one who sent him is true; they do not see that he means the Father.
v. 28: when he is lifted up, they will know.
v. 29: the Father is with him, and he always does what pleases the Father.
v. 30: many believe.
kw: John’s favourite way of naming the Father. Everything Jesus says and does comes from being sent. The theme fits this season, when the Church listens to the announcement of his coming.
John’s word with two meanings: raised on the cross and raised in glory (3:14; 12:32–33). For John these are not two events but one. The Cross is already the throne.
Literally “I am”. In the Greek Old Testament these are God’s own words (compare Isaiah 43:10), behind which stands the name given to Moses in Exodus 3:14. The same words appear in 8:24 and 8:58.
vv: the one who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him.
Jesus speaks as one who has listened before speaking. All his teaching is the overflow of what he hears from the Father.
When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own

An unexpected answer to “Who are you?”. The answer will not be given in an argument but on the Cross. The “you” is addressed to those in the debate, but the Church teaches that all sinners are the authors of the Passion (CCC 598).
he has not left me alone, for I always do what is pleasing to him.

Jesus says this on the way to the Cross, where his disciples will leave him (compare 16:32). The bond between Son and Father is the one thing nothing can break, and it is the same fellowship Paul says we are called into.
As he was saying these things, many believed in him.
John does not end with rejection. Even in a hard argument the word bears fruit. The next verses will test how deep this belief goes.
ch: The Catechism cites Jesus’ words in v. 28 when it teaches that the Resurrection confirms his divinity: the promise “I am he” is shown to be true (CCC 653). The “I am” sayings of John are read by the Church as the Son’s claim to the divine name (CCC 590).

study: Paul thanks God for the Corinthians before he corrects them. Who in my family or parish do I need to give thanks for first?
Jesus says he is not alone even on the way to the Cross. Where do I feel left alone, and how might I find the Father with me there?

lead: On the day of St Francis Xavier, the readings trace the whole road of mission. In Deuteronomy, God and Israel bind themselves to one another, and Israel becomes a people set apart. In Isaiah, the God of that one people calls to “all the ends of the earth”. In Second Corinthians, Paul shows what it costs to carry such a message. In Mark, Jesus sends the Twelve out with almost nothing in their hands. The line runs from chosen to called to sent. A people is chosen not to keep God for itself but so that all may hear.

r.h: A people holy to the Lord
set: Deuteronomy presents itself as the last words of Moses to Israel on the plains of Moab, before they cross into the land. Chapters 12–26 give the laws by which they are to live. These four verses close that long section, and the blessings and curses of chapters 27–28 follow.
The passage is one of the clearest statements of the covenant in the Bible, and it has the form of a double declaration: what Israel says about the Lord, and what the Lord says about Israel.
str: v. 16: “This very day”: the command to keep the laws with all the heart and soul.
v. 17: Israel’s side: the Lord will be their God, and they will walk in his ways.
vv. 18–19: the Lord’s side: Israel will be his treasured people, raised high, and holy to him.
kw: A rare form of the verb “to say”, found in this form only in these two verses, and translators render it in different ways. The NRSV has “obtained agreement”; the Malayalam POC has “declared”. Either way, each party solemnly commits the other.

Sĕgullâ means a personal treasure, what a king keeps as his own (compare 1 Chronicles 29:3). The same word is used at Sinai (Exodus 19:5). The First Letter of Peter applies the idea to the Church: “God’s own people” (1 Peter 2:9).
Deuteronomy’s great word, repeated three times here. Moses is speaking to people who were not at Sinai, or were children then. For every generation that hears it, the covenant is today.
vv: This very day the Lord your God is commanding you to observe these statutes and ordinances; so observe them diligently with all your heart and with all your soul.
The same pair as the great commandment in 6:5. The law is not meant to be kept only on the outside.
Today you have obtained the Lord’s agreement: to be your God; and for you to walk in his ways
This is the formula of the covenant in its simplest form: “I your God, you my people”. God allows himself to be bound by a promise to people.
for you to be a people holy to the Lord your God, as he promised.

Holiness comes last, and it is God’s gift “as he promised”. Being set “high above all nations” is not about pride. In the wider Scripture Israel’s election serves the nations, as today’s second reading will show.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that God chose the race of Israel as a people and set up a covenant with it, as a preparation for the new covenant in Christ (Lumen Gentium 9; CCC 781). The Church honours this first covenant, which was never revoked (CCC 121, 839), and receives from it the language in which she describes herself.

r.h: Turn to me, all the ends of the earth
set: This passage belongs to Isaiah 40–55, addressed to the Jews in exile in Babylon. Chapter 45 opens by naming Cyrus, the Persian king God will use to release them. Then the horizon widens beyond Israel. God summons “you survivors of the nations”, the people left after the fall of empires, to a kind of courtroom, and invites them to look at the record.
str: v. 20: the summons, and the foolishness of carrying an idol that cannot save.
v. 21: the challenge: who foretold these things?
v. 22: the invitation: “Turn to me and be saved”.
v. 23: God’s oath: every knee shall bow.
v. 24: only in the Lord are righteousness and strength.
kw: a righteous God and a Savior (v. 21)
For Isaiah, God’s justice and God’s saving do not pull against each other. He is righteous precisely in keeping his promise to save.
A simple verb of movement: turn your face. The whole of conversion is in it. Nothing is asked of the nations first except that they look in the right direction.
all the ends of the earth
The farthest places anyone could imagine. Christian missionaries travelling to Asia, like St Francis Xavier, were living inside this phrase.
vv: those who carry about their wooden idols, and keep on praying to a god that cannot save.

The next chapter draws out the contrast: the gods of Babylon are loaded on tired animals, while the Lord says to Israel “I will carry” (46:1–4). An idol has to be carried, but the true God carries us.
Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other.
This is one of the widest invitations in the Old Testament. Because there is only one God, he must be the God of all, and his salvation must be meant for all.
To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.

St Paul quotes this line twice. In Romans 14:11 it speaks of God. In Philippians 2:10–11 he applies it to Jesus: “at the name of Jesus every knee should bend”. It would be hard to find a stronger way for a Jew of that time to speak of who Jesus is.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 22–24 together with Philippians 2 in its teaching on the one God: the God revealed to Israel is the only God, and at the name of Jesus every knee bends (CCC 201). The Church reads this oracle as the Old Testament root of her mission to all peoples (compare CCC 849–851).

r.h: As having nothing, and yet possessing everything
set: Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia (2:13; 7:5), probably in the mid 50s, after a painful period in his relations with the Corinthians. Some there compared him unfavourably with more impressive preachers. So he describes his apostolic ministry, not by its successes but by what it has cost. Ancient writers, among them the Stoic philosophers, sometimes listed a wise man’s hardships. Paul uses that form to show the power of God, not his own.
str: vv. 3–4a: no obstacle: the ministry commends itself.
vv. 4b–5: under “great endurance”, three groups of three hardships.
vv. 6–7: the gifts by which it is carried out, ending in the “weapons of righteousness”.
vv. 8–10: a chain of contrasts: how the apostles look and what they are.
kw: Diakonos is one who serves or carries out a commission on behalf of another. Paul’s authority is that of a servant who has been sent.
Literally “remaining under”: staying under a load without giving way. It heads the list because all the rest depends on it.
The rhythm of vv. 8–10. The first half is how the world sees the apostles; the second half is how things truly are. The pattern comes from the Cross and Resurrection.
vv: but as servants of God we have commended ourselves in every way: through great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities,
This list comes from experience: compare 11:23–28, and the riots and imprisonments of Acts.
truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;

A soldier held a weapon in the right hand and a shield in the left. Paul’s meaning is that he is armed for attack and defence, but only with righteousness. A note on translation: In v. 6 the Greek en pneumati hagiō can mean “holiness of spirit”, as in the NRSV, or “in the Holy Spirit”, as in the Malayalam POC. Both are possible, and the second is common among interpreters.
as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.

Paul is not saying that suffering is good in itself. He is saying that those who have nothing but Christ have lost nothing. The words echo his own teaching about Christ, who became poor so that we might become rich (8:9).
ch: St John Chrysostom, the great admirer of Paul, says in his sermons in praise of the Apostle that Paul counted suffering for Christ as joy, and feared only offending God (in substance). The Council teaches that the Church, led by the Spirit, must walk the road Christ walked, a way of poverty and obedience, of service and self-sacrifice (Ad Gentes 5; CCC 852).

r.h: He began to send them out two by two
set: This passage comes straight after the rejection of Jesus in his own town of Nazareth (6:1–6). Rejection does not stop the mission: it spreads it. Jesus chose the Twelve “to be with him, and to be sent out” (3:14), and now the second part begins. Mark then places the death of John the Baptist (6:14–29) between the sending and the return of the Twelve (6:30), so that the reader knows what the preacher of repentance can expect.

The instructions fit travellers in Galilee, where a stranger depended on hospitality. Staff and sandals are for walking; the bag is what a beggar might carry for gifts received; coins were commonly kept in the belt.
str: v. 7: the sending and the authority.
vv. 8–9: what not to take.
v. 10: stay in one house.
v. 11: when they are not received.
vv. 12–13: what they did.
kw: The root of “apostle”. An apostle is one who is sent, with the authority of the one who sends him.
A way of saying “in pairs”. Under the Law a charge stood only “on the evidence of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). The message is a testimony, and testimony needs more than one voice.
Oil was a common medicine. Here, joined to healing in Jesus’ name, it becomes a sign of God’s care. Among the Gospels, only Mark mentions this anointing by the Twelve.
vv: He called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits.
They do not go on their own power. The first thing given is authority, and it is Jesus’ own.
He ordered them to take nothing for their journey except a staff; no bread, no bag, no money in their belts;
The poverty of the messenger is part of the message. Those who bring the Kingdom must themselves live on trust, and must let others give to them.
If any place will not welcome you and they refuse to hear you, as you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.

A public sign that the messenger has done his part and that the responsibility now rests with the hearers (compare Acts 13:51). It leaves judgment to God: the disciples do not stay to argue or to take revenge.
They cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them.
The Twelve do what Jesus has been doing: proclaiming, casting out, healing. The Lord’s work now goes on through other hands.
ch: The Catechism sees in this verse the Church’s ministry to the sick (CCC 1506). The Council of Trent, quoted in the Catechism, says that the Anointing of the Sick is alluded to by Mark and promulgated by James (James 5:14; CCC 1511). St Gregory the Great, on the parallel in Luke 10, says that the Lord sends disciples in twos because there are two commandments of love, and love needs at least two people (in substance). The Council teaches that the Church is missionary by her very nature (Ad Gentes 2).

qa: Mark says to take a staff and sandals, but Matthew and Luke forbid a staff. Which is right?

Matthew 10:10 and Luke 9:3 do say “no staff”. The Evangelists hand on the Lord’s teaching faithfully, but they shape the details for their readers, and the point is the same in all three: travel light and depend on God. In Mark the staff and sandals may also recall the Exodus, when Israel ate the Passover “your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand” (Exodus 12:11). The Twelve are a people on the move.
If there is “no other” god, does the Church say that followers of other religions are lost?

No. The Church proclaims Christ as the one Saviour, and she also teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel but seek God sincerely and try to do his will can attain salvation (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). She rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2). Mission is not contempt for others. It is the wish to share the best thing we have been given.
Is the anointing in Mark 6:13 the same as the sacrament?

Not yet in its full form. The Twelve’s anointing is a sign and a preparation. The Church teaches that Christ instituted the sacrament, that Mark alludes to it, and that James recommends it to the faithful and promulgates it (CCC 1511).
rite: St Francis Xavier (1506–1552), one of the first companions of St Ignatius, landed at Goa in 1542 and laboured among the fisherfolk of the southern Indian coast, and then in Malacca and Japan. In a letter he wrote that he often thought of going round the universities of Europe and crying out to the learned that souls were being lost for lack of anyone to teach them (in substance). He died on the island of Sancian, within sight of China, and his body is venerated in Goa. For Syro-Malabar Christians, who trace their faith to St Thomas long before him, his day is a reminder that an apostolic Church must be a sending Church. Our own priests and religious now serve in the mission fields of North India and beyond, carrying little and depending on others, as Mark 6 describes.
study: Deuteronomy calls Israel a “treasured” people, chosen for a purpose. What has God entrusted to me that was never meant for me alone?
Isaiah says that an idol must be carried. What am I carrying that cannot save me?
Paul lists his hardships as proof of his ministry. How do I look at the hardships in my own service of the Church?
Jesus sends the Twelve with very little. What would I find hardest to leave behind if I were sent?

lead: Both readings are about learning to see. Paul tells the Colossians that their true life is hidden with Christ, so they must look up and strip off what no longer fits. In Matthew, Jesus says that some look and do not perceive, and he calls his disciples blessed because their eyes see what the prophets longed to see. On a First Friday in this season of waiting, both ask the same thing: what are the eyes of my heart set on?

r.h: Your life is hidden with Christ in God
set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley in what is now western Turkey. The letter comes from prison (4:3, 18) and is traditionally by Paul; some scholars think a later disciple wrote it. A “philosophy” with its rules about food and festivals and its interest in angels was troubling the community (2:8, 16–18). Paul’s reply is that in baptism they have already died and risen with Christ (2:12). Chapter 3 draws the consequences.
str: vv. 1–4: look up: you have been raised, and your life is hidden until Christ appears.
vv. 5–7: put to death what belongs to the old life.
vv. 8–10: strip off the old self and put on the new.
kw: Paul’s “with” verbs are at the centre of this letter. The Resurrection is not only ahead of us. Through baptism it has already begun in us.
A perfect tense: it has been hidden and it stays hidden. No one can see the believer’s true life, not even the believer always. It is safely kept in God until it is revealed.

Literally “old man” and “new man”. The picture is of changing clothes, which may recall the clothing of the newly baptised. The new self is “renewed … according to the image of its creator”, an echo of Genesis 1:27.
vv: So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
This is not a call to ignore the world. The rest of the chapter is about speech, family and work. “Above” is where Christ reigns, and it is from there that a Christian measures everything.
for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
The sentence explains the whole of Christian hope. A believer may look like anyone else, and may look like a failure. What is true of him is out of sight.
and greed (which is idolatry).

Greed is called idolatry because what we want most becomes what we serve. A note on the text: in v. 6 some ancient manuscripts have “on those who are disobedient”, as in the NRSV, while others stop at “the wrath of God is coming”, as in the Malayalam POC. The sense is the same.
and have clothed yourselves with the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator.
“Is being renewed”: the verb is in the present. The change of clothes happened once in baptism, but the renewing goes on all through life.
ch: The Catechism teaches from this passage that Christian life is already a sharing in the Resurrection: we have in a certain way already risen with Christ, and our life remains “hidden with Christ in God” (CCC 1002–1003). The Tenth Commandment’s warning against greed takes up the same warning (CCC 2534–2536).

r.h: Blessed are your eyes
set: Chapter 13 is the third of the five great discourses in Matthew, the parables of the Kingdom. After the parable of the sower, the disciples ask why he speaks in parables (13:10). His reply is today’s Gospel. Matthew quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, the words given to the prophet at his call, in the Greek form of the Old Testament.
str: v. 12: a hard proverb: those who have receive more.
v. 13: why he speaks in parables.
vv. 14–15: Isaiah’s prophecy is fulfilled.
vv. 16–17: the blessing on those who see.
kw: In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew māšāl, which covers proverbs, riddles and comparisons. A parable invites the hearer in: to understand it you must come closer.
Literally “has grown fat, thick”. The heart has been so wrapped around that nothing gets through. In the Bible the heart is the place of understanding and decision, not just of feeling.
The word of the Beatitudes (5:3–11). It means more than “happy”: it means favoured by God, in the position everyone would wish to be in.
vv: For to those who have, more will be given, and they will have an abundance
The proverb is about openness, not wealth. Whoever receives the word finds that it grows. Whoever refuses it finds that even what he once had slips away.
The reason I speak to them in parables is that ‘seeing they do not perceive, and hearing they do not listen, nor do they understand.’

Compare Mark 4:12, which says “in order that”. Matthew’s form says “because”: the parables are a response to a closed heart. Both Evangelists are using Isaiah’s language of God’s purpose working through human refusal.
But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear.

The disciples are not cleverer than others. Their eyes are blessed because of what stands in front of them. The people Jesus calls blessed here are Jews, as he is, and the words “this people” in Isaiah are a prophet’s sorrowful warning to his own, not a sentence on a nation (CCC 597–598).
many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, but did not see it
This is one of the verses that best fits this season. All the waiting of the Old Testament reaches its goal in the one who is speaking.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the parables are a kind of mirror: one must enter the Kingdom, that is, become a disciple of Christ, in order to know its secrets, and for those who remain outside, everything remains enigmatic (CCC 546). In the liturgy of the season before Christmas, which for us is the season of Annunciation, it adds, the Church makes present the ancient expectancy of the Messiah, sharing the long preparation for his first coming (CCC 524).

qa: Does Jesus speak in parables so that people will not be healed?

No. Isaiah’s words are the language of a prophet who knows his message will be refused, and they end with what God wants: “and I would heal them.” Matthew’s “because” places the difficulty in the closed heart. A parable is also a mercy: it does not force anyone, and it stays in the memory, waiting for the day the hearer is ready.
rite: Today is a First Friday, which many Syro-Malabar families keep in honour of the Heart of Jesus, a devotion that spread from the revelations to St Margaret Mary Alacoque in the seventeenth century. Matthew’s words about a heart grown dull give it a sharp edge. The Catechism says that Jesus knew and loved each of us with a human heart (CCC 478). To come before that Heart is to ask for one’s own to be softened.
study: Paul says that greed is a kind of idolatry. What do I most want, and does it serve God or take his place?
The prophets longed to see what the disciples saw. What do I take for granted in the Holy Qurbana that they would have longed for?

lead: Both readings ask what a beginning is worth if it is not carried through. Paul asks the Galatians, “Having started with the Spirit, are you now ending with the flesh?” In Luke, three people meet Jesus on the road, and each is told what following him will really take. Abraham believed, and the plowman must not look back. Faith is both receiving what God gives and refusing to turn away from it.

r.h: Those who believe are blessed with Abraham
set: Paul had preached in Galatia, in central Asia Minor, and founded Churches of Gentile converts. After he left, other teachers told them that to belong fully to God’s people they must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. For Paul the question is not about Jewish customs as such, but whether Christ is enough. In Galatians “works of the law” refers above all to observances like circumcision and food laws, taken as the condition for being counted among God’s people. Paul’s tone here is the sharpest in his letters.
str: vv. 1–5: the appeal to their experience: how did you receive the Spirit?
vv. 6–7: Abraham believed, and believers are his children.
vv. 8–9: the Gentiles were in the promise from the beginning.
kw: A word for casting the evil eye, used here with irony. Paul can only explain their change of mind as a spell, since they had seen the Crucified so clearly.
The word for a public notice put up for all to read. Paul’s preaching was like a placard of the Cross set before their eyes.
An accounting term: entered in the ledger. Paul takes it from Genesis 15:6. Abraham is credited with righteousness because he trusted God’s word, before the Law had been given.
vv: You foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?
“Foolish” here means failing to think. Paul is not insulting their intelligence but pleading with them to look at what they know.
Are you so foolish? Having started with the Spirit, are you now ending with the flesh?
“Flesh” here carries a play on words, because circumcision is literally in the flesh. Beyond that, it means relying on what human beings can do.
Just as Abraham “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness,”
Paul goes to the root of Israel’s story. Last Monday’s reading from this same chapter (3:9–14) continues the argument: the blessing of Abraham comes to all peoples in Christ.
For this reason, those who believe are blessed with Abraham who believed.
The Gentiles do not replace Abraham’s family. They are brought into it, as God told him: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3).
ch: The Catechism presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith (CCC 144–146). It teaches that justification is God’s gift, received through faith, and that it comes before any merit of ours (CCC 1987, 1991, 1996, 2010). Paul himself says that what counts is “faith working through love” (5:6). In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, which states their common understanding of this teaching.

r.h: Looking back from the plow
set: Luke 9:51 is a turning point: “he set his face to go to Jerusalem”. From here until chapter 19 Jesus is on the road, and much of his teaching on discipleship takes place along it. Today’s three short meetings stand at the start of that journey. Matthew has the first two (8:19–22). The third is found only in Luke, and it recalls the call of Elisha, who was plowing when Elijah threw his cloak over him and who asked, “Let me kiss my father and my mother” (1 Kings 19:19–21).
str: vv. 57–58: an eager volunteer, and the warning: no place to rest.
vv. 59–60: one who is called, and asks to bury his father.
vv. 61–62: one who wants to say farewell, and the plow.
kw: The verb for the disciple’s life, used in all three meetings. It means going behind someone on a road, and here that road leads to Jerusalem.
Jesus’ own way of speaking of himself. The title recalls the glorious figure of Daniel 7, and here it is used of a homeless traveller. Glory comes through the road, not around it.
Suited or well placed, like a tool or soil that is right for its purpose. It does not mean morally worthy. It means ready for the work the Kingdom needs.
vv: Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.
This is not a refusal but an honest warning. The village that has just turned Jesus away (9:53) shows what the words mean.
Let the dead bury their own dead; but as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.

Burying a father was among the most sacred duties in Jewish life (compare Tobit 4:3–4). That is why the saying shocks, and it is meant to shock. Many interpreters read “the dead” as those who have not yet found the life of the Kingdom. The word stresses urgency: nothing, even the holiest family duty, may be placed above the call.
No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.
Anyone who has plowed with oxen knows this: if you look back, the furrow goes crooked. Elijah allowed Elisha to go home, but here one greater than Elijah is passing by, and the moment does not wait.
ch: The Catechism teaches that family ties are important but not absolute: the first vocation of a Christian is to follow Jesus (CCC 2232), and the bond with Christ takes precedence over all other bonds, familial or social (CCC 1618). Jesus’ words are not a rejection of the commandment to honour parents, which he defends elsewhere (Mark 7:9–13). They are a measure of who is calling.

qa: Is Paul against good works? Does Saint James contradict him?

No. In Galatians Paul is speaking of “works of the law” as a condition for belonging to God’s people, and he insists that the Spirit comes as a gift. He goes on at once to say what that faith does: it works through love (5:6). James insists that faith without works is dead (James 2:26). Together they say what the Church teaches: grace comes first, and it bears fruit. Paul also holds that “the law is holy” (Romans 7:12); he is not speaking against Israel’s Law as such.
study: Paul asks the Galatians to remember how they first received the Spirit. When did I first know that faith was a gift, and what has happened to that memory?
What is the “first let me” that I keep placing between myself and what the Lord is asking of me?

lead: On the second Sunday of Suvara the Church hears the announcement itself. The readings prepare for it by asking who is able to receive a word from God. In Numbers, an angel stands in the road, and a famous seer cannot see him though his donkey can. In Isaiah, God promises to pour out his Spirit on a guilty and thirsty people. In Colossians, Paul asks for a door for the word. In Luke, the angel comes to a young woman in Nazareth, she listens, and the Word becomes flesh within her. The key words are seeing, pouring out and consenting.

r.h: The Lord opened the eyes of Balaam
set: Israel has reached the plains of Moab, near the end of the desert journey (22:1). Balak, king of Moab, is afraid of them, and sends for Balaam son of Beor, a famous seer from far away, to curse them (22:2–6). Balaam is not an Israelite. An inscription found in 1967 at Deir Alla in Jordan speaks of a seer called Balaam son of Beor, so his name was known outside the Bible.

God has first told Balaam not to go (22:12). In today’s reading he allows it (v. 20), then is angry that he goes (v. 22). Scholars note the tension: the story may join older traditions, and it also suggests that God sees the heart of a man who keeps asking until he hears the answer he wants. Later Scripture remembers him as one “who loved the wages of doing wrong” (2 Peter 2:15; compare Jude 11).
str: vv. 20–21: God’s permission, with one condition.
vv. 22–27: the angel blocks the road three times, in places that grow narrower: the field, the lane between walls, the place with no room to turn.
vv. 28–30: the Lord opens the donkey’s mouth.
vv. 31–35: the Lord opens Balaam’s eyes, and the condition is repeated.
kw: Śāṭān here is an ordinary noun: someone who blocks the way or opposes. It is used of the angel of the Lord himself. An opposition can be a mercy, because this one saves Balaam’s life.
God’s messenger, whose words are God’s own (compare v. 35 with v. 20). The same kind of visit, with a word that must be received, will come to Mary, though not with a sword.

The verb used for the eyes in v. 31. Balaam is a professional seer. Later he will call himself “the man whose eye is clear” (24:3). Yet sight is God’s gift, as the opening of the donkey’s mouth has already shown.
vv: If the men have come to summon you, get up and go with them; but do only what I tell you to do.
This is the condition of the whole story. Balaam may go, but the word will not be his to sell.
The donkey saw the angel of the Lord standing in the road, with a drawn sword in his hand
The story is full of humour. The man paid to see the unseen is the only one who cannot see. Three times the donkey saves him, and three times he strikes it.
Then the Lord opened the mouth of the donkey, and it said to Balaam, “What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?”
The animal’s question is more reasonable than its master’s reply. God can speak by the lowliest means when those who should hear have stopped listening.
Then the Lord opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the Lord standing in the road
Balaam’s first words now are “I have sinned” (v. 34). He has seen what he had missed, and he must carry only God’s word: in chapters 23–24 he blesses the people he was paid to curse.
ch: 2 Peter 2:15–16 uses this story as a warning against those who preach for gain. Balaam’s later oracle, “a star shall come out of Jacob” (24:17), was read by Jews and Christians alike as pointing to the Messiah, and Origen connects it with the star of the Magi (in substance). The Church sees here the lesson Jesus gives thanks for: God reveals himself to the lowly (Luke 10:21). On this Sunday the contrast is clear: the seer who could not see the angel, and the unknown girl who receives him.

r.h: I will pour my spirit upon your descendants
set: These verses speak to the exiles in Babylon (Isaiah 40–55). They knew why Jerusalem had fallen, and they wondered if there could be any future for a people so guilty. The passage has two movements. First comes a courtroom scene in which God proves the case against Israel and then forgives the debt. Then comes a promise, marked by “But now hear” (44:1), of water, Spirit and new growth.
str: 43:25: God blots out sin “for my own sake”.
43:26–28: the trial: from the first ancestor on, Israel has sinned, and the exile has followed.
44:1–2: “Do not fear”: chosen and formed from the womb.
44:3–4: water on thirsty land, and the Spirit on the children.
44:5: people will gladly claim the name of the Lord.
kw: The verb for wiping writing from a scroll or wiping a dish clean. The record is not filed away but erased.
A poetic name for Israel, probably from a root meaning “upright” (Deuteronomy 32:15; 33:5, 26). It is a gentle name to use for a guilty people: God calls them what he intends them to be.
The verb is used for pouring out water or oil. The same promise, in a different wording, is in Joel 2:28 and is quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:17).
vv: I, I am He who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.

“For my own sake”: forgiveness is grounded in who God is, not in what Israel can offer. A note on translation: In v. 28 the Hebrew has “I profaned the princes of the sanctuary”, which the NRSV follows, while the ancient Greek has the princes profaning the holy things, close to the Malayalam POC. Both describe the same catastrophe.
For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my spirit upon your descendants, and my blessing on your offspring.
In dry country, water means life. Water and the Spirit stand side by side in this verse, as they will in John 3:5 and in the font of baptism.
yet another will write on the hand, “The Lord’s,”

A mark on the hand showed whose a person was. The exile’s shame becomes something people will be glad to claim. These may be foreigners joining Israel or Israelites returning to their name; either way, belonging is now a joy.
ch: The Catechism teaches that only God forgives sins (CCC 1441) and that the prophets’ promises of the Spirit look forward to the Messiah and to the whole messianic people (CCC 715, 1287). It explains the seal of Confirmation with the same picture as 44:5: a seal is a sign of ownership, as soldiers were marked with their leader’s seal (CCC 1295). On a Sunday of Suvara, the promise of Spirit on dry ground prepares for the Spirit who comes upon Mary (Luke 1:35).

r.h: A door for the word
set: These are the last instructions of the letter, before the greetings (4:7–18). After teaching the household about daily life (3:18–4:1), Paul turns to the two things that link the Christian to God and to those outside: prayer and speech. He writes in chains: “for which I am in prison”. The letter is sent in his name (4:18); on the question of authorship, Catholic scholars differ.
str: v. 2: keep praying, alert and thankful.
vv. 3–4: pray for us, that God may open a door.
v. 5: walk wisely toward outsiders.
v. 6: let your speech be gracious.
kw: The word means to hold on firmly, to stay at something. Acts uses the same verb of the first community, devoted to prayer (Acts 1:14; 2:42).
A prisoner asks for a door, but not for his own release. The door he wants is for the message.
making the most of the time
Literally “buying up the time”, as a trader buys up what is scarce. The word for time is again kairos, the moment of opportunity.
vv: Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping alert in it with thanksgiving.
Alert prayer recalls the Lord’s word in the garden: “Keep awake and pray” (Mark 14:38). Thanksgiving keeps prayer from becoming only a list of needs.
At the same time pray for us as well that God will open to us a door for the word, that we may declare the mystery of Christ, for which I am in prison,
“The mystery of Christ” is God’s plan, once hidden and now revealed: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27). Today’s Gospel shows that mystery beginning in the womb of Mary.
Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer everyone.

“Gracious” is literally “in grace”. Salt brings out flavour and preserves, and it recalls Jesus’ word in Mark 9:50. The Malayalam POC gives the sense without the picture of salt. The Christian’s speech should have some taste to it, and should be kind without being empty.
ch: The Catechism’s section on persevering prayer, “Pray constantly”, is built on texts like this one (CCC 2742–2745). The Second Vatican Council takes up Paul’s phrase in its decree on mission: wherever God opens a door for the word, the mystery of Christ is to be proclaimed to all (Ad Gentes 13). 1 Peter 3:15 gives the same advice: always be ready to answer, “with gentleness and reverence” (3:16).

r.h: Here am I, the servant of the Lord
set: Last Sunday’s Gospel told of Gabriel’s visit to Zechariah in the Temple. Luke now sets the second scene against it. Then, an old priest in Jerusalem; now, a young woman in Nazareth, a town the Old Testament never mentions. Then, a couple past child-bearing; now, a virgin. Then, doubt and silence; now, a question and consent.

Mary is “engaged”. A Jewish betrothal was a binding legal bond, and the woman normally stayed in her family’s home for a time before moving to her husband’s. Joseph is “of the house of David”, and this is how Jesus will belong legally to David’s line.
str: vv. 26–27: place, people, and the sixth month.
vv. 28–29: the greeting, and Mary’s pondering.
vv. 30–33: the promise: Jesus, Son of the Most High, heir of David.
vv. 34–35: Mary’s question and the answer: the Holy Spirit.
vv. 36–37: the sign: Elizabeth; nothing is impossible with God.
v. 38: Mary’s consent.
kw: A perfect passive participle of the verb from charis, grace: “you who have been graced, and remain so”. The verb is rare (elsewhere in the New Testament only at Ephesians 1:6). The angel uses it in place of her name, as if it were her name. The Latin has gratia plena and the Malayalam POC “full of God’s grace”.

This verb is used in the Greek of Exodus 40:35, where the cloud settles on the tent of meeting and God’s glory fills it. Luke uses it again at the Transfiguration (9:34). Mary becomes the new dwelling of God.
The Greek form is a wish, not mere resignation. Mary does not simply accept what will happen. She wants it. The Latin gives the word that has passed into every language: fiat.
vv: And he came to her and said, “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you.”

Chaire, “greetings”, was an ordinary greeting, but it means “rejoice”. Many scholars hear behind it the prophets’ call to daughter Zion (Zephaniah 3:14). “The Lord is with you” are words said in the Old Testament to those given a task beyond their strength.
He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give to him the throne of his ancestor David.
Here the promise to David in 2 Samuel 7:12–16 is taken up. At the same time v. 35 goes beyond it: he is “Son of God”, in a way no king of Israel ever was.
Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, since I am a virgin?”

The Greek says “since I do not know a man”, as the Malayalam POC does. St Augustine and others took her question to mean that she had resolved to remain a virgin (in substance). Luke’s text does not say so directly, but what it clearly teaches is that the child’s conception is the work of the Spirit, without a human father (CCC 496–497).
The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be holy; he will be called Son of God.
The promised Spirit of Isaiah 44:3 comes down here. Father, Son and Spirit are all named in this one scene.
For nothing will be impossible with God.
An echo of what was said about Sarah: “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” (Genesis 18:14). Last Sunday’s Genesis story was the same promise.
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
“Servant” here means a slave woman, a title of humility and also of honour, like the “servants of the Lord” of Israel’s history. God does not take flesh without being welcomed.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Father willed the Incarnation to be preceded by the consent of the predestined mother (Lumen Gentium 56; CCC 488, 494). St Irenaeus, quoted there, says that the knot of Eve’s disobedience was untied by Mary’s obedience. St Ephrem the Syrian sings that death entered through Eve’s ear, and that through Mary’s ear the Word entered (in substance). St Bernard, in his fourth homily in praise of the Virgin Mother, pictures all creation waiting for her answer: “Answer quickly, O Virgin”. The Catechism sees in the angel’s greeting the Church’s growing understanding that Mary was “full of grace” from the first moment of her life (CCC 490–491).

qa: Did the donkey really speak?

The Church has given no ruling on this detail. The Church asks us first to consider what kind of writing we are reading (Dei Verbum 12). 2 Peter 2:16 mentions the event, and many readers take it as told. Others read the story as a vivid popular narrative with a touch of humour. Either way the teaching is the same: the prophet who thinks that he sees everything is corrected by the humblest of creatures, and he can say only what God gives him to say.
Is “full of grace” a good translation, and does this verse teach the Immaculate Conception?

“Favored one” and “full of grace” both translate one Greek word, which says that Mary has been and remains filled with God’s favour. The verse alone does not state the doctrine. The Church, reflecting on it over the centuries, came to understand that to be so graced for this mission, Mary was redeemed from the moment of her conception (CCC 490–492), and Pope Pius IX defined this in 1854. The feast comes this Tuesday, 8 December.
Could Mary have said no?

Yes. The Church insists that her consent was real: she was not used as an instrument but cooperated by faith and obedience (Lumen Gentium 56; CCC 494). The fullness of grace did not lessen her humanity. It set her fully able to answer God, as the angel’s courteous greeting and her careful question show.
rite: In the East Syriac year, Suvara means the announcement, and its Sundays are built around God’s messages to Zechariah, Mary and Joseph. Today’s Gospel is the heart of the season, and the Twenty-five Day Fast continues around it. The East Syriac tradition loves the Fathers’ poetry on this mystery. St Ephrem’s picture of the ear is a good one for us, who come to the Holy Qurbana first to listen: Mary heard, consented and bore the Word, and we hear the same Word proclaimed, and receive him at the altar. The Bema, the place of the word in the East Syriac tradition, reminds us that a Church must first be a listening Church.
study: Balaam was a professional seer who could not see what his donkey saw. What might God be trying to show me through someone or something I look down on?
Isaiah promises the Spirit to a people who feel that they have no future. Where is the “dry ground” in my life or my family?
Paul, in prison, asks not for release but for a door for the word. What would I ask for if I were in his place?
Mary’s question and her consent stand side by side. What am I asking God at this time, and what would my “let it be” sound like?

lead: On the day of St Ambrose, the readings speak of growing up and of doing greater things. Ephesians wants the Church to stop being tossed about like children by “every wind of doctrine” and to grow up into Christ. In John, Jesus promises that those who believe will do even greater works than his, and that he will do what they ask in his name. Ambrose, a bishop who stood firm in a storm of false teaching and who helped to bring Augustine to Christ, shows what both mean.

r.h: Grow up into him who is the head
set: The letter comes from prison (4:1) and is traditionally by Paul; some scholars think a later disciple wrote it. Its first half (chapters 1–3) sings of God’s plan to unite all things in Christ. Its second half (chapters 4–6) describes the life that follows. Just before today’s verses, the author lists the gifts Christ has given to the Church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers (4:11), who are given to equip the saints “until all of us come to the unity of the faith”.
str: v. 13: the goal: unity, knowledge, maturity.
v. 14: the opposite: children tossed by every wind.
v. 15: speaking the truth in love, we grow into the head.
v. 16: the whole body grows, as each part does its work.
kw: The word is singular. The goal is not many mature individuals but one whole person, the Church grown into Christ.
The word for playing with dice. False teachers treat the truth like a dice game, with a skilful throw of the hand.
Literally “truthing”, doing and living the truth, not only speaking it. In the Greek the words “truth” and “love” are side by side, and the Christian needs both at once.
vv: until all of us come to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to maturity, to the measure of the full stature of Christ.
“All of us”: maturity is a goal for the whole Church. No one reaches it alone, and it is measured by Christ himself, not by comparison with others.
We must no longer be children, tossed to and fro and blown about by every wind of doctrine
This is a sailor’s picture: a small boat with no steering. In the fourth century, Ambrose faced such a wind in Arianism, which denied the full divinity of the Son and had powerful friends at court.
But speaking the truth in love, we must grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ,
Truth without love wounds, and love without truth deceives. The growth is “into him”: the Church is not growing toward some idea, but toward a person.
from whom the whole body, joined and knit together by every ligament with which it is equipped, as each part is working properly, promotes the body’s growth in building itself up in love.
The sentence is long and tangled, as a body is. Every part matters, down to the least. The body’s growth comes from the head and is built up by what each member gives.
ch: The Catechism draws on this passage to teach that Christ, the head, provides in his Body, the Church, the gifts and helps by which we support one another on the way of salvation (CCC 794). The Council speaks of the same growth of the whole body toward its head (Lumen Gentium 7).

r.h: Greater works than these
set: This is the Last Supper in John’s Gospel. Jesus has said that he is going away, and the disciples are troubled. Philip has just said, “Lord, show us the Father”, and Jesus has replied, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (14:8–9). Today’s verses continue that reply and turn it into a promise for the time after he has gone.
str: v. 11: believe in the unity of Son and Father, or at least believe because of the works.
v. 12: the promise: greater works, because he is going to the Father.
vv. 13–14: the promise about prayer in his name.
kw: John’s word for what Jesus does, including his signs. They are the Father’s works in him (14:10), and they show who he is.
Greater not in power but in reach. Jesus ministered in one small land for a few years; after his return to the Father, his Church will carry the word to the nations.
In the Bible a person’s name stands for the person. To ask “in his name” is not a formula added at the end of prayer. It means asking as one united with him, wanting what he wants.
vv: Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me; but if you do not, then believe me because of the works themselves.
Jesus accepts a beginning of faith. Those who cannot yet trust his word may at least look at what he has done.
Very truly, I tell you, the one who believes in me will also do the works that I do and, in fact, will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.
The reason given is striking: “because I am going”. His departure is not the end of his work but its widening, through the Spirit he will send (14:16).
I will do whatever you ask in my name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
The goal of the promise is the Father’s glory. This sets the limit of the prayer, and its joy.
If in my name you ask me for anything, I will do it.

A note on the text: Many ancient manuscripts have “ask me”, as the NRSV and the Malayalam POC do, and some leave out “me”. With “me”, Jesus himself receives the prayer. The Church has prayed to him from the beginning.
ch: St Augustine, commenting on this Gospel, says that the justification of the wicked is a greater work than the creation of heaven and earth; the Catechism quotes him (CCC 1994). The Catechism also teaches that prayer in Jesus’ name is the heart of the new prayer he gives (CCC 2614–2615), and that “There is no other way of Christian prayer than Christ” (CCC 2664).

qa: Jesus says that he will do “whatever” we ask. Why are some prayers not answered?

The promise is for prayer “in my name”, that is, in union with him, and “so that the Father may be glorified”. It is not a way of getting what we want. The Catechism speaks of this difficulty directly: we should ask whether our prayer is that of a child who trusts, and we should remember that God’s gift is greater than what we ask (CCC 2735–2737). Jesus’ own prayer in Gethsemane is the model.
rite: St Ambrose (c. 340–397) was a Roman governor at Milan and still a catechumen when the people acclaimed him bishop in 374. His feast falls on the anniversary of his ordination. He stood firm against Arianism, taught the people through sermons and hymns, and did not hesitate to make the Emperor Theodosius do penance after the massacre at Thessalonica. St Augustine tells in his Confessions how Ambrose’s preaching opened the Old Testament to him; Ambrose baptised him at Easter in 387. In that one baptism the “greater works” of John 14 can be seen, and every parish priest who preaches and baptises shares that work.
study: Ephesians says that we must speak the truth “in love”. In my family or parish, do I find it harder to speak truth or to speak love?
What “greater work” might the Lord want to do through me, my family or my parish in this season?

lead: Today, in the second week of the season of Annunciation, the Church honours the grace God gave to Mary at the first instant of her existence: she was preserved from every stain of original sin, by the merits of the Son she would one day bear. No reading states this doctrine in so many words. Together they prepare the ground for it. In Sirach, Wisdom looks for a resting place and God chooses her tent. In Isaiah, the Lord himself promises a sign: a woman and a son called Immanuel. In Hebrews, the Son who is the reflection of God's glory takes hold of our human race. In Luke, Mary herself sings and gives all the credit to “God my Savior”. The line runs from a tent, to a mother, to the Son, to her song, and its key words are dwelling, sign and mercy.

r.h: Wisdom looks for a resting place
set: Ben Sira, the son of Sirach, taught in Jerusalem about 180 BC. His grandson translated the book into Greek in Egypt some decades later, and tells us so in his prologue. Parts of the Hebrew have been recovered, but this chapter is known to us mainly through the Greek. Chapter 24 stands near the centre of the book. Wisdom, spoken of as a woman, praises herself before the heavenly court.

The speech has a clear aim. Greek culture was attractive to Jews of that time, and Ben Sira answers that the highest wisdom is not far away. A few verses after our reading he identifies her with the Law given through Moses (24:23). The one who ruled the whole world was given her home in Israel.
str: vv. 1–2: introduction: Wisdom speaks among her people and before the hosts of the Most High.
vv. 3–7: her origin and her search: from God's mouth, over all the earth, looking for a place to rest.
vv. 8–12: God's command: she pitches her tent in Jacob and is established in Zion.
vv. 13–14: she grows like the great trees of the land, from Lebanon and Hermon to En-gedi and Jericho.
kw: Here wisdom is more than cleverness. She is the plan and the skill by which God made and guides the world, spoken of as a person. The New Testament will call Christ “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).
The word for Israel's tent of meeting in the Greek Old Testament. John uses the related verb when he says the Word “lived among us”, literally pitched his tent (John 1:14).
She who rules every nation is still looking for somewhere to settle (v. 7). God's plan is told as a search for a home.
vv: Among all these I sought a resting place; in whose territory should I abide?
The great lady of the universe asks a homeless person's question. It prepares the surprise of the next verse.
Then the Creator of all things gave me a command, and my Creator chose the place for my tent.
Wisdom does not choose her own home; God chooses it for her. On this feast the Church hears a likeness: before the Word came, God prepared the place where he would dwell.
I took root in an honored people, in the portion of the Lord, his heritage.
The image moves from a tent to a tree. What came down from above now grows in the soil of one people. The Son of God too will have his roots in Israel, through a daughter of Israel.
ch: The first and literal sense of the chapter concerns Wisdom and the Law. Christians came to see its fullness in Christ, the Word who pitched his tent among us. The Church also applies such passages to Mary, not because Mary is divine Wisdom, but because she is the place where Wisdom came to live. The Catechism says that the Church's Tradition has often read the most beautiful texts on wisdom in relation to Mary, who is acclaimed in the liturgy as the “Seat of Wisdom” (CCC 721).

r.h: The Lord himself will give you a sign
set: The year is about 734 BC. Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel have marched against Jerusalem to force King Ahaz of Judah into their alliance against Assyria (7:1–6; 2 Kings 16:5–9). Their threat is to remove Ahaz and put another man on David's throne. Isaiah has already told the king to stand firm: “If you do not stand firm in faith, you shall not stand at all” (7:9). Ahaz has privately decided to buy help from Assyria instead.
str: vv. 10–11: God offers Ahaz any sign he wants, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven.
v. 12: the king refuses, with pious words.
v. 13: Isaiah's rebuke to “the house of David”.
v. 14: the sign: a woman, a son, a name.
vv. 15–16: before the child can tell good from evil, the two enemy kingdoms will be deserted.
kw: A visible token that God is at work. Ahaz refuses the sign, and God gives it anyway, to the whole house of David.

A young woman of marriageable age. The word does not itself specify virginity. The Greek Old Testament translated it parthenos, “virgin”, and Matthew 1:23 quotes that Greek. The Malayalam POC here has “young woman”.
A name and a promise. God has not abandoned David's house, even when its king will not trust him.
vv: But Ahaz said, I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.
It sounds devout (compare Deuteronomy 6:16), but it hides a decision already made. God himself had told him to ask.
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Look, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall name him Immanuel.
Scholars discuss who the woman was in Ahaz's own day; many think of a royal wife, whose son would continue David's line. The prophecy says more than that first horizon could hold.
For before the child knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land before whose two kings you are in dread will be deserted.
The sign has a short-term point: the threat will soon pass. The curds and honey of v. 15 are probably the food of a land laid waste (see 7:21–22).
ch: Matthew reads this verse as fulfilled when Mary conceives by the Holy Spirit and bears Jesus, God with us (Matthew 1:22–23). The Catechism sees here the fulfilment of the divine promise given through Isaiah (CCC 497). The sign refused by a king of David's line is received by a humble woman of David's people. The verse speaks directly of the Son's coming, not of Mary's own beginning, but the feast reads the two together: the mother of Immanuel was prepared by God for this mission (CCC 490).

r.h: He spoke by a Son who became our brother
set: Hebrews is a sermon to tired Christians (“a word of exhortation”, 13:22). Its author is not named. It opens with one long, carefully built Greek sentence (1:1–4), among the most polished in the New Testament. Today's reading joins that opening to the close of chapter 2, so that the Son of glory and the brother who suffers stand side by side.
str: 1:1–2a: two times of speaking: long ago by the prophets, now by a Son.
1:2b–3: who the Son is: heir, agent of creation, reflection of glory; and what he did: purification, and his seat at God's right hand.
2:16–18: why he became one of us: to be a merciful and faithful high priest.
kw: Light shining out from its source. The Son is not a second light apart from the Father. The Council of Nicaea says “Light from Light”.
The mark a seal leaves in wax or a die on a coin. To see the Son is to see what the Father is.

The verb in 2:16 means to take hold of. The NRSV gives “come to help”; the POC gives “took to himself”. St John Chrysostom took it to mean that the Son took on our nature, not that of angels (in substance). Both readings fit what follows.
vv: but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son,
In Greek there is no “the” here: “by a Son”, one who is Son by nature. The prophets spoke God's word; the Son is that Word.
He is the reflection of God’s glory and the exact imprint of God’s very being,
The two images say what the Church would later state at Nicaea: the Son is one in being with the Father.
Therefore he had to become like his brothers and sisters in every respect,
The Son of glory wants a human body, a human family and a human mother. This is why Mary matters: the flesh of the eternal Son was taken from her.
ch: The Catechism uses these verses to teach that in his Son, God has said everything (CCC 65). It uses Hebrews 1:3 for the Son's oneness with the Father (CCC 241). The Council of Chalcedon teaches that he is like us in all things except sin. The feast adds a further thought: the one who would be like us without sin received his flesh from a mother whom God had kept from sin by his grace (CCC 490–492).

r.h: God my Savior
set: Mary has travelled to Elizabeth's house and has been called blessed. Luke gives her answer as a song, which the Latin tradition calls the Magnificat, from its first word. It is close to the song of Hannah, who also received a child from God (1 Samuel 2:1–10), and it is woven from the Psalms and the Prophets. Pope Benedict XVI wrote that the Magnificat is entirely woven from threads of Holy Scripture (Deus Caritas Est 41).
str: vv. 46–49: what God has done for Mary.
v. 50: his mercy for all who fear him, in every generation.
vv. 51–53: what God does in the world: he overturns the proud and lifts up the lowly.
vv. 54–55: his promise to Israel, from Abraham onward.
kw: To declare great. Mary does not add to God's greatness; she makes it known. The song begins with God and stays with him.
The key word for today. Mary calls God her own Savior. The Immaculate Conception does not take her out of the circle of the redeemed. She is its first and most complete fruit.
Low condition, not the virtue of humility as such. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Hannah's affliction (1 Samuel 1:11). God looks on Mary's littleness.
vv: and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,
The Church does not say that Mary had no need of a Saviour. She needed him as all do, and she was saved by being kept from sin, not by being cleansed after it (CCC 491–492).
for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant.
This is the whole theology of the feast in one line: the initiative is God's. Mary's greatness starts in the way God looked at her.
for the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name.
“The Mighty One” echoes Old Testament language for the God who saves (compare Zephaniah 3:17). The “great things” are not Mary's achievements. They are God's work in her.
ch: The Catechism calls the Magnificat the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church (CCC 2619). Pope Pius IX defined the Immaculate Conception in Ineffabilis Deus (8 December 1854): by a singular grace, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ the Saviour, Mary was preserved from all stain of original sin from the first instant of her conception (CCC 491). St Ambrose, preaching on this passage, wishes that the soul of Mary might be in each of us to magnify the Lord, and her spirit in each of us to rejoice in God (in substance). The grace given to her at the start is the grace promised to all of us at the end.

qa: Is the Immaculate Conception the same as the virgin birth?

No. They are often confused. The Immaculate Conception concerns Mary's own beginning in her mother's womb: she came into being through her parents in the natural way, and from that first moment she was kept from original sin. The virginal conception concerns Jesus, conceived in Mary by the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:35; CCC 496–497).
If Mary was without sin, did she need Jesus as Saviour?

Yes, and she says so herself (Luke 1:47). St Thomas Aquinas hesitated over the doctrine for this very reason, wanting to guard Christ as the Saviour of all. Blessed John Duns Scotus helped the Church see the answer: to be preserved from a fall is a more perfect rescue than to be lifted up after it. So the Catechism says she was “redeemed in a more exalted fashion” in view of her Son's merits (CCC 492; Lumen Gentium 53).
Where is this doctrine in the Bible?

No verse states it in so many words. The Church reads it in the enmity between the woman and the serpent (Genesis 3:15), in the angel's greeting “favored one” (Luke 1:28), and in the role of the mother of the Holy One. The Fathers praised Mary's holiness, especially in the East (CCC 493). The Church's understanding grew over the centuries, and the doctrine was solemnly defined in 1854.
rite: The Syriac tradition has sung Mary's purity since its earliest poets. St Ephrem the Syrian (4th century) says to the Lord that he and his Mother alone are entirely beautiful, for there is no blemish in him and no stain in his Mother (in substance, Nisibene Hymns 27). He did not use later Western terms, but the love and the wonder are the same. Among St Thomas Christians the Carmelites of Mary Immaculate, the congregation of St Kuriakose Elias Chavara, carry this title in their very name. In the season of Annunciation, we keep this feast while waiting for the birth of her Son. At the Holy Qurbana we too receive him, and ask to be made a fitting dwelling.
study: Wisdom looks for a resting place and God prepares one. How can my family and my home be made ready for Christ this Christmas?
Ahaz refused God's sign because he had already chosen his own plan. Where do I use pious words to avoid trusting God?
Mary calls God “my Savior”. What does it change in me to see her as the first of the redeemed, not as someone far from us?
Why is it good news for sinners that God did something so complete in one of us?

lead: The day after the feast of the Immaculate Conception, the readings take up its two great themes. Paul's hymn says that God chose us in Christ “before the foundation of the world”, to be holy and blameless. Luke shows the moment when one young woman of Nazareth, already prepared by God, says yes. God's plan is older than the world, and it passes through one person's willing word of consent.

r.h: Chosen before the foundation of the world
set: The letter comes from prison (3:1; 4:1) and is traditionally by Paul. Some of the oldest manuscripts lack the words “in Ephesus” in 1:1, and many scholars think it was meant for several churches of the region; some think a later disciple wrote it. In Greek, vv. 3–14 are one long sentence of blessing, shaped like the Jewish berakah, the prayer that begins “Blessed be God”. Today's reading takes most of it.
str: v. 3: the blessing: God has blessed us in Christ.
vv. 4–6: chosen and adopted, to the praise of his grace.
vv. 7–8: redemption and forgiveness through his blood.
vv. 9–10: the mystery made known: all things gathered up in Christ.
vv. 11–12: our inheritance and our hope.
kw: The same root is used three times in v. 3. We bless God because he first blessed us.
In Paul not a riddle, but God's hidden plan, now made known (v. 9).
To bring together under one head. St Irenaeus built on this idea: Christ sums up in himself the whole of creation and human history, and heals it (in substance; CCC 518).
vv: just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
Choice comes first, holiness follows. We are not chosen because we are holy, but so that we may become holy. The word “blameless” is also used of an unblemished sacrifice.
He destined us for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ,
Adoption was a serious legal act in the Roman world: the adopted son received the full rights of a son. By baptism, God's only Son shares his place with us.
as a plan for the fullness of time, to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
Salvation is not only for souls. The whole universe is to find its head and its peace in Christ.
ch: The Catechism applies these words directly to Mary: the Father blessed her more than any other created person with every spiritual blessing and chose her in Christ before the foundation of the world, to be holy and blameless (CCC 492). It also takes this hymn as the model of all Christian liturgy, which blesses the Father for his blessings (CCC 1077–1083). What God did perfectly in Mary is what he wants for each of us.

r.h: Here am I, the servant of the Lord
set: Gabriel has greeted a young woman of Nazareth, engaged to Joseph of the house of David, and has told her that she will bear a son, the heir of David's throne (1:26–33). In the Jewish custom of the time, engagement was a binding legal bond, though the couple did not yet live together. Nazareth was a small, unimportant village of Galilee. Our reading is the second half of the scene: her question and her answer.
str: v. 34: Mary's question.
v. 35: the angel's answer: the Holy Spirit, the power of the Most High, the Son of God.
vv. 36–37: a sign, Elizabeth, and the reason: nothing is impossible with God.
v. 38: Mary's consent; the angel leaves.
kw: The same verb is used in the Greek of Exodus 40:35 for the cloud of God's glory covering the tent, and in Luke 9:34 for the cloud at the Transfiguration. Mary becomes the new place of God's presence.
A woman slave. Mary takes this as a title of honour, in the line of Moses and David, who were called servants of the Lord.
A form of the Greek verb that expresses a wish. Mary does not merely accept; she desires what God desires.
vv: Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, since I am a virgin?”
The Greek says, “since I do not know a man”, which the POC keeps. “Know” is the biblical word for marital union. Her question is about how, not whether.
For nothing will be impossible with God.”
These words echo what the Lord said to Abraham about Sarah (Genesis 18:14 in Greek). The God of the first barren mother is the God of Elizabeth and of the virgin of Nazareth.
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
After this Luke simply says that the angel departed. She is left with the promise, and no further explanation.
ch: The Catechism presents Mary's answer as the obedience of faith (CCC 148, 494). St Irenaeus, quoted there, says that the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by Mary's obedience, and Lumen Gentium 56 teaches that she was not a passive instrument but cooperated by her faith and obedience. St Augustine says that she conceived Christ in her heart by faith before she conceived him in her womb (in substance). St Bernard of Clairvaux, in a famous homily, imagines the whole world waiting for her reply (in substance).

qa: Zechariah was struck silent for asking a question. Why was Mary not?

The two questions differ. Zechariah asks for a guarantee: “How will I know that this is so?” (1:18), and the angel himself says that he did not believe (1:20). Mary already accepts the promise and asks how it will come about, since she does not know a man. Elizabeth later says of her, “blessed is she who believed” (1:45).
