study: Ephesians says that I was chosen before the world began. How would it change my day if I really believed this?
Mary's “let it be” was said with no further explanation given to her. What is God asking of me that I do not yet fully understand?

lead: Paul's list of the works of love and Luke's scene of the Visitation explain each other. Paul says, “extend hospitality”, “rejoice with those who rejoice”, “associate with the lowly”. In Luke we see this lived: a pregnant young woman hurries to help an older relative, and two women rejoice together over what God has done. Love shows itself in going out to someone.

r.h: Let love be genuine
set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome, a church he had not yet visited, probably from Corinth in about AD 57. After eleven chapters on God's mercy to Jews and Gentiles, he turns in chapter 12 to how the redeemed should live: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (12:1). Our passage is a chain of short commands, many without a main verb in the Greek, like the sayings of the wise. The Sermon on the Mount can be heard behind vv. 14 and 17.
str: vv. 9–13: love within the community.
vv. 14–16: blessing, sharing joy and grief, living in harmony.
vv. 17–18: toward all people: no revenge, peace as far as it depends on you.
kw: Literally “without hypocrisy”. The hypokritēs was a stage actor. Love must not be a mask.
A word for the warm love within a family, used only here in the New Testament. The Church is to be a home.
Literally “love of strangers”. The Greek says to pursue it, not merely to wait for guests.
vv: Let love be genuine; hate what is evil, hold fast to what is good;
Genuine love is not soft. It has a clear view of good and evil.
Contribute to the needs of the saints; extend hospitality to strangers.
Travelling Christians depended on such welcome in those days. “Saints” means all the baptised, as in all Paul's letters.
Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.
Sharing another's joy without envy may be the harder half of this verse.
ch: The Catechism names Romans 12–15 among the apostolic teachings that hand on the moral teaching of Christ, and quotes these verses (CCC 1971). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, remarks that it takes more greatness of soul to rejoice with the one who rejoices than to weep with the one who weeps, for envy is overcome only with difficulty (in substance).

r.h: The mother of my Lord comes to me
set: Gabriel had given Mary a sign: Elizabeth, too old to bear, was in her sixth month (1:36). Mary goes at once. Nazareth in Galilee is several days' journey from the hill country of Judea. Luke does not name the town; a later Christian tradition places it at Ein Karem, near Jerusalem. Luke tells the meeting with echoes of the story of the ark in 2 Samuel 6.
str: vv. 39–40: Mary's journey and her greeting.
v. 41: the child leaps, and Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit.
vv. 42–44: Elizabeth's cry of blessing and her question.
v. 45: the beatitude of faith.
kw: Eagerly. St Ambrose says that the grace of the Holy Spirit knows nothing of slow efforts (in substance).
The word is used for Jacob and Esau in Rebekah's womb (Genesis 25:22, Greek) and for leaping with joy in Luke 6:23. Luke sees John already beginning his work.
In Luke's Greek this is the title of the God of Israel, here given to the child in Mary's womb. This is the seed of the later title Mother of God.
vv: Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.

Words like those said of Jael (Judges 5:24) and Judith (Judith 13:18), women through whom God saved his people. Here Mary's blessing and that of her child are spoken together. The Church repeats it in the Hail Mary (CCC 2676).
And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?

Many commentators hear David's words: “How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (2 Samuel 6:9). In that story too there is a journey in the hills of Judah, leaping for joy, and a stay of three months (compare Luke 1:56). Mary carries the presence of God.
And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her by the Lord.”
This is the first beatitude in Luke's Gospel, and it is about faith. Mary is blessed not only for what happened in her, but for how she received it (CCC 148).
ch: Lumen Gentium 57 sees here the union of Mother and Son in the work of salvation: Mary is called blessed for her faith, and the forerunner leaps in the womb. Elizabeth's “mother of my Lord” stands behind the title Theotokos that the Council of Ephesus confirmed in 431 (CCC 495). St Ambrose remarks that Elizabeth was first to hear the voice, but John was first to feel the grace (in substance).

qa: Was John made holy before he was born?

Luke says that John would be filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb (1:15), and the Catechism repeats this (CCC 523, 717). This is not the same as Mary's Immaculate Conception. John's leap is the first sign of that promise, and he leaps because of the presence of Jesus.
study: Mary went at once to someone who might need her. Whom could I visit or help this week, before Christmas?
Which is harder for me: to weep with those who weep or to rejoice with those who rejoice? Why?

lead: Paul asks the Corinthians to finish their collection for the poor Christians of Jerusalem, so that there may be “a fair balance”. Mary sings of the God who “has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty”. On the feast of 8 December we dwelt on the first half of this song, about what God did for her. Today we listen especially to its second half, about what God does in the world. Her song and Paul's collection point the same way: God's coming changes who has what.

r.h: A fair balance
set: For years Paul organised a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:10; Romans 15:25–27). For him it was more than relief: it was a sign that Jews and Gentiles are one body in Christ. The Corinthians had begun it eagerly a year earlier (8:10), then let it drop. Paul, writing from Macedonia, gently urges them on. Just before our reading he gives the deepest reason: though Christ was rich, he became poor for our sake (8:9). Our passage begins in the middle of a sentence.
str: vv. 11–12: finish what you began, according to what you have.
vv. 13–14: the principle: not a burden, but a fair balance.
v. 15: the proof from Scripture: the manna.
kw: Readiness of heart. Paul uses it several times in these chapters. God looks at it first, not at the amount.
The key word, used twice here. Paul does not ask anyone to become destitute; he asks that no one be left with too little while others have too much.
vv: For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has
A comfort to the poor who give little, and a question to those who could give more. Compare the widow's coin (Luke 21:1–4).
your present abundance and their need, so that their abundance may be for your need, in order that there may be a fair balance.
Today one gives; tomorrow one may receive. Perhaps Paul is also thinking of what Jerusalem gave the Gentiles: the spiritual riches of the Gospel (Romans 15:27).
As it is written, “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little.”
Exodus 16:18. In the desert, however much each one gathered of the manna, each had enough. Paul sees in the Church the same providence, now working through human hands.
ch: The Catechism refers to this passage when it explains “our daily bread”: poverty in the spirit of the Beatitudes means sharing, not by force but out of love, so that the abundance of some may remedy the needs of others (CCC 2833). It teaches the universal destination of the earth's goods (CCC 2402–2406) and quotes St John Chrysostom: not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them (CCC 2446).

r.h: He lifted up the lowly
set: The Magnificat stands in the line of Israel's songs of deliverance: Miriam's (Exodus 15), Deborah's (Judges 5) and above all Hannah's (1 Samuel 2:1–10). Its second half turns from Mary's own story to God's way with the whole world. The speaker is a poor woman of a land under Rome's power, in the time of Herod. Israel's “poor of the Lord” had long hoped for this.
str: vv. 46–50: God and his servant (see 8 December).
vv. 51–53: three reversals: the proud, the powerful, the rich.
vv. 54–55: the reason: his mercy and his promise to Abraham.
v. 56: Mary stays about three months, then goes home.
kw: The “outstretched arm” is the language of the Exodus (Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 4:34). What God did in Egypt, he does again.
A Hebrew term, not used in Luke's Greek, for the humble who rely on God alone (see Zephaniah 2:3; 3:12). Mary “stands out among the poor and humble of the Lord” (Lumen Gentium 55; compare CCC 64).
Used in vv. 50 and 54. In the Greek Old Testament it often translates ḥesed, God's faithful covenant love. It frames these three verses of reversal.
vv: He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly;
The Greek verbs are past tenses: Mary sings of the future as if it had already happened, as the prophets do, because in the child she carries God has already begun it.
he has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty.

This agrees with Luke's own beatitudes and woes (6:20–26). Being rich is not the fault in itself; the danger is the self-sufficiency that needs nothing from God. Hannah sang the same thing (1 Samuel 2:5).
according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever.”

The song ends with memory: this is no new God. A note on the text: at v. 46 a few old Latin witnesses read “And Elizabeth said”, but nearly all manuscripts, and the Church's constant reading, give the song to Mary.
And Mary remained with her about three months and then returned to her home.
Three months, like the stay of the ark in the house of Obed-edom (2 Samuel 6:11). Luke mentions it simply. The one who sings of reversals also stays and helps.
ch: St Paul VI wrote that Mary of Nazareth, while completely devoted to God's will, was far from timidly submissive; she proclaims that God vindicates the humble and the oppressed (Marialis Cultus 37). St John Paul II saw in the Magnificat the source of the Church's love of preference for the poor (Redemptoris Mater 37). The Catechism takes the song as a model of adoration: to adore God is to confess with Mary that he has done great things (CCC 2097).

qa: Is the Magnificat a call to political revolution?

Not as a program of violence. The one who acts here is God, and the reversal begins with the proud “in the thoughts of their hearts” (1:51). But it is not merely “spiritual” either. The poverty and hunger it speaks of are real, and the Church has drawn from it a real duty toward the poor (Redemptoris Mater 37; CCC 2448). Both sides must be kept.
study: In the coming feast of Christmas, who in my parish or neighbourhood has “too little”? What is my part in a fair balance?
Mary sings of what God has done before she can see it. What promise of God can I give thanks for today, though it is not yet complete?

lead: Both readings ask about the inner state of the heart and the eye. Hebrews warns against a heart that hardens slowly, and takes Israel in the desert as its example. Jesus says that the eye is the lamp of the body, and asks whether the light in us is really light. Nearing Christmas, the Church asks us not only whether we are busy for God, but what we are looking at, and whether we can still hear his voice today.

r.h: Today, if you hear his voice
set: The author has just quoted Psalm 95 (Hebrews 3:7–11), with its memory of Israel's testing of God in the desert (Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 14). The whole generation that left Egypt, except Joshua and Caleb, failed to enter the land. The readers of Hebrews are believers growing tired under pressure, and they face the same danger. This passage is a preacher's commentary on the psalm.
str: vv. 12–14: the warning: encourage one another today; hold firm to the end.
v. 15: the psalm repeated.
vv. 16–19: three questions and the answer: unbelief kept them out.
kw: The psalm's key word. For the preacher it has not expired: it remains God's “today” as long as this age lasts (v. 13).
The root of our word “apostasy”. It is not a sudden act here, but the end of a slow hardening.
In the psalm, the promised land. Hebrews 4 will widen it to mean God's own rest, which believers are invited to enter.
vv: Take care, brothers and sisters, that none of you may have an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
The danger is described as a condition of the heart, not of the intellect. Note “none of you”: the author is concerned for each one.
But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
The remedy is shared. Christians are responsible for each other's faith. Sin “deceives”: it hardens without our noticing.
So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.
They had seen the wonders of the Exodus. Having seen wonders is not the same as trusting God now.
ch: The Catechism writes that when the Church celebrates the mystery of Christ, one word marks her prayer: “Today!” (CCC 1165). It also teaches, quoting this same psalm, that it is in the present that we meet God, not yesterday or tomorrow but today (CCC 2659). So every Holy Qurbana is an answer to the psalm: God speaks now, and the hearer responds now.

r.h: Your eye is the lamp of your body
set: Jesus has been speaking to crowds who ask for a sign (11:16, 29). He has said that the only sign is Jonah, and that the queen of the South and the people of Nineveh will judge this generation. The light is already among them; the trouble is in the eyes that look at it. Immediately afterward he eats at a Pharisee's house (11:37). Matthew has similar sayings in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:15; 6:22–23).
str: v. 33: a lamp is put where it can be seen.
v. 34: the eye as the lamp of the body: healthy or not.
v. 35: the warning: check your light.
v. 36: the promise: a body full of light.
kw: Literally “single” or “simple”, without folds. It can also mean generous. The undivided eye sees clearly.
An “evil eye” in biblical language often means a stingy, envious way of looking at others (Deuteronomy 15:9; Sirach 14:8–10). So the saying touches both sight and generosity.
A small clay oil lamp, the ordinary light of a house. In the image, the eye does for the body what the lamp does for the house.
vv: No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar, but on the lampstand so that those who enter may see the light.

A note on the text. The POC has “or under a measure” (പറയുടെ കീഴിലോ). Some ancient manuscripts have those words, as in Matthew 5:15, and others, followed by the NRSV, omit them. The sense does not change. Christ is not a hidden light.
Your eye is the lamp of your body. If your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light;
The problem is not lack of light but how we look at it. The same Jesus was seen by some as God's envoy and by others as a threat.
Therefore consider whether the light in you is not darkness.
One of the most searching sentences in the Gospels: what I take as my light may itself be darkness. It calls for honest self-examination.
ch: St Augustine, commenting on Matthew's form of this saying, takes the eye to be the intention with which we act: if the intention is pure, the whole work is full of light (in substance). The Catechism says that intention lies at the voluntary source of our actions, though a good intention does not by itself make a wrong act right (CCC 1752–1753). Vatican II opens its teaching on the Church with Christ as the light of the nations, a light that shines out on the face of the Church (Lumen Gentium 1).

qa: Can a baptised believer really lose faith, as Hebrews warns?

Yes. Faith is God's gift, but we can lose it if we do not care for it. The Catechism says that to live, grow and persevere in faith we must nourish it with the word of God and beg the Lord to increase it (CCC 162). Hebrews does not aim to frighten but to keep us near each other and near God.
study: Who is the person I should encourage “today”, so that he or she is not worn down?
What do I look at most in a day: on my phone, in people, in myself? Is this filling me with light?

lead: This Sunday of the season of Annunciation celebrates a birth: John the Baptist. Three of the four readings tell of children given to women who could not hope for them: Sarah in Genesis, the wife of Manoah in Judges, and Elizabeth in Luke. Each time God's promise comes first, and the child arrives as pure gift, with a task for the whole people. In between stands Paul, who like John exists to point to someone else: the mystery of Christ, now open to all the nations. The line runs from a tent at Mamre to a tablet in Zechariah's hand, and its key words are welcome, promise and name.

r.h: Visitors at the tent of Abraham
set: Abraham lives as a stranger in Canaan. God promised him descendants long ago (12:2; 15:5), and has just repeated that Sarah herself will bear the son (17:15–21). Abraham is ninety-nine and Sarah ninety (17:17, 24). Mamre is near Hebron, in the southern hills of Canaan. The story is told with a storyteller's care, and it leaves open a question which the reader only slowly understands: who are these three men?
str: vv. 1–2: the Lord appears; Abraham sees three men and runs to them.
vv. 3–5: the invitation: a little water, a little bread.
vv. 6–8: the great meal, prepared in haste.
vv. 9–10: the question about Sarah and the promise.
kw: These two verbs drive the scene (vv. 2, 6, 7). An old man, in the heat of the day, runs. He promises “a little bread” and serves a feast: three measures of flour are far more than three guests could eat.

The traditional Hebrew vowels of v. 3 are those used for God's title, though the sentence can be heard as courtesy. Abraham speaks to one, and then to more than one (vv. 3–5). The text moves between “the Lord” and “three men”.
A rare phrase, literally something like “at the time of life”. It probably means this time next year. The NRSV has “in due season”, and the POC has “in spring”.
vv: The Lord appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day.
The narrator tells the reader what Abraham does not yet know. He thinks he is receiving passing travellers.
He said, “My lord, if I find favor with you, do not pass by your servant.
Here it is the host who begs a favour of the guest. Compare Luke 24:28–29, where two disciples urge a stranger to stay.
Then one said, “I will surely return to you in due season, and your wife Sarah shall have a son.”

The promise comes at the end of a meal, and Sarah overhears it behind the tent door. Just after the reading she laughs, and the Lord asks: “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” (18:14). The Greek of that verse is echoed by the angel's word to Mary in Luke 1:37.
ch: Hebrews 13:2 alludes to this scene: “by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.” Many Fathers saw in the three visitors a hint of the Trinity, and St Augustine notes that Abraham sees three yet speaks as to one Lord (in substance). Eastern iconography paints the scene in this light, most famously in the icon of Andrei Rublev. The Catechism says that Abraham's remarkable hospitality at Mamre foreshadows the annunciation of the true Son of the promise (CCC 2571), a fitting word for this season.

r.h: Consecrated from birth
set: The Philistines have ruled Israel for forty years (13:1), and this time, unlike earlier episodes in Judges, the people do not even cry out. The tribe of Dan is barely holding its land near the coastal plain; Zorah lies on the edge of Philistine country. God takes the initiative anyway. The mother is never named, yet the angel comes first to her, and she sees more clearly than her husband (13:22–23). The reading skips the longer story of Manoah's offering and goes to the birth.
str: v. 2: the family and the sorrow: a barren wife.
vv. 3–5: the angel's message: a son, a rule of life, a mission.
vv. 6–7: the woman tells her husband.
v. 24: the birth, the name, and God's blessing.
kw: God's messenger, so close to God in these stories that the one who sees him may say “we have seen God” (13:22).
Numbers 6:1–21 describes the nazirite vow, usually for a limited time: no wine, no razor, no contact with a corpse. Samson's is unusual: God imposes it, from birth, for life.
The same root as the name Yeshua, Jesus. Samson will only “begin” this deliverance. It will take Samuel and David to complete it.
vv: Although you are barren, having borne no children, you shall conceive and bear a son.
The words of barrenness are said plainly. God begins from what the woman lacks. Luke's angel echoes this announcement form when he speaks to Mary (Luke 1:31).
It is he who shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.
“Begin” is an honest word. The hero is strong, and also flawed, as the next chapters show. Yet Hebrews 11:32 names him among the people of faith.
The woman bore a son, and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the Lord blessed him.
The name Šimšôn is probably linked to šemeš, “sun”. Compare the growth notices for Samuel (1 Samuel 2:26) and John (Luke 1:80).
ch: The Catechism says that God chooses those considered powerless and weak, to show his faithfulness to his promises (CCC 489), and that line of women prepares for Mary. Samson's flaws remind us that God's call is a gift, not a reward: the Lord works even through weak vessels. Luke's account of John draws on this story: “wine or strong drink” (Luke 1:15), a child set apart, and a promise of deliverance.

r.h: The boundless riches of Christ
set: Paul writes as “a prisoner for Christ Jesus”; his chains are the price of his mission to the Gentiles. In chapter 2 he has said that Christ broke down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile. He begins a prayer here (3:1), breaks off to explain his own role, and returns to the prayer at 3:14. The passage is a long aside, and it contains the letter's definition of the mystery.
str: vv. 1–4: the prisoner and the mystery revealed to him.
vv. 5–6: its content: the Gentiles are co-heirs.
vv. 7–9: Paul's call, the least of all.
vv. 10–12: God's many-sided wisdom, shown through the Church.
v. 13: do not lose heart over my sufferings.
kw: Literally the management of a household. Used for Paul's task (v. 2) and for God's own plan (v. 9). Paul is a steward in God's house.

In v. 6 three Greek words begin with this prefix: fellow heirs, members of the same body, sharers. Paul piles up words of togetherness. The Gentiles join Israel's inheritance; they do not replace her.
Literally “many-coloured”, used of embroidered cloth or flowers. The Church, with all her peoples, rites and tongues, shows God's wisdom.
vv: that is, the Gentiles have become fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
The secret is not a teaching for a few. It is the opposite: everyone is invited.
Although I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given to me to bring to the Gentiles the news of the boundless riches of Christ,

“The very least” renders a strange Greek form, a comparative made from a superlative, as if “leaster”. The word for “boundless” means that one cannot trace it to its end. The POC gives “hard to grasp” (ദുർഗ്രഹമായ).
in whom we have access to God in boldness and confidence through faith in him.
Parrēsia, boldness, is the frank speech of a citizen. A prisoner writes this: chains cannot take away access to God.
ch: The Catechism reads these verses when it says that God's plan is fulfilled and revealed in the Church (CCC 772). Vatican II teaches that the pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature (Ad Gentes 2). The Church remains linked with Israel, whose covenant God has not revoked (CCC 121, 839). Paul's words on the wisdom shown “through the church” also fit the Eastern Churches: the Council says that such variety, far from harming the Church's unity, makes it clearer (Orientalium Ecclesiarum 2, in substance).

r.h: His name is John
set: Luke has set up two parallel stories: the announcements to Zechariah and to Mary, and now the birth of John and, in the next chapter, the birth of Jesus. Zechariah has been unable to speak since the angel's visit (1:20). A child's circumcision on the eighth day followed God's command to Abraham (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). The custom of naming the child at that moment is reflected here. Family names were common; the relatives' surprise is natural.
str: vv. 57–58: the birth and the joy of the neighbours.
vv. 59–61: the eighth day and the dispute over the name.
vv. 62–63: the father writes.
v. 64: his mouth is opened.
vv. 65–66: fear, and the question of the whole region.
kw: Literally “magnified his mercy”. It is the same verb as Mary's “My soul magnifies” (1:46), a few verses earlier.
A Hebrew name meaning “the Lord has been gracious”. The name is itself the message of the season.
The Old Testament expression for God's power at work in a person (1 Kings 18:46; Ezekiel 1:3). It ends the scene and answers the question.
vv: Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown his great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
Gabriel had promised this: “many will rejoice at his birth” (1:14). Her shame among the people is now over (compare 1:25).
But his mother said, “No; he is to be called John.”

Elizabeth speaks first and speaks firmly. Luke does not say how she knew the name, whether from Zechariah in writing or from the Spirit. The name does not come from the family. It comes from God, and it breaks a custom.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And all of them were amazed.

He does not write “let his name be” but “his name is”: the matter has already been decided by God. They have to motion to him (v. 62), which suggests that he may have been deaf as well. The word for his condition in 1:22 can mean both.
Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue freed, and he began to speak, praising God.
The first act of his obedience opens his mouth, and the first use of his tongue is praise. The words of that praise come in the Benedictus (1:68–79).
All who heard them pondered them and said, “What then will this child become?” For, indeed, the hand of the Lord was with him.
The question stays open until chapter 3. Luke's readers know the answer: the voice in the wilderness.
ch: The Catechism calls John the Lord's immediate precursor, sent to prepare his way, filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb (CCC 523, 717–718). St Augustine, in his preaching on John's birth, says that John was the voice and Christ the Word: the voice passes when the word has reached the heart (in substance). So the feast is not about John alone. He lives to make room for another (John 3:30).

qa: Why does Elizabeth insist on the name before Zechariah can write it?

Luke does not explain, and we should not claim more than he says. Some think she knew by the Holy Spirit; others think that Zechariah had made it known in writing during those months. What matters is that husband and wife agree, against all the relatives, in obeying God's word (1:13).
Are the three visitors in Genesis 18 really the Trinity?

The text itself speaks of the Lord and of three men, and later calls two of them angels (19:1). Jewish tradition sees here angels sent by the Lord, and many Christians read it as the Lord with two angels. The Trinity is not revealed at this point in Scripture. But many Fathers, reading in the light of Christ, saw it as a hint, and so does Christian art. Both are honest ways of reading.
Was Paul the only one given this mystery?
No. He himself says it was revealed “to his holy apostles and prophets” (3:5). He sees his own call as a share in a gift given to the whole apostolic Church.
rite: For us St Thomas Christians, Paul's “fellow heirs” is our own story. By our ancient tradition, St Thomas the Apostle brought the Gospel to Malabar, and Gentiles of this land became members of the same body. The Syro-Malabar season of Annunciation reads these birth stories slowly, so that we arrive at Christmas having learned how God works: with the barren, with the silent, with the small. At this Sunday's Holy Qurbana we can ask for Zechariah's grace, that our tongue may be opened in praise. We might also bless our children, and ask of each: “What then will this child become?”
study: Abraham ran to welcome strangers without knowing who they were. Whom does my parish or home need to welcome more readily?
The wife of Manoah has no name in the text, but she hears God's word first. Who are the unnamed people through whom God has spoken to me?
Paul calls himself “the very least” and still preaches boldly. How can real humility and real boldness go together in me?
Zechariah's silence ended when he obeyed. Where would obedience open my own mouth to praise?

lead: Paul tells a Corinthian church that has grown proud to clear out the old yeast, for Christ our paschal lamb has been sacrificed. Jesus says that a tree is known by its fruit, and that the mouth speaks from what fills the heart. Both readings look for the source of what we do, and both call for purification. The Church keeps today the memory of St John of the Cross, who taught that the heart must be emptied so that God alone may fill it.

r.h: Clean out the old yeast
set: Paul founded the church at Corinth, a busy Greek port under Roman rule, and wrote this letter from Ephesus in the mid-50s AD (16:8). He has been told of a scandal: a man is living with his father's wife, presumably his stepmother, which both the Law (Leviticus 18:8) and Roman law forbade. What grieves Paul most is that the community is proud of itself and does nothing.
str: vv. 1–2: the case, and the community's arrogance.
vv. 3–5: Paul's judgment: the assembly must act, for the man's own salvation.
vv. 6–8: the image of the yeast: Passover and Christian life.
kw: A broad word for sexual sin. Here it is a specific case that Paul says even pagans do not accept.
Old leaven, fermented dough kept from one batch to the next. It is a picture of something small that affects the whole. Before Passover, Jewish homes clear out all leaven (Exodus 12:15).
The word for Passover and for its lamb. Here is one of the earliest Christian statements that the Cross is the true Passover.
vv: you are to hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
The goal of this severe step is salvation, not revenge. On the wording: the POC reads “flesh” as the man's base passions (അധമവികാരങ്ങൾ); the Greek word is sarx.
Do you not know that a little yeast leavens the whole batch of dough?
A proverb, also used in Galatians 5:9. Tolerated sin is not a private matter.
For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.

Paul does not say “become holy, and then Christ will save you”. It is the other way round: the Lamb has already been sacrificed, so live as the people of the Passover. The moral command rests on what God has done.
Therefore, let us celebrate the festival, not with the old yeast, the yeast of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
The whole Christian life is a feast of Passover, kept not once a year but every day, with sincerity and truth as its bread.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ is the Paschal Lamb (CCC 608) and that the Eucharist is the Lord's own Passover (CCC 1340). Exclusion from communion remains a serious, healing remedy of the Church, and is lifted when the sinner repents (CCC 1463). The Church's discipline serves the conversion of the one who has sinned and protects the holiness of the community.

r.h: From the abundance of the heart
set: These sayings come near the end of the Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:20–49). Jesus has told his disciples to love their enemies, not to condemn, and to see the log in their own eye first (6:41–42). Now he explains how such a life is possible: everything grows from the inner life. Matthew uses similar words in 7:16–20 and 12:33–35. The next verses say that hearing without doing is a house without a foundation (6:46–49).
str: vv. 43–44: tree and fruit: what is known by what.
v. 45: the heart as a treasure store: the mouth shows what is kept there.
kw: Rotten, useless, spoiled. It can describe a tree that bears nothing good.
A storehouse. What I keep in my heart today I will have to draw on tomorrow.
Overflow. Speech is what spills over from the heart when it is full.
vv: No good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit;
This concerns character more than single acts. Jesus does not deny that people can change. The whole Gospel calls for conversion: by grace a bad tree can be made good.
for each tree is known by its own fruit.
A test for ourselves before it is a test for others, since the verses just before warn against judging (6:37, 41–42).
for it is out of the abundance of the heart that the mouth speaks.
In the Bible the heart is the seat of thought and choice, not only of feeling. The way we speak of others shows what we have stored inside.
ch: The Catechism says that the heart is the seat of moral personality (CCC 2517) and the hidden centre where we choose life or death (CCC 2563). Good works are therefore not a way to buy grace, but the fruit of the tree that grace has made good. St John of the Cross, whose words the Catechism quotes, gives the final test: at the evening of life, we shall be judged on our love (CCC 1022).

qa: What does “hand this man over to Satan” mean?

Most understand it as a form of exclusion from the community: put outside the Church's fellowship, the man stands in the realm that is not under Christ's protection. It is not a curse, for its stated aim is “that his spirit may be saved”. What “destruction of the flesh” means exactly is debated: suffering, or the death of his sinful way of life. 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 asks the Church to forgive a repentant offender; St John Chrysostom thought it was the same man, though many modern scholars doubt it.
rite: St John of the Cross (1542–1591), a Spanish Carmelite, worked with St Teresa of Ávila to reform the Carmelite order. Carmelite brothers who opposed the reform imprisoned him at Toledo for months in 1577–78, and there he began his great poem, the Spiritual Canticle. Pope Pius XI named him a Doctor of the Church in 1926. Carmel's spirituality is well known among us in Kerala, through St Kuriakose Elias Chavara and St Euphrasia, among others. His “dark night” fits today's Gospel: God clears the storehouse of the heart, so that only love remains.
study: What small “old yeast” have I learned to live with, in myself or in my community?
If those close to me heard everything I said this week, what would they conclude about what is stored in my heart?

lead: Both readings ask what comes first, God's action or ours. Paul looks back at the Christians of Asia Minor as people who were dead, and says that God made them alive by grace alone. In the Gospel John the Baptist stands in the wilderness and calls for repentance, because the kingdom has already come near. In the season of the Annunciation, the two belong together: God's gift comes first, and repentance is how we open the door to it.

r.h: Dead, and made alive by grace
set: Ephesians comes from prison (3:1; 4:1; 6:20) and is traditionally by Paul; some scholars think a later disciple wrote it. It looks at the whole plan of God for the Church. Chapter 1 ended with the power God used "when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places" (1:20). Now Paul makes a daring step: what God did for Christ, he has done for us.
str: vv. 1–3: what we were: dead in sin, and "by nature children of wrath", Jews and Gentiles alike ("all of us").
vv. 4–7: what God did: "But God" made us alive, raised us and seated us with Christ.
vv. 8–10: the conclusion: salvation is a gift, and it is given for a life of good works.
kw: The first of three Greek verbs in vv. 5–6 that begin with syn, "with": made alive with, raised with, seated with. This language says that we share in what happened to Christ. Baptism has already joined us to him.
by grace you have been saved
The verb is in the Greek perfect tense: a completed act whose effect continues. Paul says it twice (vv. 5, 8), and the second time he adds "through faith".

A thing made, a work of art or craft. The word appears in the New Testament only here and in Romans 1:20, where it means God's works in creation. The Christian is a work of the same Creator, a new creation.
vv: But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ
Everything turns on the words "But God". Paul has given a dark picture of human life without grace, and God interrupts it. The dead cannot help themselves, and so the initiative is entirely his.
For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God
The word "this" is neuter in Greek, so most commentators take it to mean the whole event of being saved, and not faith alone. Even our response is held up by grace.
created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.
Not saved by works (v. 9), but saved for works. Paul holds the two together without strain. Good works are not the price of salvation; they are the road God has laid out for the saved to walk on.
ch: The Catechism teaches that justification comes from the grace of God, and that since the initiative belongs to God, no one can merit the first grace of forgiveness (CCC 1996, 2010). St Augustine says that when God crowns our merits he crowns his own gifts (in substance; see CCC 2006). In the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), Catholics and Lutherans together confessed that we are accepted by God by grace alone, and not because of any merit of ours, and that good works follow.

r.h: A voice in the wilderness
set: After the infancy stories, Matthew moves straight to the adult John with the words "In those days". John's place is important. The wilderness is where Israel was formed after the Exodus, and the Jordan is the river Israel crossed to enter the land (Joshua 3). People go out from the city, back to where it all began, to start again.
str: vv. 1–2: John appears and gives his one message.
v. 3: Isaiah 40:3 explains who he is.
v. 4: his clothing and food.
vv. 5–6: the crowds come, are baptized and confess.
kw: Literally, change your mind, in the deep biblical sense of turning your whole life around. It is more than feeling sorry.
Matthew's usual phrase. Like many Jews of his time, he reverently says "heaven" in place of the name of God. It means God's own reign, and not only a place after death.
The verb says that the kingdom is at the door. Jesus begins his preaching with exactly the same sentence (4:17). John does not preach a message of his own; he goes ahead and prepares the way.
vv: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.
The order matters. The kingdom is not a reward for those who first repent. It is coming, and that is the reason to turn.
Now John wore clothing of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist

Any reader who knew the Scriptures would recognize Elijah, "a hairy man, with a leather belt around his waist" (2 Kings 1:8). Malachi had promised Elijah's return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5), and Jesus will say that John is the one to come (Matthew 11:14). Locusts were clean food under the Law (Leviticus 11:22).
and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
The baptism goes together with a spoken confession. Repentance is not left vague; people name what they have done.
ch: The Catechism calls John the Lord's immediate forerunner, sent to prepare his way (CCC 523), and teaches that his baptism was one of repentance (CCC 535). Inner repentance, it says, is a radical reorientation of the whole life, a turning back to God with all our heart (CCC 1431). The days before the Lord's birth are a time for this turning, and for the Sacrament of Reconciliation.

qa: Was John's baptism the same as Christian baptism?

No. John's baptism was a sign of repentance that prepared for the one to come. Christian baptism is given in the name of Jesus and joins us to his death and resurrection, with the gift of the Spirit. See Matthew 3:11 and Acts 19:3–5.
study: Paul says, "But God" (Ephesians 2:4). Where in my own life has God interrupted a story that was going badly?
John's hearers named their sins aloud. What would I name in a good confession before the feast of the Lord's birth?

lead: Today's two readings are about being faithful with what has been entrusted to us. Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians kept the word of God even under pressure. Jesus says that faithfulness is learned in very small things, and that no one can have two masters. The word of God and the things of daily life make the same demand: a single heart.

r.h: Not a human word
set: This is very probably the earliest of Paul's letters, written about AD 50 or 51, from Corinth, to a young Church he had to leave in a hurry (Acts 17:1–10). The whole of chapter 2 is a look back at his time with them. He is anxious for them, and he is writing with relief and affection.
str: v. 13: thanksgiving: they received the word as God's word.
vv. 14–16: they have suffered as the churches in Judea suffered; Paul's sharp words against those who opposed the mission.
v. 17: Paul's longing to see them.
kw: Two different verbs in v. 13. The first is the usual word for receiving something handed on, a tradition. The second means to welcome, as one welcomes a guest. The Gospel is both handed on and welcomed from the heart.
The English word "energy" comes from the same root. The word of God does not lie still in those who believe. It keeps on working.
A tender and unusual word (v. 17). Paul has already called himself a nurse and a father to them (2:7, 11). Now he says that being apart from them has left him an orphan.
vv: you accepted it not as a human word but as what it really is, God’s word, which is also at work in you believers.
Paul knows that he is the human voice, yet he insists that it is God who speaks. This is one reason we stand when the Gospel is proclaimed: another is speaking.
you suffered the same things from your own compatriots

The Thessalonians, mostly Gentiles, were being troubled by their own neighbours. Sharing in suffering makes them one with the mother churches far away in Judea. On the hard words that follow, see the question below.
we longed with great eagerness to see you face to face.
The teacher of the Gospel is not a lecturer who has moved on. Paul's theology and his affection cannot be separated.
ch: The Catechism applies 2:13 to the whole of Scripture: in it the Church finds her nourishment and strength, because she welcomes it not as a human word but as what it really is, the word of God (CCC 104; Dei Verbum 24). The Second Vatican Council also uses this verse to describe the sense of faith of the whole people of God (Lumen Gentium 12).

r.h: Faithful in a very little
set: These sayings follow the parable of the dishonest manager (16:1–9), which ended with the puzzling advice to "make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth". Luke now gathers sayings about money that explain how a disciple should use it. Later in the same chapter comes the rich man and Lazarus (16:19–31).
str: v. 10: the principle: little and much.
vv. 11–12: two applications: dishonest wealth and true riches; what belongs to another and what is your own.
v. 13: the conclusion: two masters are impossible.
kw: In v. 11 Luke plays on this word: if you are not pistoi with money, who will pisteusei, entrust, the true riches to you? Trust is earned through faithfulness.
An Aramaic word for wealth or property, which the Gospels keep untranslated in Greek, so that older English Bibles say "mammon". Jesus speaks of it almost as of a person, a rival lord.
This is more than having a job. A slave belongs to a master completely. So the saying is not about owning things, but about who owns us.
vv: Whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much
Character is not built on great occasions. It is built in the small honesty of ordinary days, and great occasions only show what is there.
who will entrust to you the true riches?
Money, Jesus says, is a small thing, a test. The true riches are the goods of the kingdom. How we handle the first shows whether we can be given the second.
You cannot serve God and wealth.
Jesus does not say that it is difficult; he says that it cannot be done. There is room for only one Lord. The same saying stands in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:24).
ch: The Catechism lists money among the things that people can honour in the place of God, and quotes this saying under the sin of idolatry (CCC 2113). It also quotes St John Chrysostom, who says that not to let the poor share in our goods is to steal from them (CCC 2446). Chrysostom says this in his sermons on Lazarus, the story that follows today's Gospel in Luke.

qa: Does 1 Thessalonians 2:14–16 blame the Jewish people?

No, and it must not be read that way. Paul is himself a Jew (Romans 11:1). He is writing in the heat of a particular conflict about those in Judea who persecuted the first Christians and those who were blocking his mission. The meaning of "God’s wrath has overtaken them at last" is debated by scholars, but it is not a judgment on a whole people. Paul's last word is in Romans: "the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" (Romans 11:29). The Church teaches that the Passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597), and that sinners were the authors of Christ's sufferings (CCC 598).
study: The Thessalonians received the word as God's word, and it went on working in them. How do I listen to the readings at the Holy Qurbana, as a human word or as God's word?
What "very little" thing is God asking me to be faithful in this week?

lead: Today's Gospel continues directly from last Sunday's, where John was born and named. Zechariah, silent for months, opens his mouth and sings. Paul's few verses to the Galatians tell us what the song has come to mean for us: all those clothed with Christ have become the heirs of the promise made to Abraham. God has remembered his promise, and now it reaches everyone.

r.h: Clothed with Christ
set: Paul is writing to Gentile Christians in Galatia who were being told that they had to accept circumcision and the Law of Moses to be true children of Abraham. Chapter 3 is his answer: the promise to Abraham came before the Law, and it is fulfilled in Christ. Today's verses are the high point. Many scholars think v. 28 echoes words already used at baptisms in the early Church.
str: v. 26: all are children of God through faith.
v. 27: baptism has clothed you with Christ.
v. 28: the old dividing lines no longer decide who belongs.
v. 29: therefore you are Abraham's offspring and heirs.
kw: The ordinary word for putting on a garment. Clothes in the Bible stand for what a person is and how he is seen (compare Isaiah 61:10). The baptized now go about clothed in Christ, and the Father sees his Son in them.
Paul does not say that you are all one thing, in the neuter, but uses the masculine: one person, one new man, in Christ Jesus.
Heirs do not earn an inheritance. They receive it because of who they are. This is what Paul has been defending all through the chapter.
vv: As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.
Paul does not offer an idea here, but points to something that has happened to them, in water, on a day they can remember.
There is no longer Jew or Greek, there is no longer slave or free, there is no longer male and female; for all of you are one in Christ Jesus.

Paul does not mean that these differences have disappeared. He still writes as a Jew, and to men and women. He means that none of them gives anyone a better place before God. The phrase "male and female" is the wording of Genesis 1:27.
And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise.
Gentile Christians are brought into the promise made to Israel, and they do not take it away from Israel. Compare the olive tree in Romans 11:17–18.
ch: The Catechism says that the baptized have "put on Christ" (CCC 1227), and that the white garment of baptism is the sign of it (CCC 1243). The Second Vatican Council draws the conclusion from this verse: in Christ and in the Church there is no inequality on the basis of race or nationality, social condition or sex (Lumen Gentium 32).

r.h: The dawn from on high
set: In the Temple, Zechariah did not believe the angel and was struck dumb (1:20). When he writes the name "John" at the child's circumcision, his tongue is freed (1:63–64). Luke says he was "filled with the Holy Spirit". The first words of the old priest, after his silence, are not a complaint or an explanation but a blessing of God. The song is full of the language of the Psalms and the prophets.
str: vv. 68–75: God is blessed for what he has done: he has visited his people, raised up a savior from David's house, and kept his oath to Abraham.
vv. 76–77: the song turns to the child: he will go ahead of the Lord.
vv. 78–79: the promised dawn.
kw: Literally, he has visited. The same verb comes back at v. 78, where the dawn "will break upon us", so the visit of God frames the song. In v. 78 the manuscripts differ between "will visit" and "has visited"; the promise holds either way.
Literally, "a horn of salvation", as in Psalm 18:2. An animal's horn stands for strength. Here it is the strength of a king from David's line.

The rising of the sun or a star. The Greek Old Testament uses the same word for the messianic "Branch" (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8), so it may carry both pictures: a shoot rising from the ground and a light rising in the sky.
vv: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has looked favorably on his people and redeemed them.

The verbs are in the past tense, although Jesus is not yet born. For the prophet, what God has begun is as good as done. Names are at work too: Zechariah means "the Lord has remembered", and the song is about God remembering (v. 72).
And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways,
An old man speaks to an eight-day-old baby. The child is great, but only as one who goes ahead. The song is not finally about John; it soon moves past him to the dawn.
By the tender mercy of our God, the dawn from on high will break upon us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.

The picture comes from Isaiah 9:2. The last word of the song is "peace", which is also what the angels will sing at the birth of Christ (Luke 2:14). "Tender mercy" is, literally, mercy felt in the depths of one's being.
ch: The Catechism sees John as the last of the prophets and the one who goes before the Lord in the Spirit (CCC 523, 717–719). The Latin Church sings this canticle at Morning Prayer every day, as the sun comes up. For us it is a good prayer of the last days before the feast of the Lord's birth.

study: "Clothed with Christ." In what part of my daily life do I most easily forget what I am wearing?
Zechariah's long silence ended in praise. What has God been teaching me in my own silences this season?

lead: Today the Syro-Malabar calendar keeps the memory of the Miraculous Cross at Mylapore, and the four readings open up the meaning of the Cross. In Exodus, water for a dying people comes from a rock that has been struck. In Acts, Peter proclaims that the crucified Jesus has been raised and has poured out the Spirit. In Ephesians, the Cross breaks down the wall between peoples and makes them one house of God. In John, on the night before he dies, Jesus tells Thomas that he himself is the way to the Father. The line runs from the struck rock to the Father's house, and its key words are water, peace and way. It is a fitting set of readings for the Church of St Thomas, a week before the birth of the Lord: the child we are waiting for was born for the Cross.

r.h: Water from the rock
set: Israel has crossed the sea and been fed with manna (Exodus 14–16). Now they camp at Rephidim, and there is no water. The people quarrel with Moses and ask: "Why did you bring us out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and livestock with thirst?" (17:3). The story ends with a question that lies under all their complaints: "Is the Lord among us or not?" (17:7).

The reading is short, but the place became famous. Moses named it Massah and Meribah, "testing" and "quarrelling" (17:7), and Psalm 95:8 still warned later generations not to harden their hearts as at Meribah. A similar event at Kadesh is told in Numbers 20:1–13.
str: v. 4: Moses cries out to the Lord: the people are about to stone him.
v. 5: God's command: go ahead of the people with the elders, and take the staff.
v. 6: God's promise to stand on the rock; Moses strikes it, and water flows.
¶ The people deserve judgment, yet the staff that struck the Nile (7:20) is not used on them. It is used on the rock where God has said that he will stand.
kw: A word from the law court: to bring a case against someone. It gives the place its name, Meribah. Israel has in effect put God on trial.
The root of the name Massah. The people demand that God prove himself. Jesus answers the tempter with this very memory: "Do not put the Lord your God to the test" (Matthew 4:7; Deuteronomy 6:16).
Often a title of God himself in the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 18:2). That makes this scene even more striking.
vv: So Moses cried out to the Lord, “What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me.”
Moses brings the anger of the people to God, and does not throw it back at them. This is what a mediator does.
take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go.
The same staff brought plague on Egypt and life to Israel. The elders are to go as witnesses, as at a trial, but the trial turns out strangely.
I will be standing there in front of you on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it, so that the people may drink.

God stands on the rock, and Moses strikes it. God does not strike the people. In a sense the blow falls where God is standing, and life comes out of it. Christian readers could not hear this verse without thinking of Calvary.
ch: St Paul writes that the Israelites drank from a spiritual rock, "and the rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). Jesus promises rivers of living water (John 7:37–39), and John records that from his pierced side "at once blood and water came out" (John 19:34). The Catechism sees in this blood and water the types of Baptism and the Eucharist (CCC 1225), and speaks of the Spirit as the living water welling up from Christ crucified (CCC 694). St Ambrose tells the faithful: Drink Christ, for he is the rock from which water gushed (in substance; Commentary on Psalm 1).

r.h: This Jesus whom you crucified
set: This is the end of Peter's speech on the day of Pentecost, in Jerusalem, to Jews who have come from every nation (Acts 2:5). The crowd has heard the disciples speaking in many tongues. Peter explains what has happened, first by the prophet Joel (2:17–21) and then by the Psalms. David, whom his hearers revere, becomes the main witness. The speech is the earliest public preaching of the Resurrection that Luke records.
str: v. 29: David died, and his tomb is here.
vv. 30–31: so David, as a prophet, was speaking of someone else (Psalm 132:11; Psalm 16:10).
v. 32: God raised Jesus, and we are witnesses.
v. 33: exalted, he has poured out the Spirit.
vv. 34–35: David did not ascend (Psalm 110:1).
v. 36: the conclusion.
kw: The boldness to say things openly (v. 29). Peter denied the Lord weeks earlier in this very city, and now he stands up in public. This change is itself evidence for what he is claiming.
The decay of the body in the grave. The Greek Old Testament of Psalm 16:10 uses this word, and the argument of Acts rests on it: David's body decayed, and Jesus' body did not.
Kyrios is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the name of God. Christos is the anointed king, the hope of Israel. Peter applies both to a man crucified a few weeks before.
vv: he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day.
Peter's argument is plain enough for anyone to check. A well-known tomb in Jerusalem holds David. The tomb of Jesus does not hold him.
This Jesus God raised up, and of that all of us are witnesses.
This is the centre of the apostolic preaching. It is said simply, and it rests on people who can be asked.
Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you both see and hear.
The Father, the Son and the Spirit are all here in one sentence. The Cross, the Resurrection and Pentecost belong to a single movement.
God has made him both Lord and Messiah, this Jesus whom you crucified.

The word "made" does not mean that Jesus was not Lord before. The Resurrection shows and establishes in his risen humanity what he always was (see CCC 445). On "whom you crucified", see the question below.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the title "Lord" given to Jesus is the divine name of the Old Testament, and that it gives him the honour due to God (CCC 446–449). It sees in Pentecost the outpouring by the risen Lord of the Spirit he received from the Father (CCC 731). When we confess at the Holy Qurbana that he is seated at the right hand of the Father, we are confessing what Peter preached that morning (CCC 659, 663).

r.h: He is our peace
set: The passage comes just after the reading we heard earlier this week, on being saved by grace (2:1–10). Paul now turns to what that grace has done to human divisions. The Gentiles were "far off" and the Jews were "near" (compare Isaiah 57:19). Paul writes as a Jew who honours the covenants: he says that what the Gentiles lacked was precisely a share in "the covenants of promise" (2:12).

Many commentators think that the "dividing wall" may recall a real barrier in the Temple at Jerusalem. A stone wall kept Gentiles from going further into the courts, and Greek inscriptions warning them of death have been found. Paul himself was accused of bringing a Greek past it (Acts 21:28–29).
str: vv. 14–16: Christ has made the two one, through the Cross.
vv. 17–18: he proclaimed peace to both; both now have access to the Father.
vv. 19–22: so you are one house, built on the apostles and prophets, with Christ as cornerstone.
kw: Behind it stands the Hebrew shalom: wholeness and right relationship, more than the absence of war. Paul uses the word four times in this passage, and he says more than that Christ brings peace. He says that Christ is our peace.
This word appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Walls keep people apart, and they also make enemies of them, so Paul adds at once: "that is, the hostility".
The word used for being brought into the presence of a king. In v. 18 the whole Trinity is at work: through the Son, in one Spirit, to the Father.
Compare Isaiah 28:16. The stone that sets the line and holds the walls together. Paul's picture of a building grows as he writes, into a temple where God lives.
vv: For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
"In his flesh": peace has not come through a treaty or a good idea. It has come through the body of a man who was put to death.
He has abolished the law with its commandments and ordinances,

This does not mean that the moral law has been cancelled. Paul elsewhere says that we "uphold the law" (Romans 3:31). He means the Law as a boundary that kept Gentiles out. In Christ, entering God's people no longer depends on it. Compare Matthew 5:17.
and might reconcile both groups to God in one body through the cross, thus putting to death that hostility through it.
Those who killed Jesus thought that they were ending something. Paul says that what was put to death on the Cross was hostility itself. "One body" may mean his crucified body and also the Church.
So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
The readers of this letter had no claim on Israel's God. Now they are at home. So are we, far from Jerusalem, on the coasts of India.
built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone.
The Church rests on people who actually knew him, and the Catechism builds its teaching on the apostolic Church on this verse (CCC 857). For us, one of those stones has a name: Thomas.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes this passage directly when it speaks of the Jewish people: by his Cross Christ our peace reconciled Jews and Gentiles, making both one in himself (Nostra Aetate 4). The Church does not replace the root of the olive tree, but is fed by it (Romans 11:17–18). The Catechism says that earthly peace is the image and fruit of the peace of Christ, who by the blood of his Cross killed the hostility in his own person (CCC 2305), and it describes the Church as the building of God, resting on Christ the cornerstone (CCC 756).

r.h: I am the way
set: It is the night of the Last Supper. Jesus has washed the disciples' feet (13:1–20). Judas has gone out: "And it was night" (13:30). Jesus has said that he is going where they cannot follow (13:33), and that Peter will deny him (13:38). Into that fear he speaks these words. They are the start of the long farewell discourses (John 14–17).

Thomas is one of the few disciples who come alive in this Gospel. He is the one who said, "Let us also go, that we may die with him" (11:16), and later the one who will say, "My Lord and my God!" (20:28). Here he is the honest man who says that he does not understand.
str: v. 1: do not be troubled; believe.
vv. 2–3: the Father's house and the promise to come back.
v. 4: "you know the way".
v. 5: Thomas's objection.
v. 6: the answer.
kw: A strong word, for being shaken and stirred up. John has used the same verb for Jesus himself, at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33), in his hour (12:27), and just before this at the supper (13:21). He is not speaking from a safe distance. He knows what it is to be troubled.

From the verb menein, to remain, one of John's favourite words. These are places to remain, and the only other use in the New Testament is in this chapter: the Father and the Son will make their home with the one who loves (14:23). Older translations say "mansions", following the Latin.
Jesus does not only show a way; he says that he is the way. In Acts, the first Christians were themselves called "the Way" (Acts 9:2).
vv: Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me.
The Greek form of "believe" can be read as a statement or as a command. Either way, faith in Jesus is set right next to faith in God, which no mere teacher could ask.
In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.
"My Father's house" was the Temple in 2:16. Now it means the Father's own presence, and there is room in it. On the night he is betrayed, what Jesus has in mind is the place he is going to prepare.
I will come again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, there you may be also.
Heaven is described here in terms of a person: being where he is.
Thomas said to him, “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?”

We should be grateful for this question, since the greatest answer in the Gospel was given to it. The man who asks it is the Apostle who, according to our tradition, walked the farthest way of all, to India.
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.

Three words, and one "I". The way leads to the Father, and he is also the truth about the Father and the life of the Father. This is said by a man hours away from the Cross, and it is the Cross that makes him the way.
ch: The Catechism teaches that human beings, left to their own powers, have no access to the Father's house, and that only Christ can open it (CCC 661), and it presents him as the way and the model of holiness (CCC 459). St Augustine puts it this way: Christ as God is the homeland to which we are going, and Christ as man is the way by which we go (in substance; Sermon 123). The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse in Nostra Aetate 2, in the same place where it says that the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions.

qa: What is the Miraculous Cross at Mylapore?

It is a carved stone cross with an inscription in Pahlavi, the Persian language of the first Christian millennium, found on St Thomas Mount near Chennai in the sixteenth century and venerated there. Scholars date it long after the Apostle, and they have read its inscription in more than one way. It is a witness to very old links between the Christians of India and the Church of Persia. Tradition records that it showed miraculous signs during the Eucharist. Reports like these do not belong to the deposit of faith (compare CCC 67), and no one is bound to accept them. The faith of the St Thomas Christians in the Cross as a sign of victory stands whether one does or not.
When Peter says "whom you crucified", is he blaming the Jewish people?

No. Peter is a Jew speaking to fellow Jews, about the events of those weeks in that city, and he is calling them to repentance. The next verses show three thousand of them baptized (Acts 2:37–41). The Church teaches that the Passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living, nor against Jews today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597), and that sinners, all of us, were the authors of Christ's sufferings (CCC 598).
"No one comes to the Father except through me." Does this mean that non-Christians cannot be saved?

All salvation comes through Christ; the Church does not soften that. But she also teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel and yet seek God with a sincere heart can be saved, by the grace of Christ, even if they do not know that it is his (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 846–848). The verse says who the way is. It does not say that those who have not heard of him are beyond his reach.
rite: The St Thomas Christians have long honoured the Cross, and many Syro-Malabar churches display a cross without a corpus, of the kind known from the stone crosses at St Thomas Mount and in Kerala, for instance at Kottayam. It is called the Mar Thoma Sliva, and it proclaims the Cross as the sign of victory and life. The readings of today say the same. The struck rock gives water, the crucified one is Lord, the Cross makes peace, and the way to the Father runs through it. The Holy Qurbana makes present the sacrifice of the Cross, and from the altar, as from the rock, flows the living water of grace.
study: At Rephidim the people asked, "Is the Lord among us or not?" (Exodus 17:7). When have I asked this, and where did the water come from?
Peter denied the Lord, and then spoke with boldness in the same city. What has changed in me since I first believed?
"He is our peace" (Ephesians 2:14). What wall in my family, my parish or my town needs to be brought to the Cross?
Thomas said honestly that he did not know the way. What is the honest question I need to bring to Jesus today?

lead: Both readings ask where the Gospel comes from. Paul says that his Gospel did not come from any human being, but from a revelation of God's Son. John's Gospel says that the one who comes from above speaks what he has seen and heard. Our faith, then, is not a human invention. It is an answer to someone who has come to us from God.

r.h: He was pleased to reveal his Son
set: Others had apparently been saying that Paul had his Gospel second-hand and had trimmed it to please Gentiles. To answer them he tells his own story, one of the fullest he gives us in his letters. Paul is a Jew and is proud of it (compare Philippians 3:5). He does not present what happened as leaving a bad religion. He describes it as a prophet's call, by the God he had always served.
str: vv. 11–12: the thesis: the Gospel came through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
vv. 13–14: his earlier life: persecutor and zealot.
vv. 15–16: God's call.
v. 17: he goes to Arabia, not to Jerusalem.
kw: An unveiling. In v. 12 it is the same word that gives its name to the Book of Revelation. Paul does not mean that he reasoned his way to Christ. Christ was shown to him.
The word recalls Phinehas and Elijah, men zealous for God. Paul's persecution did not come from a lack of faith. It came from sincere zeal, and this should make us careful about our own.
The Greek of v. 16 is literally "in me", which NRSV renders "to me". The revelation was given to Paul, but it was also a change within him. Christ was to be shown through his whole life.
vv: for I did not receive it from a human source, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
This is not a denial that Paul learned from the Church; see the question below. He means that his certainty that the crucified Jesus is the Son of God came from God.
I was violently persecuting the church of God and was trying to destroy it.
Paul never forgets this (1 Corinthians 15:9). The honesty about his past is part of his preaching, because it shows what grace can do.
But when God, who had set me apart before I was born and called me through his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles,
The words come from the call of the prophets: Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1. The whole sentence has God as its subject. Paul does the persecuting, but God does the calling.
but I went away at once into Arabia, and afterwards I returned to Damascus.
"Arabia" here probably means the Nabataean kingdom, east and south of Damascus. Paul does not say what he did there, and we should not claim to know.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses to show that Paul's vision on the road to Damascus was a revelation of Jesus as the Son of God, and that this became the heart of his preaching (CCC 442). Pope Benedict XVI, in his catechesis on St Paul, said that the change in him was not the fruit of a process of thinking or moral growth, but came from outside, from meeting Christ (in substance; General Audience, 3 September 2008).

r.h: From above
set: This passage follows John the Baptist's last witness in this Gospel: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (3:30). Commentators differ on whether vv. 31–36 are still the Baptist speaking or the evangelist reflecting on what has been said. The themes are those of the talk with Nicodemus earlier in the chapter: above and below, witness and believing, life and judgment.
str: v. 31: the one from above and the one from the earth.
vv. 32–33: his testimony, refused and accepted.
vv. 34–35: the Son, the Spirit and the Father.
v. 36: the choice.
kw: The same word Jesus uses to Nicodemus: "born from above" (3:3). No one can rise by his own effort to where Jesus comes from. He has to come down, and we have to be born from there.
Literally, has set his seal on. In the ancient world a seal made a document binding. Whoever believes puts his own seal to the statement that God tells the truth.

The picture is of something not measured out in a small jar. The Greek of v. 34 does not state the subject outright, so it may be read as God giving the Spirit to the Son (so the Malayalam POC, and CCC 504), or as the Son giving the Spirit to believers (NRSV leaves it open with "he"). Both are true.
vv: The one who comes from above is above all; the one who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks about earthly things.
This is said with no contempt for John. He himself pointed the way. Every other teacher speaks from below, and only this one speaks of what he has seen.
Whoever has accepted his testimony has certified this, that God is true.
Faith is more than an opinion about Jesus. It is a personal act, a trust that stakes itself on God's truthfulness.
The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands.
In the middle of warnings, here is the deepest thing in the passage: the love between Father and Son. What the world is offered in Christ comes out of that love.
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever disobeys the Son will not see life, but must endure God’s wrath.

The verb is in the present: "has" eternal life, already. In John, believing and obeying go together, because the opposite of believing here is disobeying. The verse speaks of the choice that lies before each person, and it is not a verdict on anyone.
ch: The Catechism says that from his conception Christ's humanity was filled with the Holy Spirit, for God gives the Spirit without measure (CCC 504). St Augustine, preaching on this verse, says that the Spirit is given to each member of the Church in a measure, one gift to one and another to another, but that the Son does not receive by measure (in substance; Tractates on John 14). The Church also teaches that believing in Christ is necessary for salvation (CCC 161), and that God's grace can reach those who through no fault of their own do not know him (CCC 847).

qa: If Paul learned nothing from anyone, why does he say that he "received" the faith from others?

Both are true. In 1 Corinthians 15:3 he says he handed on "what I in turn had received", and in 1 Corinthians 11:23 he hands on the Lord's Supper. He was baptized by Ananias (Acts 9:18), and he later went to see Peter (Galatians 1:18). What Paul says in Galatians is that no human being convinced him that Jesus is the Son of God. The content of the Church's tradition he received, and he guarded it faithfully.
study: Paul's zeal once led him to violence. How can I tell the difference between zeal for God and my own anger?
"Has certified this, that God is true." Where in my life this week am I being asked to stake something on God's truthfulness?

lead: On the last Sunday before the feast of the Lord's birth, the season of the Annunciation comes to its final announcement, to St Joseph. The four readings show God at work in families and in marriages, and they all ask how a person recognizes God's will and says yes to it. Rebekah's family says, "The thing comes from the Lord", and she says, "I will". Hannah pours out her soul in silence and goes away at peace. Paul tells the Ephesians to find out what pleases the Lord. Joseph wakes from a dream and takes Mary home. In each case God's plan comes into an ordinary home by way of someone's quiet consent. The key words are discerning, consenting and receiving.

r.h: “I will”
set: This is the end of the longest chapter in Genesis. Abraham is old, and Sarah has died (Genesis 23). So that the promise may continue, Abraham sends his senior servant back to his homeland to find a wife for Isaac among his own kin. At the well the servant prays for a sign, and Rebekah gives water to him and to his camels (24:12–20). When he has told this to the family, today's reading begins.

Gifts from the groom's side and a long send-off were the normal custom. It is less expected that her family should ask the young woman herself. The veil in v. 65 belongs to the custom of a bride coming to her husband.
str: vv. 50–51: Laban and Bethuel recognize the Lord's hand.
vv. 52–54: the servant worships; gifts and a meal.
vv. 55–58: the family asks for a delay; Rebekah is asked, and she answers.
vv. 59–61: blessing and departure.
vv. 62–67: Isaac and Rebekah meet; she comes into Sarah's tent.
kw: the thing comes from the Lord
A phrase of plain faith from a family that does not know Abraham's God as Abraham does. They recognize that this cannot be argued with. Discernment here means reading the events.
One word in Hebrew. Abraham once left his homeland at God's word (12:1, 4). Rebekah now does the same, with the same verb, and so she becomes a true partner in the promise.

A rare Hebrew word, and its meaning is not certain. NRSV has "to walk"; the Latin Vulgate has "to meditate", and the Malayalam POC also says that Isaac was deep in thought. Christian and Jewish readers have often seen Isaac at prayer here, in the evening.
vv: The thing comes from the Lord; we cannot speak to you anything bad or good.
"Anything bad or good" is an idiom: we have nothing to add. When God has clearly spoken, even a careful family steps back.
And they called Rebekah, and said to her, “Will you go with this man?” She said, “I will.”

She is going hundreds of miles to marry a man she has never seen. The whole chapter has been about God's guidance, but it pauses here for a young woman's own word. God's plan does not go around human consent; it waits for it.
Isaac went out in the evening to walk in the field; and looking up, he saw camels coming.
The two look up at the same moment (vv. 63–64). The servant's long journey and Isaac's quiet evening meet in a single scene.
Then Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah’s tent. He took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.

This is the first time the Bible says that a man loved his wife. Love comes here after the marriage, and it does not depend on a first romance. It is the love that brings comfort after grief. The tent of Sarah, empty since chapter 23, has a mother in it again.
ch: The Fathers often read this chapter as a figure: Isaac for Christ, Rebekah for the Church or the soul, the well for the word of God. Origen preaches on Rebekah at the well in his homilies on Genesis, and St Ambrose wrote a whole book, On Isaac, or the Soul (both in substance). The Catechism teaches that the exchange of consent is the indispensable element that makes a marriage (CCC 1626). Rebekah's "I will" is not yet the sacrament, but it does show God's respect for a person's own word.

r.h: Pouring out her soul
set: This is the time of the Judges, before there was a king. Israel's central sanctuary, with the ark, is at Shiloh, and its priests are not doing well (2:12–17). The nation needs a new beginning, and the story opens not with a battle but with a childless woman. In this she stands with Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Samson's mother. Each time God's new work starts in a place where human hope has run out.
Having two wives was permitted in that society, but the Bible shows what it did. Peninnah has children and Hannah has none, and the wound is reopened every year at the feast.
str: vv. 1–3: Elkanah's family and its yearly pilgrimage.
vv. 4–8: the portions, the rival, Hannah's tears, and her husband's kind but limited comfort.
vv. 9–11: Hannah's prayer and vow.
vv. 12–16: Eli thinks she is drunk; her answer.
vv. 17–18: Eli's blessing; Hannah's peace.
kw: This title appears here for the first time in the Bible (v. 3), and Hannah is the first person in Scripture we hear address God by it (v. 11). The least powerful person in the story calls on the God of all armies.
Hannah's name comes from this word. It means grace, favour. Her last words in the reading are that she may "find favor" (v. 18). The woman called Grace goes away having found it.
I have been pouring out my soul
