The Hebrew nepeš is the whole living self. She has not said a formal prayer. She has emptied herself out before God, like water (compare Psalm 62:8).
vv: Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart sad? Am I not more to you than ten sons?

Elkanah truly loves her, and he cannot reach her. A note on the text: v. 5 is obscure in Hebrew. NRSV says that he gave her "a double portion", and POC says only one portion. Either way the wound remains.
She made this vow: “O Lord of hosts, if only you will look on the misery of your servant, and remember me, and not forget your servant,

Three times she calls herself "your servant". NRSV's next words about a nazirite follow other ancient witnesses; the traditional Hebrew text, which POC is closer to, says that she will give him to the Lord all his life, and that no razor will touch his head. What she asks for she will give back. She prays for a child, and at the same moment she lets him go.
Hannah was praying silently; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard; therefore Eli thought she was drunk.
In her time people usually prayed aloud. The official priest of the sanctuary misjudges the most real prayer offered there that day. It is a comfort to anyone whose prayer has been misunderstood.
I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have been pouring out my soul before the Lord.
She corrects the priest respectfully and without bitterness. This is how a person of faith speaks to authority when it is wrong.
Then the woman went to her quarters, ate and drank with her husband, and her countenance was sad no longer.
Nothing has changed yet; she is not pregnant. Only her prayer has been handed over. This is the peace of having truly left something with God.
ch: The Catechism names Hannah among the holy women of the Old Covenant whose mission prepared for that of Mary (CCC 489). Her song (1 Samuel 2:1–10) lies behind the Magnificat, and Mary's words about God looking on the lowliness of his servant (Luke 1:48) echo Hannah's. St Cyprian holds her up as a model of prayer, praying not with loud demands but quietly from the heart (in substance; On the Lord's Prayer 5). Jewish teachers too learned rules of prayer from her (Talmud, Berakhot 31a).

r.h: Find out what is pleasing to the Lord
set: In the second half of Ephesians, Paul moves from what God has done to how the Church should live. Chapters 4–5 use the verb "walk" again and again (NRSV often says "live"). Today's passage comes between the call to imitate God (5:1) and the teaching on Christian households (5:21–6:9). The readers live in a pagan world, and Christian life was visibly different from what went on around them.
str: vv. 5–7: a warning: some ways of life have no inheritance in the kingdom.
vv. 8–14: once darkness, now light. Live as children of light and find out what pleases the Lord.
vv. 15–17: live wisely; understand the will of the Lord.
vv. 18–21: be filled with the Spirit: song, thanksgiving, and mutual submission.
kw: The word used for testing metal to see if it is genuine (v. 10). Discerning God's will is not a matter of waiting for a voice. It is a daily, careful testing of what is good, by people who have been changed.
Literally, someone who wants to have more. Paul calls such a person an idolater (v. 5), because what we always want more of has become our god. Compare Colossians 3:5.
making the most of the time
Literally, buying up the time, as a merchant buys up something valuable while it is on the market. Kairos means the opportune moment, and not simply the time on the clock.
A command in the present tense: keep on being filled. The verb is passive, because it is the Spirit who does the filling. Paul sets it against being filled with wine (v. 18).
vv: For once you were darkness, but now in the Lord you are light. Live as children of light
Paul does not say that they were in the dark but that they were darkness, and that they are now light. The change goes all the way through, and behaviour must catch up with what has already happened.
Try to find out what is pleasing to the Lord.
This verse gives the Sunday its theme. Rebekah's family, Hannah and Joseph were all doing just this, in very different ways.
Sleeper, awake! Rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.

This is probably a line from an early Christian hymn, and many think that it was sung at baptism. St Clement of Alexandria preserves what seems to be more of it (in substance; Exhortation to the Greeks 9).
making the most of the time, because the days are evil.
Paul has no illusions about the world. He does not advise escape from evil days, but good use of them.
Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ.
This verse closes today's reading and opens the teaching on the household that follows. Before anything is said to wives, husbands, children or slaves, all are told to be subject to one another.
ch: The Catechism says that the baptized, enlightened by Christ, are to walk as "children of light" (CCC 1695), and that Baptism is called enlightenment (CCC 1216). It quotes v. 19 on the place of song in the Church's worship (CCC 1156), and it sees greed for money as a form of idolatry (CCC 2113). The Holy Qurbana is where this passage is lived in the most concentrated way: the Church sings to the Lord in the Spirit and gives thanks to the Father in the name of Jesus (v. 20).

r.h: He took her as his wife
set: Matthew has just given the genealogy of Jesus, from Abraham to "Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born" (1:16). The Greek of "of whom" is feminine: Jesus was born of Mary, not of Joseph. So the genealogy leaves a question, and these verses answer it: how does Jesus belong to the line of David? Through Joseph, who receives him and gives him his name.

Among Jews of that time, a betrothal was more than our engagement. It was legally binding; the couple were already called husband and wife, and it could be ended only by divorce. The bride usually stayed with her family for some time before moving to her husband's home. A pregnancy in that interval raised a serious question under the Law (Deuteronomy 22:23–24).
str: v. 18: the situation: Mary is with child from the Holy Spirit.
v. 19: Joseph's decision.
vv. 20–21: the angel's message in a dream.
vv. 22–23: the first of Matthew's fulfilment quotations (Isaiah 7:14).
v. 24: Joseph wakes and obeys.
kw: In the Bible, a just man is one who lives by the Law and the will of God. In Joseph's case, justice and mercy turn out to be one: he will not ignore what seems to be a breach of the Law, and he will not shame her either.
The word for ending a betrothal or marriage (compare Matthew 5:31–32). Joseph looks for the quiet way, without bringing Mary's case before a public court (deigmatisai, to expose to public disgrace).

The Hebrew name means "the Lord saves". It is the name of Joshua, and in Syriac it is Īšō‘, from which our own Malayalam name Eesho comes. The angel gives the meaning: "he will save his people from their sins".
Matthew's Gospel begins with this name and ends with its promise: "I am with you always" (28:20). God-with-us is the frame of the whole Gospel.
vv: she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit.
Matthew tells the reader at once what Joseph does not yet know, so we may watch him struggle with sympathy. Mary says nothing in this story.
Her husband Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her to public disgrace, planned to dismiss her quietly.
Before any angel speaks, Joseph has already chosen mercy, in the dark. He does not know the whole truth, and he acts on what he knows in the kindest way the Law allows.
Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for the child conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.

"Son of David" is the key title, used in this Gospel only of Jesus and Joseph. Joseph is told who he is and what he must do. "Do not be afraid" is what God's messengers say all through this season (Luke 1:13, 30; 2:10).
She will bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.

Giving the name is a father's right. By naming the child, Joseph takes him legally into his own family, and so into the house of David. The kind of salvation is also defined: from sins, and not only from Rome.
“Look, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall name him Emmanuel,” which means, “God is with us.”
Matthew quotes Isaiah 7:14 in the Greek. See the question below.
When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him; he took her as his wife,
Joseph says nothing in the whole of the Gospels. His reply is this sentence. He does just what he was told, at the cost of whatever people would say.
ch: St John Chrysostom admires Joseph's gentleness and self-control, in not wishing to shame Mary even before he understood the mystery (in substance; Homilies on Matthew 4). St Jerome says that Joseph, knowing Mary's purity and astonished at what had happened, covered with silence a mystery he did not yet understand (in substance; Commentary on Matthew). The Catechism teaches that God called Joseph so that Jesus should be born into the messianic line of David (CCC 437), and that the angel's words announce both the virginal conception (CCC 497) and God's mercy to sinners (CCC 1846). St John Paul II calls Joseph's response an obedience of faith, parallel to Mary's (Redemptoris Custos 3–4), and Pope Francis has written of him as an accepting, courageous father in the shadows (Patris Corde, 2020).

qa: Did Joseph suspect Mary of sin?

The text does not say what he thought, and the Fathers read it in different ways. Some take it that he saw the facts and could not explain them. Others, like St Jerome, think that he knew her virtue too well to accuse her and stepped back in reverence before something he did not understand. Either way, the Gospel praises him: he would not shame her. He should be our model when we hear something about another person that we cannot explain.
Isaiah says "young woman" in Hebrew. Does Matthew misquote him?

The Hebrew ‘almâ of Isaiah 7:14 means a young woman of marriageable age. The Greek Old Testament, made by Jews before the time of Christ, translated it parthenos, "virgin", and Matthew quotes that. The Church, reading the prophecy in the light of what God did, sees here the virginal conception of Jesus (CCC 497). The following verse (1:25) says that Joseph had no relations with her "until" she bore a son. As St Jerome argued, the word "until" says nothing about what came after, and the Church confesses Mary's perpetual virginity (CCC 499).
If Joseph is not the natural father, how is Jesus a son of David?

In the Jewish understanding, a man who accepted a child and named him was that child's legal father, with all that this gave the child. This is why Matthew traces the line through Joseph, and why the angel addresses him as "son of David". Jesus truly belongs to David's house by Joseph's obedience (CCC 437).
rite: Our Annunciation season has moved through the announcements of salvation: to Zechariah, to Mary, the birth of John, and now to Joseph. The Twenty-Five Day Fast is nearly over, and this Sunday asks whether there is room in our house for the one who is coming. Joseph received Mary and the child into his home; at the Holy Qurbana we receive Christ, not into a house but into ourselves. St Ephrem the Syrian, in his Hymns on the Nativity, has Joseph marvel at the child he carries (in substance). In families getting ready for the feast, Joseph's quiet yes may be the most useful example we have: wake up, do what the Lord commands, and take him home.
study: Rebekah said, "I will", to something she could not see. What does God seem to be asking me to go towards, without seeing the end?
Hannah prayed in a way the priest misunderstood. Have I learned to pour out my soul before the Lord, and do I judge others' prayer too quickly?
Ephesians 5:10 tells us to test what pleases the Lord. What helps our family discern God's will in practical matters?
Joseph chose mercy before any angel spoke. To whom do I need to show mercy, even though I do not yet understand the whole story?

lead: With four days to go before the feast of the Lord's birth, the readings set two things side by side: a prisoner asking his friends to pray for him, and one of the highest statements in all of Scripture about who is coming. The Word who was with God from the beginning is the one the Church now waits to welcome in a manger. And so she prays, at all times.

r.h: Pray at all times
set: These verses come straight after the armour of God (6:10–17): the belt of truth, the shield of faith, the sword of the Spirit. Grammatically v. 18 still belongs to that sentence. Prayer is not one more piece of the armour. It is how the soldier stays awake inside it.
str: v. 18: pray always, in the Spirit, for all the saints.
vv. 19–20: pray also for me, that I may speak boldly.
kw: Literally, staying awake, losing sleep. It is the word for a watchman on duty through the night. The word "all" sounds four times in the Greek of v. 18: every prayer, all times, all perseverance, all the saints.
The right of a citizen to speak openly in the assembly. It appears in v. 19, and the related verb in v. 20. Even Paul asks for this; it is not something he assumes he has.
I am an ambassador in chains
An ambassador was protected and honoured, so this is a striking picture. His captors have put the envoy of the King of kings in chains, and he goes on with his embassy.
vv: Pray in the Spirit at all times in every prayer and supplication.
Praying in the Spirit means letting the Spirit pray in us (see Romans 8:26). Paul asks for a whole life held in prayer, not a life without other work.
Pray also for me, so that when I speak, a message may be given to me to make known with boldness the mystery of the gospel,
The great Apostle does not ask for release from prison. He asks for the right word at the right moment. Those who preach and teach need this prayer from their people.
Pray that I may declare it boldly, as I must speak.
"As I must": the Gospel is a duty laid on him. Compare 1 Corinthians 9:16.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it teaches that we must pray constantly and that this is possible, because prayer and Christian life are one (CCC 2742, 2745). It describes prayer for others as a sharing in the prayer of Jesus, and it recalls that the first Christian communities lived this form of prayer intensely (CCC 2634–2636).

r.h: In the beginning was the Word
set: The Gospel of John opens with its famous Prologue (1:1–18), which many scholars think has the form of a hymn. Matthew begins Jesus' story with Abraham, and Luke with Zechariah in the Temple. John goes back before all of them, to the first words of the Bible: "In the beginning" (Genesis 1:1).
str: vv. 1–2: the Word with God, and the Word as God.
v. 3: all things through him.
vv. 4–5: life and light; the darkness does not overcome it.
kw: Greek readers would hear in it reason, the order of the world. Jewish readers would hear the word by which God created (Genesis 1; Psalm 33:6) and the Wisdom who was with him (Proverbs 8:22–31). John gathers all this up and then says what no one had yet said: this Word became flesh (1:14).
pros ton theon / theos ēn ho logos
with God / the Word was God

The two phrases must be kept together. "With God" means that the Word is distinct from the Father. "Was God" means that he is truly divine. Without the article, theos here says what the Word is, and it does not lessen his divinity. Here we meet the seed of the Church's faith in the Trinity.
The Greek verb can mean both to overcome and to grasp, to understand. Both meanings fit the Gospel: the darkness has not put out the light, and it has not understood it either.
vv: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The verb "was" in Greek describes a state that continues. At the beginning, the Word already was. He does not begin to exist; he is there when everything else begins.
All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being.

Nothing lies outside his reach, which is why nothing created is evil in itself. A note on the text: the earliest manuscripts have no punctuation. NRSV takes the end of v. 3 with v. 4, as many early writers did, while the Malayalam POC ends the sentence at v. 3.
What has come into being in him was life, and the life was the light of all people.
This light is for "all people", and not for one people alone.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.
"Shines" is in the present tense. The verse is not only about the past. On the darkest day of our own lives, it is still true.
ch: The Council of Nicaea (325) confessed, against Arius, that the Son is true God, of one being with the Father, and that all things were made through him (CCC 242, 465). The Catechism teaches that God created everything by his eternal Word (CCC 291). St Augustine says in his Confessions that he found something like "In the beginning was the Word" in the books of the Platonists, but that he did not find there that the Word became flesh (in substance; Confessions 7.9). That is exactly what the Church is about to celebrate.

qa: If the Word is God and is also with God, are there two Gods?

No. The Church confesses one God in three Persons. John holds together that the Word is distinct from the Father and that he is truly God. The Father and the Son are one in being (John 10:30), and they are distinct as Persons (CCC 253–254).
study: Paul asks for prayer, not for release. Who in my parish, perhaps my priest or my catechist, needs me to pray that they may speak boldly?
The light still shines in the darkness (John 1:5). Which darkness in my family or my town do I most want the Lord's birth to reach?

lead: Three days before Christmas, both readings ask how the Son came and what his coming does to us. Paul says it in one sentence: God sent his Son, born of a woman, so that we might be adopted. John says it with an image: the true light came into the world, and those who received him became children of God. The two readings arrive at the same word: children.

r.h: Born of a woman, so that we might be children
set: Paul writes to Gentile Christians in Galatia who are being urged by other teachers to take on circumcision and the whole Mosaic law. He has just told them that all who belong to Christ are “Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise” (3:29). Now he explains what an heir is, with a picture from family law that everyone in his world understood.
str: vv. 1–2: the young heir owns everything, yet lives under guardians until the date his father has set.
v. 3: so were we, under “the elemental spirits of the world”.
vv. 4–5: the date arrives: God sends his Son.
vv. 6–7: God sends the Spirit of his Son, and the slave becomes a child and an heir.
kw: Time is pictured as a vessel that God fills to the brim. The coming of the Son is not an accident of history but the date the Father set (4:2).
A legal word from the Greek and Roman world: an adopted son had the full rights of a son. Christ is Son by nature; we become children by grace, through him.
An Aramaic word for father, kept untranslated by the Greek-speaking Church. Jesus prays with it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and Paul uses it again in Romans 8:15.
vv: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law,

“Sent” means that the Son was already with the Father before he was born. “Born of a woman” means that he is truly one of us. This is the only mention of Jesus’ mother in Paul’s letters, and she stands at the centre of the great turning point of time. “Born under the law” means that he lived as a son of Israel.
in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as children.
He takes our condition so that we may receive his. The word “redeem” recalls the price paid to release a slave.
God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!”
God sends twice: the Son, then the Spirit of the Son. It is the Spirit who cries “Abba” within us. Christian prayer is the voice of the Son in us, speaking to his Father.
ch: The Catechism quotes Galatians 4:4–5 as the heart of the Good News: God has visited his people (CCC 422). Vatican II opens its teaching on Our Lady with this very verse (Lumen Gentium 52). The Catechism sees in this passage the joint mission of the Son and the Spirit (CCC 689), and it recalls the teaching of the Fathers, St Irenaeus among them, that the Son of God became the son of man so that we might become children of God (CCC 460).

r.h: He came to witness to the light
set: The reading comes from the Prologue of John’s Gospel (1:1–18). The great poem about the Word has just said that “the light shines in the darkness” (1:5). Then, without warning, it turns to a man with a name and a task. The fourth Gospel never calls him “the Baptist”. For this Gospel his whole identity is to be a witness.
str: vv. 6–8: John is sent as a witness; he is not the light.
v. 9: the true light was coming into the world.
vv. 10–11: the world and his own people do not receive him.
vv. 12–13: those who receive him are born of God.
kw: A word from the law court, and a favourite of this Gospel. A witness speaks of what he knows and points away from himself. The later word “martyr” comes from this root.
“True” here means real and final. Every other light is a lamp lit from this one. Jesus later calls John “a burning and shining lamp” (5:35).
Those who receive him are given the right and the authority to become God’s children. It is a gift, not an achievement.
vv: He himself was not the light, but he came to testify to the light.
The whole of John’s greatness lies in that “not”. He later says, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30).
He came to what was his own, and his own people did not accept him.
The Word came to the world he made and to the people he had prepared. The verse describes the sadness of every refusal, not the guilt of one nation: see the question below.
But to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave power to become children of God, who were born, not of blood or of the will of the flesh or of the will of man, but of God.

A note on the text. Almost all Greek manuscripts have the plural, “who were born”, meaning believers. A few early Latin witnesses, with St Irenaeus and Tertullian, have the singular, “who was born”, meaning Christ, and some modern versions have followed it. The plural is the accepted reading; the Virgin birth stands on Matthew and Luke, not on this verse.
ch: St Augustine loved the contrast between John and Jesus: John is the voice, Christ is the Word; the voice passes and the Word remains (Sermon 293, in substance). The Catechism uses John 1:12–13 when it teaches that to become children of God we must be “born from above” (CCC 526).

qa: Who are “his own people”? Does John blame the Jews?

No. Mary, Joseph, the shepherds, John himself and all the apostles were Jews, and they received him. The verse speaks of the human refusal that the world as a whole shares (1:10). The Church teaches that the Jewish people as such are not to be blamed for the rejection and death of Christ (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598).
rite: Abba is an Aramaic word, and Syriac, the language of our liturgical heritage, is a form of Aramaic. When the Syro-Malabar Church calls God “Father”, she stands very close to the speech in which Jesus himself first said it.
study: Paul says that I am “no longer a slave but a child”. What in my prayer still sounds like a slave speaking to a master?
John the witness points away from himself. In my family or parish, whom do my words and actions point towards?

lead: The official readings for this day are still awaited from the 2026–27 calendar, so this study takes the verse given for the day: Isaiah 9:6. Two days before Christmas it is a good verse to stay with. Isaiah announces a birth and gives the child four names, and each name says something about what God intends to do through him.

r.h: Four names for one child
set: Isaiah speaks in a dark time for his people. In about 733–732 BC the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III took Galilee and the land of Naphtali from the northern kingdom (2 Kings 15:29), the very region named at the start of this oracle (9:1). Into that darkness comes a song of light and of broken yokes (9:2–5), and its reason is a birth in the house of David.

In the Hebrew Bible this verse is numbered 9:5. Many scholars hear in it the language of a Davidic king’s birth or enthronement, when a new king received solemn titles. Its first hearers looked for a good king. The Church sees that its words reach further than any king of Judah.
str: “A child has been born for us”: the event, spoken of as already done.
“Authority rests upon his shoulders”: the rule he will carry.
Four double names: Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.

¶ The next verse completes the thought: his authority and peace will have no end, on David’s throne, and “the zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this” (9:7). The whole promise rests on God’s own passion, not on human skill.
kw: Pele’ is the word for a wonder that only God works. A counselor is one who plans and guides. This king’s wisdom is not ordinary statecraft. The Greek Old Testament renders the title “Angel of great counsel”.
The same phrase is used of the Lord himself in the next chapter (Isaiah 10:21). It is the name that most clearly goes beyond the language of an ordinary king.
Šālôm is more than the absence of war: wholeness and things set right. Śar is a ruler or commander. His command is peace.
vv: For a child has been born for us, a son given to us;
“For us”, twice. He is not born for himself. The verbs are in the past tense, as the prophets often speak of what God has already decided. The Church hears this verse at Christmas as now fulfilled.
authority rests upon his shoulders;

The rod of the oppressor had lain across the people’s shoulders (9:4). Now the burden of rule lies on one shoulder instead, and it is his. Christian readers have long thought also of the wood of the Cross carried on those shoulders.
and he is named Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
A name in the Bible says what a person is for. Together these names promise wisdom, strength, lasting care and peace, the four things a people in darkness most needs.
ch: Gabriel’s words to Mary echo the next verse of this oracle: God will give him “the throne of his ancestor David” and “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33). Paul says of Christ, “he is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). The Catechism teaches that earthly peace is the image and fruit of the peace of Christ, the messianic “Prince of Peace” (CCC 2305).

qa: How can the Son be called “Everlasting Father”?

The title does not confuse the Son with the Father. The Father and the Son are distinct Persons (CCC 254). The Hebrew ’ăbî‘ad means “father for ever”: a king who cares for his people as a father does, without end. It speaks of his care for us, not of his place within the Trinity.
study: Which of the four names do I most need this Christmas, and why?
The child is born “for us”. Who around me needs to hear that this is also for them?

lead: The official readings for this day are still awaited from the 2026–27 calendar, so this study takes the verse given for the day: Micah 5:2. On the eve of Christmas the Church looks at a small town. Micah promises that Israel’s ruler will come from a place nobody would choose, and yet that his origin is older than the town itself.

r.h: The little town and the ancient origin
set: Micah came from Moresheth, a village in the Judean foothills (1:1), and he prophesied in the same years as Isaiah, in the late eighth century BC, when Assyria threatened Judah. The verse just before this one shows Jerusalem under siege and its ruler struck on the cheek (5:1). Micah turns away from the humiliated capital to the country town where David’s family began.
David was the son of “an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah” (1 Samuel 17:12). In the Hebrew Bible this verse is numbered 5:1.
str: “But you, O Bethlehem of Ephrathah”: God addresses the town directly.
“one of the little clans of Judah”: its smallness.
“from you shall come forth for me”: God’s own choice of a ruler.
“whose origin is from of old”: the mystery of where he really comes from.
kw: This is the usual understanding of the name, and Christian preachers have loved it. Ephrathah is the name of the clan and district to which Bethlehem belonged (Ruth 4:11).
Literally “the thousands of Judah”, the units into which a tribe was divided. Bethlehem hardly counts among them.
It comes from the same root as “shall come forth” earlier in the verse. He comes forth from Bethlehem, and yet his comings forth reach back “from ancient days”.
vv: But you, O Bethlehem of Ephrathah, who are one of the little clans of Judah,

God’s habit is to begin small. David was the youngest son, left out with the sheep (1 Samuel 16:11). When Matthew quotes the verse he turns it around: “by no means least” (Matthew 2:6), because the birth of the Child has changed the town’s rank for ever.
from you shall come forth for me one who is to rule in Israel,
“For me”: the ruler belongs to God before he belongs to the people. In 5:4 his rule is described as a shepherd’s: he “shall stand and feed his flock”.
whose origin is from of old, from ancient days.

In its first setting this points to the ancient roots of David’s house. Many Fathers heard more in it, a hint of the Son’s eternal origin. Both are true of Jesus: he is a son of David, and he is “from the beginning” with God (John 1:1–2).
ch: The chief priests and scribes quote this verse to Herod when the Magi ask where the Messiah is to be born (Matthew 2:4–6; compare John 7:42). The Catechism says that the coming of God’s Son is an event of such immensity that God willed to prepare for it over centuries (CCC 522). St Gregory the Great, preaching on Christmas, draws the lesson from the name: the One who says “I am the living bread” is rightly born in the “house of bread”, and is laid in a manger to feed the faithful (Homily 8 on the Gospels, in substance).

rite: For the Syro-Malabar faithful tonight ends the 25 Days’ Fast, and the parish gathers for the Christmas night Holy Qurbana. The fast and the feast belong together: we have kept hungry for the Bread that comes from the house of bread.
study: God chose a town that hardly counted. What in my life or my parish do I dismiss as too small for God to use?
How can I keep a few minutes of silence tonight before the crib, among all the preparations?

lead: Yalda, the Syriac word for birth, gives this feast its name, and the four readings tell how long that birth was prepared. Isaiah gives a frightened king a sign and gives a people in darkness a child. Micah shows the nations streaming to God’s mountain and a shepherd coming from Bethlehem. Paul traces the promise from Abraham through the law to the moment when God sent his Son. Luke then tells it plainly: a decree, a journey, a manger, shepherds at night. The line runs from a promise to a Person, and its key words are sign, peace and today.

r.h: The sign and the great light
set: About 734 BC, Rezin king of Aram (Damascus) and Pekah king of Israel marched against Jerusalem to force Judah into an alliance against Assyria (Isaiah 7:1–2; 2 Kings 16:5). King Ahaz and his people shook “as the trees of the forest shake before the wind” (7:2). Ahaz was inclined to buy Assyria’s protection, which he went on to do (2 Kings 16:7). Isaiah comes to him with one message: trust God.
The second part of the reading (chapter 9) comes after the Assyrians had taken Galilee from the northern kingdom. It promises that the land which saw the darkness first will see the light first.
str: 7:10–12: God offers a sign, and Ahaz refuses it with pious words.
7:13–14: God gives a sign anyway: the child Immanuel.
7:15–16: before the child is grown, the two enemy kings will be gone.
9:1–3: Zebulun and Naphtali see a great light; joy like harvest.
9:6–7: a child born, four names, and a peace with no end.
¶ The reading passes over 9:4–5, the breaking of the oppressor’s rod and the burning of soldiers’ boots.
kw: A young woman of an age to marry. The Hebrew does not itself specify virginity, for which the usual word is bĕtûlâ. See the question below.
The Greek Old Testament, made by Jews before the time of Christ, rendered ‘almâ here by parthenos. Matthew quotes this form (1:23).
A promise in the shape of a name. Matthew begins his Gospel with it (1:23) and ends it with Jesus’ words: “I am with you always” (28:20).
vv: But Ahaz said, I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.
It sounds devout and echoes Deuteronomy 6:16. In fact he has already decided where his help will come from. There is a false piety that uses God’s name to keep God at a distance.
Look, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall name him Immanuel.

In Ahaz’s day the sign was probably a child soon to be born, perhaps in the royal house, who would show that God had not abandoned David’s line. The Church, with Matthew, reads its fullness in the virgin Mary’s Son, the one in whom God is with us in person.
The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light;

Matthew quotes these verses when Jesus begins his preaching in Galilee (Matthew 4:14–16). On this night the Church hears them with shepherds in the dark and “the glory of the Lord” shining around them.
The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this.
Peace will not come from human cleverness. God’s own burning love will bring it about.
ch: The Catechism reads Isaiah 7:14 through Matthew when it teaches that the conception of Jesus was the work of God beyond all human understanding: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (CCC 497). St Justin Martyr, in the second century, already discussed this verse with a Jewish teacher in his Dialogue with Trypho, showing how early Christians read it of Christ (in substance).

r.h: Swords into plowshares, and a shepherd of peace
set: Micah preached in the same years as Isaiah, when the Assyrian army came through Judah. The hope of 4:1–3 appears almost word for word in Isaiah 2:2–4. Between this vision and the Bethlehem oracle stands a Jerusalem under siege (5:1): the mountain of all nations is at this moment a city that has been humiliated.
str: 4:1–3: in days to come, the nations stream to the mountain of the Lord, and weapons become farming tools.
5:1: the present: siege, and the ruler struck on the cheek.
5:2: the ruler from little Bethlehem.
5:3: until she who is in labor has brought forth.
5:4–5: he will feed his flock, and “he shall be the one of peace”.
5:8–9: the remnant among the nations, like a lion.
kw: “Out of Zion shall go forth instruction” (4:2). Tôrâ is teaching for life. The nations come not to be conquered but to learn.
A woman giving birth (5:3), which echoes the mother of Isaiah 7:14. Lumen Gentium 55 reads the two texts together of Mary.
The verb in 5:4. The ruler from David’s town rules as David once kept sheep, by feeding them. That is why the first visitors on Christmas night are shepherds.
vv: For out of Zion shall go forth instruction, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.
The movement is first inward, nations coming to Zion, then outward, the word going forth. Christians hear in it the word that went out from Jerusalem through the apostles (Luke 24:47).
they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation,
Weapons are not merely laid aside but remade to feed people. Peace begins where the nations let God be their judge (“He shall judge between many peoples”).
And he shall stand and feed his flock in the strength of the Lord,
and he shall be the one of peace.
In Hebrew the words are very short, “this one shall be peace”. Peace is here a Person. Compare Ephesians 2:14.
ch: St Justin Martyr quotes this passage of Micah and says that Christians, once full of war and slaughter, have changed their swords into plowshares and their spears into farming tools (Dialogue with Trypho 109–110, in substance). Vatican II sees in “she who is in labor” a foreshadowing of Mary (Lumen Gentium 55). The Catechism says that God willed to prepare for his Son’s coming over centuries (CCC 522). The fierce image of the lion in 5:8–9 is a besieged people’s hope that God will not let them be destroyed. It is no licence for revenge: the Prince of Peace has taught his Church to love her enemies (Matthew 5:44).

r.h: The promise, the guardian, and the Son
set: Paul is answering a real pastoral question. If God’s promise came through Abraham, and then the law came through Moses, must Gentile Christians now keep the whole law? He answers by telling salvation history as one story with three stages: promise, law, Christ. Christmas is the point at which the story reaches its goal.
str: 3:15–18: a ratified will cannot be changed; the promise to Abraham and his offspring stands.
3:19–22: why then the law? It is not opposed to the promises.
3:23–25: the law as a guardian until Christ.
3:26–29: all are children of God in Christ, one in baptism.
4:1–6: the heir comes of age: God sends his Son and the Spirit of his Son.
kw: The same Greek word means a last will and a covenant, and Paul plays on both. God’s promise is like a will that has been ratified: what came later cannot cancel it.
In Genesis the word is collective (Genesis 12:7; 22:18). Paul, in the way of a Jewish teacher, leans on its singular form: all Abraham’s line finds its point in one person, Christ.
Not a schoolteacher but the household slave who took a boy to school and watched over his conduct. It is an honest role, and a temporary one: the boy grows up.
vv: Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring;
Christmas does not begin in Bethlehem. It begins with God’s word to an old man with no child.
Therefore the law was our disciplinarian until Christ came,
Paul does not call the law bad. It is “holy” (Romans 7:12). It kept and guided God’s people until the one it pointed to had come.
As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.
A picture of baptism, in which a person puts on new clothes. The Word has put on our flesh, and in baptism we put on him.
But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law,
The story of 3:15 onward reaches its goal here. The eternal Son is born into the people of the promise and under their law, a son of Abraham indeed.
ch: The Catechism calls the Old Law a preparation for the Gospel, and quotes St Irenaeus that it is “a pedagogy and a prophecy of things to come” (CCC 1964). The covenant with Israel has never been revoked (CCC 121). The white garment of baptism signifies that the baptized person has “put on Christ” (CCC 1243).

r.h: Today, in the city of David
set: Luke writes as a historian of salvation. He sets the birth under Augustus, who ruled the Roman world from 27 BC to AD 14. An inscription from Priene in Asia Minor (9 BC) calls the birthday of Augustus the beginning of “good news” for the world, and hails him as a saviour who brought peace. Luke uses the same language deliberately. The Emperor issues a decree and, without knowing it, sends a poor couple to the town where the Scriptures said the ruler would be born.
str: vv. 1–5: the decree, and the journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem.
vv. 6–7: the birth, in one plain sentence.
vv. 8–12: the angel and the shepherds: the good news and the sign.
vv. 13–14: the song of the heavenly host.
vv. 15–18: the shepherds go, find, and tell.
vv. 19–20: Mary keeps the words in her heart; the shepherds return praising God.
kw: This may mean a guest room rather than a commercial inn. Luke uses the same word for the upper guest room of the Last Supper (22:11), and a different word for the inn of the Good Samaritan (10:34). Either way, there was no suitable place for a birth, and the child is laid where the animals eat.

A feeding trough, named three times (vv. 7, 12, 16), so it matters. Isaiah 1:3, where the Greek Old Testament has this word, complains that the donkey knows its master’s manger but God’s people do not know him. Here some people come to the manger, and know.

A key word of Luke: “today” in the city of David (2:11), “today” in Nazareth (4:21), “today” in Zacchaeus’ house (19:9), “today” on the Cross (23:43). Salvation is not only a memory or a hope; it happens now.
The verb behind “I am bringing you good news”. Its word family was used for imperial announcements. Here it comes from an angel to men on the night shift.
vv: And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in bands of cloth, and laid him in a manger,

No wonders are described. Mary herself does what every mother does. Solomon too, a king, was “nursed with care in swaddling cloths” (Wisdom 7:4): the Son of God does not ask for an exemption from being a baby.
to you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is the Messiah, the Lord.

Three titles, each of them enormous, and “to you” addressed to shepherds. Savior is the word used of the Emperor. Messiah is the hope of Israel. Lord is the word that the Greek Old Testament uses for God.
and on earth peace among those whom he favors!

A note on the text. Older Greek manuscripts read “people of his favour”, which the NRSV and the Latin (“of good will”) follow, while many later ones read “good will among people”. The Syriac Peshitta, the Bible of our own tradition, reads “peace and good hope to the sons of men”. Peace is God’s gift to those he loves; it is not earned, and it is not a reward for good manners.
But Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart.

The Greek word for “pondered” means to put together, to place one thing next to another. Mary lays the angel’s words beside the manger. Everyone else in the scene is moving; she is the still centre, and she is the source of the Church’s meditation on this night.
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus was born in a humble stable into a poor family and that simple shepherds were the first witnesses, and it says that the mystery of Christmas is accomplished in us when Christ is formed in us (CCC 525–526). The angel’s message is the announcement of the Messiah promised to Israel (CCC 437). St Leo the Great, preaching on this day, said that there is no room for sadness on the birthday of life, and called out: “Christian, remember your dignity” (Sermon 21; CCC 1691). St Ephrem, in his Hymns on the Nativity, never tires of the paradox that the Lord of all lay as a small child at the breast of his mother (in substance).

qa: Isaiah says “young woman” and the caption says “virgin”. Which is right?

Both words belong to the Church’s reading. The Hebrew ‘almâ means a young woman. The Greek Old Testament has parthenos, virgin, and Matthew quotes it (1:23). The NRSV and the POC translate the Hebrew, as they are entitled to do. The Church’s faith that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary does not rest on one word in Isaiah. It rests on the Gospels (Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:26–38) and on the constant faith of the Church (CCC 496–498).
Was Jesus really born on 25 December? And what about the census of Quirinius?

The Gospels give no date. The earliest clear record of 25 December comes from Rome in the fourth century, and scholars still discuss how the date was chosen. The Church is celebrating the fact of the birth, not a date of record. On the census, there is a real difficulty: Matthew and Luke place the birth in the days of Herod, who died about 4 BC, and Josephus records a census under Quirinius about AD 6. Various solutions have been proposed and none is agreed. Luke’s purpose is clear in any case: the world’s ruler issues a decree, and God’s plan goes forward.
Does “firstborn” mean that Mary had other children?

No. “Firstborn” is a legal title for the son who opens the womb, who is to be consecrated to God (Exodus 13:2; Luke 2:23). An only son is still a firstborn son. The Church teaches that Jesus is Mary’s only child, while her spiritual motherhood extends to all people (CCC 500–501).
rite: In the Syro-Malabar Church the 25 Days’ Fast ends and the season of Nativity begins. Today’s Gospel touches our Holy Qurbana very closely: we begin it with the angels’ song, in the words handed down in our Syriac tradition, with its promise of peace and good hope. So every Qurbana opens on the fields of Bethlehem, and it brings us, like the shepherds, to the One who lay in the feeding trough and now gives himself as food. What the shepherds saw in the manger, we receive at the altar.
study: Ahaz refused a sign with pious words. Where do I use religious language to avoid really trusting God?
Micah says that swords will become plowshares. What weapon of mine, a harsh word or an old grudge, could I turn into something that feeds others this Christmas?
Paul says I have “clothed” myself with Christ in baptism. What difference does that make to how I treat the people I think are unlike me (Galatians 3:28)?
Mary “pondered”. What can I lay beside the manger today, and hold there in silence?

lead: The day after Christmas the Church moves from the crib to the stones. Acts tells how Stephen died, and the Gospel gives the warning Jesus had already spoken to his disciples: they will be handed over, and the Spirit of the Father will speak through them. Stephen is the first in whom that word comes true. The note for this day also lists the weekday readings, 1 John 2:26–29 and John 1:19–29, which are not studied here.

r.h: He saw the heavens opened
set: Stephen is one of the seven chosen to serve the Greek-speaking widows of the Jerusalem Church, “a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (6:5). He does more than wait on tables. He argues in a synagogue of Greek-speaking Jews and is brought before the council on a charge of speaking against the Temple and the law (6:11–14). His long speech (7:2–53) retells the story of Israel and ends with a hard rebuke. The reading passes over the speech and goes straight to its end.
Luke’s account reads more like a rush of fury than an orderly sentence. Stoning, outside the city, was the penalty the law set for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:14).
str: 6:8–10: grace, power and wisdom that his opponents cannot withstand.
7:54: the fury of his hearers.
7:55–56: the vision of Jesus standing at God’s right hand.
7:57–58: he is dragged out of the city and stoned; a young man named Saul keeps the coats.
7:59–60: two prayers, and his death.
kw: The ordinary word for a witness in court. Paul later speaks of “the blood of your witness Stephen” (Acts 22:20). In the early Church the word came to mean one who bears witness with his life: a martyr.
Stephen’s Greek name means a crown or wreath, like the wreath of a victor in the games. Christian writers often played on this: he was the first to receive the crown he was named for.
The Greek that the NRSV gives as “he died” is literally “he fell asleep”. It is a Christian way of speaking of death after such violence: he dies as one who will wake.
vv: “Look,” he said, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”

Elsewhere the risen Lord is said to “sit” at God’s right hand (Luke 22:69). Here he stands. Many have seen in this the witness who rises to speak for his servant, or the Lord who rises to welcome him. Apart from Jesus himself, hardly anyone in the New Testament uses the title Son of Man.
Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.

Jesus prayed on the Cross, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). Stephen prays the same prayer to Jesus. It is one of the earliest signs of Christian prayer directed to Christ as Lord.
Lord, do not hold this sin against them.

This is the mirror of “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). Luke wants us to see that the disciple dies like the Master. The young man holding the coats will one day write the letters we read at the Holy Qurbana.
ch: St Fulgentius of Ruspe joins the two feasts: yesterday we celebrated the birth in time of our eternal King; today we celebrate the triumphant suffering of his soldier. The love that brought Christ down from heaven to earth raised Stephen from earth to heaven (Sermon 3, in substance). A saying long attributed to St Augustine holds that if Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul. The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473), and it points to Stephen’s prayer as a model of intercession even for those who do us harm (CCC 2635).

r.h: Sheep among wolves
set: This belongs to the second of the five great discourses in Matthew: Jesus sends out the Twelve (10:1–42). The first part is about their mission in the towns of Israel. From v. 16 his eye reaches further, to what will happen to his messengers among the Gentiles as well. Matthew’s first readers already knew such things from experience.
str: v. 16: sheep among wolves: wise and innocent.
vv. 17–18: handed over, and led before councils, governors and kings as a testimony.
vv. 19–20: do not worry about what to say: the Spirit of the Father will speak.
vv. 21–22: division in families, hatred, and endurance to the end.
kw: Akeraios means pure, unmixed, like unmixed wine. The disciple needs both: open eyes and a clean heart. Cleverness without purity becomes cunning; purity without wisdom becomes naivety.
The word Matthew also uses of Jesus himself, “handed over” to be crucified (20:18–19; 26:2). The disciple walks the Master’s road.
Not passive suffering but standing firm under a load. The same word family is at the root of Christian “patience”.
vv: See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves;
“I am sending”: the danger is not an accident of the mission. He sends them knowingly, and he goes on being their Shepherd.
for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.

Luke notes that Stephen’s opponents “could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke” (Acts 6:10). This is the first place in the discourse where God is called “your Father”, and it comes at the worst moment.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
The “end” may be the end of a life or the end of the age. The promise holds for both.
ch: The Catechism defines fortitude as the virtue that lets us conquer fear, even fear of death, and face trials and persecutions, and it may lead a person even to give up his life for a just cause (CCC 1808). Witnesses of this kind are many in our own century too. The Church holds up the “acts of the martyrs” as an archive of truth written in letters of blood (CCC 2474).

qa: Do these readings blame the Jewish people?

No. Stephen himself was a Jew, and so were all the first Christians, Jesus and the apostles. Those who killed him were some angry men of one city at one time. Luke also shows many Jews believing (Acts 6:7), and Matthew’s “their synagogues” reflects a painful quarrel inside one family. The Church firmly rejects any blaming of the Jewish people as a whole (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598).
rite: In the season of Nativity the Syro-Malabar Church places a martyr next to the crib. We are the Church of an Apostle whom our tradition remembers as a martyr in India, St Thomas, and we know that the faith of the Child costs something. Stephen teaches the deepest lesson of that witness: to die without hatred.
study: Stephen forgave at the very moment he was being hurt. Whom do I find it hardest to forgive, and can I say his prayer for that person today?
“Wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” Which of the two do I lack more in the way I live my faith among others?

lead: Two days after Christmas the Church looks at the home in which the Son of God grew up, and the readings build that home from the foundation upward. Genesis gives the foundation: man and woman together are the image of God, and they are blessed. Sirach gives the walls: honour between the generations. Colossians gives the daily rule: love, respect and gentleness “in the Lord”. Matthew then shows a real family living this under pressure: warned at night, driven out by violence, settling at last in an unknown town. The key words are image, honour, in the Lord and get up.

r.h: Male and female, in the image of God
set: Genesis 1 is a solemn, ordered account of creation, which many scholars think received its final form around the time of the exile in Babylon. Other stories known in that world described human beings as made to serve the gods and spare them labour. Genesis says something far greater: every man and woman bears the image of God and is blessed by him.

After the repeated “God said” of the earlier days, the rhythm changes at v. 26. God does not simply command; he says “Let us make”. Humanity is the crown of the sixth day, and the only creature said to be in God’s image.
str: v. 26: God’s decision: “Let us make humankind in our image”, and the task of dominion.
v. 27: the act of creation, told in three short lines in which the verb “created” appears three times.
v. 28: the blessing: be fruitful, fill the earth, care for it.
¶ The family is not an arrangement added later. It stands within the blessing of the first page of the Bible.
kw: In the ancient world a king set up his image to mark his rule in a distant province. Here every human being, not only a king, stands in the world as God’s image. Dignity comes from the Creator, not from wealth, health or usefulness.
In the Old Testament this verb always has God as its subject. Its threefold use in v. 27 shows that the creation of man and woman is a high point.
The difference of the sexes belongs to God’s good design, and it is named in the same breath as the image of God. Neither is the image more than the other.
Strong royal words, but kings in Israel were meant to be shepherds. Dominion here means care on God’s behalf, not plunder.
vv: Then God said, “Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness;

The Hebrew plural has been explained as a plural of majesty or as God speaking to his heavenly court. Many Fathers heard in it a first hint of the Trinity, which the Christian may read in the full light of the New Testament. The word “humankind” translates ’ādām, used here for the whole human race.
So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.
The verse moves from “him” in the Hebrew (’ōtô) to “them”. One humanity, two persons who face each other. Jesus returns to this verse when he speaks of marriage (Matthew 19:4).
God blessed them, and God said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it;
The first words God speaks to the human couple are a blessing. Children appear in the Bible first as blessing, not as burden.
ch: The Catechism teaches that man and woman were willed by God in perfect equality as persons (CCC 369), and that Scripture begins with the creation of man and woman in God’s image and ends with the wedding feast of the Lamb (CCC 1602). The family is “a communion of persons, a sign and image of the communion of the Father and the Son in the Holy Spirit” (CCC 2205). “Subduing” the earth is the task of stewards, not arbitrary and destructive domination (CCC 373). St Irenaeus distinguishes the image from the likeness to which we grow by the Spirit (in substance). St John Paul II taught that to be in God’s image means to exist in relationship, in a communion of persons (Mulieris Dignitatem 7).

r.h: Honour your father by word and deed
set: Jesus son of Sirach, or Ben Sira, was a teacher in Jerusalem about 180 BC. His grandson translated the book into Greek in Egypt some decades later, as the book’s own prologue says. Large portions of the Hebrew text have been recovered in modern times. The Catholic Church receives the book as inspired Scripture. Its old Latin name, Ecclesiasticus, reflects its long use in the Church.

Ben Sira’s world was changing quickly under Greek culture, and the young were drawn to new ways. He takes the commandment of Exodus 20:12 and turns it into a small sermon, showing what it means inside a home.
str: vv. 1–2: a teacher speaks as a father; God himself upholds the authority of father and mother.
vv. 3–6: the promises: sins atoned, treasure laid up, joy in one’s own children, prayer heard, long life.
vv. 7–9: honour in practice: word and deed, and the power of a parent’s blessing.
kw: The word of the commandment (Exodus 20:12) comes from a Hebrew root meaning “to be heavy”. To honour parents is to give them their full weight, not to treat them lightly.
A word from the language of Temple worship. Ben Sira dares to use it of the home: daily love of parents has a place in the healing of sin.
Like saving for the future. What is given to a mother is not lost; it is stored up with God.
vv: For the Lord honors a father above his children, and he confirms a mother’s right over her children.
Father and mother stand side by side throughout this passage. In a society that gave the father most of the power, this equal naming matters.
Those who honor their father atone for sins,
A strong saying. It does not compete with the sacrifice of Christ. It says that sin is healed also through love that repairs what selfishness has damaged.
Those who respect their father will have long life, and those who honor their mother obey the Lord;

The Malayalam POC reads the second half differently (the one who obeys the Lord gladdens his mother). The ancient texts of Sirach differ in places. In both forms, obeying God and honouring a mother belong together.
Honor your father by word and deed, that his blessing may come upon you.
Honour is spoken and done: a respectful voice, a visit, a hospital bill paid. The chapter goes on to speak of the care of a father in old age (3:12–13), just beyond today’s reading.
ch: The Catechism draws on this teaching for the fourth commandment: respect for parents comes from gratitude to those who gave us life (CCC 2214–2215), and grown children owe their parents material and moral support in old age, sickness, loneliness or distress (CCC 2218). This commandment opens the second table of the Decalogue and shows the order of charity (CCC 2197).

r.h: A home under the Lord
set: Colossians is written from prison (4:3, 18) to a young Church in the Lycus valley, in what is now western Turkey. Just before this passage Paul has listed the clothing of the new life: compassion, kindness, patience, forgiveness and, above all, love (3:12–14), and he has said, “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). Today’s verses apply that to the home.

Scholars call such passages “household codes” (see also Ephesians 5:21–6:9; 1 Peter 2:18–3:7). Ancient writers on the household usually addressed its head. Paul speaks directly to wives and children as well as to husbands and fathers, and he gives duties to every side.
str: v. 18: wives.
v. 19: husbands.
v. 20: children.
v. 21: fathers.
¶ The pattern is mutual. Each of the two pairs has a word for the one with less power and a stronger limit for the one with more.
kw: Literally “place yourselves under”, a voluntary ordering. Paul’s word to the Ephesians first asks all to “be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). The same verb describes the boy Jesus at Nazareth (Luke 2:51).
Rare in the ancient lists of a husband’s duties, and the verb Paul uses for Christ’s own love. It sets the husband’s duty far above mere provision.
Do not stir up or irritate. Constant criticism and harshness can break a child’s spirit; “lose heart” (athymōsin) means to become discouraged.
vv: Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
“In the Lord” sets the measure. Nothing that goes against the Lord can be demanded in his name.
Husbands, love your wives and never treat them harshly.
The Greek speaks of becoming bitter toward someone. Paul forbids the sourness and hardness of a man who has power in the house.
Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is your acceptable duty in the Lord.
Written to children who were expected to be present when the letter was read in the assembly. They are members of the Church in their own right.
Fathers, do not provoke your children, or they may lose heart.
The ancient father held wide legal power over his children. Here he is told to think of how his child feels. This was a quiet revolution.
ch: St John Paul II read such texts in the light of Ephesians 5:21: the subjection in Christian marriage is mutual (Mulieris Dignitatem 24). Pope Francis says the same: what we must keep from this teaching is the revealed call to mutual love and service, not any form of domination (Amoris Laetitia 156). St John Chrysostom, preaching on Ephesians, calls a household “a little Church” (in substance). The Second Vatican Council speaks of the family as “domestic Church” (Lumen Gentium 11; CCC 1655–1657, 2204).

r.h: Get up, take the child and his mother
set: The Magi have gone home by another road. Matthew now tells three short episodes, each ending with a prophecy, the first and last led by a dream: the flight to Egypt (2:13–15), the killing at Bethlehem (2:16–18, read tomorrow) and the return (2:19–23).

Herod the Great was a capable and feared ruler who killed even members of his own family when he suspected a threat, as the historian Josephus records. He died in 4 BC. His kingdom was divided among his sons: Archelaus received Judea, and Antipas received Galilee. Josephus reports that Archelaus began his rule with a bloody repression at Passover; Rome removed him in AD 6.
str: vv. 13–14: the first dream and the flight by night.
vv. 19–21: Herod’s death, a second dream and the return.
vv. 22–23: Joseph’s fear, a further warning, and the home in Nazareth.
¶ Each time the angel says “Get up”, and each time Matthew reports that Joseph “got up”. The obedience is told in almost the same words as the command.
kw: to paidion kai tēn mētera autou
The phrase comes again and again in this chapter (2:11, 13, 14, 20, 21). The child is at the centre, and Joseph is never called his father here, yet everything depends on Joseph’s care.
An everyday word, also used for rising from the dead. It marks prompt action. In the whole Gospel record Joseph speaks no word; he acts.
Israel’s Lord asks the Holy Family to run. Egypt was a traditional place of refuge (1 Kings 11:40), and a large Jewish community lived there at this time.

No Old Testament verse says these exact words, and Matthew speaks of “the prophets” in general. He may be playing on nēṣer, the “branch” from the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1), and perhaps on nāzîr, one consecrated to God (Judges 13:5), as well as on the name Nazareth.
vv: Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you;

Joseph is given no date and no plan, only the next step. St John Chrysostom notes that the angel no longer says “your wife”, as in 1:20, but “his mother” (in substance): the child born of Mary is now the centre of Joseph’s life.
Then Joseph got up, took the child and his mother by night, and went to Egypt,
“By night”: he does not wait for morning. The Son of God begins his earthly life as a refugee, carried over a border in the dark.
“Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who were seeking the child’s life are dead.”

These words echo what the Lord told Moses in Midian: “all those who were seeking your life are dead” (Exodus 4:19). Jesus relives the story of Moses and Israel: threatened by a king, saved, called out of Egypt.
And after being warned in a dream, he went away to the district of Galilee.
Joseph is afraid, and the text does not hide it. Faith does not mean having no fear. God leads him through ordinary caution as well as through dreams.
There he made his home in a town called Nazareth,
A small village never mentioned in the Old Testament. The great journey of the infancy story ends in an unknown place, where the Son of God will live most of his life.
ch: The Catechism says that the flight into Egypt and the killing of the innocents show the opposition of darkness to the light, and that Jesus’ whole life was lived under the sign of persecution, while his departure from Egypt recalls the Exodus (CCC 530). His hidden life at Nazareth, in obedience, is the way of most human beings (CCC 531–533). Pope Pius XII opened his constitution on migrants, Exsul Familia (1952), with the Holy Family in exile. Pope Francis writes that every family should look to the icon of the Holy Family, whose daily life had its burdens and even nightmares, and he thinks of refugee families today (Amoris Laetitia 30). Pope Francis describes St Joseph as an obedient and creatively courageous father (Patris Corde 3, 5).

qa: Does Colossians 3:18 mean a husband may dominate his wife?

No. The verse says “as is fitting in the Lord”, and it stands next to the command that husbands love and never treat their wives harshly. The Church reads these words in the light of mutual subjection in Christ (Ephesians 5:21; Mulieris Dignitatem 24; Amoris Laetitia 156). The text gives no support to violence or fear in a home.
Must I obey my parents “in everything”, even as an adult, or if they ask something wrong?

Paul writes to children living in the home. The Catechism teaches that a child must obey in all that is asked for his or her good or that of the family, but must not obey if conscience sees that the request is morally wrong (CCC 2217). Once grown, children no longer owe the same obedience, but honour and care remain for life (CCC 2217–2218). Honouring a parent who has hurt a child does not mean denying the wound; it may mean care from a safe distance, with prayer.
Did the flight to Egypt really happen? Is there any other record?

Only Matthew tells it. Yet it fits what is known: Herod’s violence, the Jewish community in Egypt and the division of the kingdom after his death. Matthew tells real events and shows, through Scripture, what they mean.
rite: Many Syro-Malabar families live what this Gospel describes: a father or mother working in the Gulf or far from home, children raised across borders, journeys made for the sake of the family. The Holy Family knew the road and the unfamiliar land. Family prayer in the evening, long loved in Kerala homes, is the practice of what Colossians asks. On this Sunday of the Nativity season the Holy Qurbana gathers these scattered families around the Child whom Mary and Joseph carried, and the home becomes again a little Church.
study: Genesis 1:27 says each person is the image of God. How would my home change if we treated one another with that in mind?
Sirach asks us to honour parents “by word and deed”. What is one concrete thing I can do this week for a parent or an elder?
Which of the words in Colossians 3:18–21 do I find hardest, and what does “in the Lord” add to it?
St Joseph was given only the next step, not the whole plan. Where is God asking me to “get up” today?

lead: The joy of Christmas is followed at once by the tears of Bethlehem. Today’s readings draw one line of innocent blood through the whole Bible. Genesis shows the first murder, of a brother, by a man who would not master his anger. Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping and carries God’s promise that her children will come back. Hebrews remembers those who suffered for their faith and of whom “the world was not worthy”. Matthew shows the children of Bethlehem, killed by a frightened king, while the Child he sought is carried away. The key words are blood, weeping and hope.

r.h: Where the killing began
set: Genesis 3 told how the first man and woman turned from God. Genesis 4 shows what follows outside the garden: sin moves from the relation with God to the relation with a brother. The story is short and bare, and the word “brother” sounds seven times in vv. 1–11.
The names may be meaningful. Abel (hebel in Hebrew) means “breath” or “vapour”, the word used in Ecclesiastes for what passes away. His life is short, and he never speaks in the story.
str: vv. 3–5a: two offerings; the Lord regards one and not the other.
v. 5b: Cain’s anger and his fallen face.
vv. 6–7: God speaks to Cain before the crime, warning him as a father would.
v. 8: the field and the killing.
kw: A gift or tribute. Both brothers bring one. The text does not explain why only Abel’s is regarded. It only notes that Abel brought the “firstlings” and “their fat portions”, the best that he had.
Crouching, lying in wait, like an animal at a door. Sin is pictured as a beast waiting for Cain to open.
The same rare word as in Genesis 3:16. Sin wants to possess Cain, yet the verse says he “must master it”. Temptation is real, and so is human responsibility.
vv: but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his countenance fell.
The hidden wound is envy. The Hebrew says literally that it burned in him. His face tells what his heart is doing.
If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is lurking at the door; its desire is for you, but you must master it.
God does not reject Cain. Before the crime he speaks to him, questions him and offers a way out. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, but its main sense is clear: nothing is yet decided.
Cain said to his brother Abel, “Let us go out to the field.” And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel, and killed him.

A note on the text. The standard Hebrew text says “Cain said to his brother Abel”, and then gives no words. The words “Let us go out to the field” come from ancient versions, including the Greek and the Syriac, and both the NRSV and the POC include them. Two lines later a brother is dead.
ch: Jesus himself names “righteous Abel” as the first in the line of those who shed innocent blood (Matthew 23:35). Hebrews says that Christ’s blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (12:24), for Abel’s blood cries out for justice, and Christ’s for mercy. The Catechism sees in this story the anger and envy that are the consequences of original sin (CCC 2259). St John Paul II opens Evangelium Vitae with a long meditation on Cain and Abel (EV 7–9). The Syriac teacher Aphrahat, in his Demonstration on Prayer, says that Abel’s offering was accepted because of the purity of his heart (in substance).

r.h: Rachel weeping, and a word of hope
set: Jeremiah 30–31 is often called the Book of Consolation, a bright section in a dark book. The prophet lived through the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC. The northern tribes had been taken away by Assyria more than a century earlier.

Ramah lay a few miles north of Jerusalem, in the land of Benjamin, and Jeremiah says that exiles were gathered there in chains (Jeremiah 40:1). Rachel, Jacob’s beloved wife, was the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and so the grandmother of the great northern tribes. She had died long before; the prophet imagines her crying from her grave for her lost descendants.
str: v. 15: the voice in Ramah: Rachel refuses to be comforted.
vv. 16–17: the Lord’s answer: stop weeping; they will come back.
¶ “Thus says the Lord” opens both parts. God is the one who reports her grief, and God is the one who answers it.
kw: A very similar phrase is used of Jacob when he thinks Joseph is dead (Genesis 37:35). God does not scold this refusal; he answers it with a promise.
“A reward for your work”, as if her tears were labour that God takes into account.
From the same root as the verb for waiting with eager hope. Jeremiah uses the word for the future God plans for his people (29:11).
vv: Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted for her children, because they are no more.
The Bible lets a mother cry with no easy words offered. It gives this grief the dignity of Scripture.
Keep your voice from weeping, and your eyes from tears; for there is a reward for your work, says the Lord: they shall come back from the land of the enemy;
God alone can say “stop weeping” without being cruel, because he alone can bring the children back.
there is hope for your future, says the Lord: your children shall come back to their own country.
Later in this same chapter comes the promise of the new covenant (31:31–34).
ch: Matthew quotes v. 15 today and stops there. A reader who knows Jeremiah hears what comes next, the promise of return, and so the Gospel’s silence is not despair. Jewish tradition has also treasured Rachel as the mother who weeps and intercedes for her children; a well-known passage in the Midrash on Lamentations says that God was moved by her plea (in substance). For Christians the final answer to every Rachel is the Resurrection.

r.h: Of whom the world was not worthy
set: Hebrews 11 is the great roll call of faith. It opens by defining faith as “the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (11:1), and it runs from Abel (11:4) through Abraham and Moses. At v. 32 the author runs out of time and hurries on.
The readers are tired Christians who have already known suffering (10:32–34). The chapter tells them that the people of God has always walked by faith, in victory and in defeat alike.
str: v. 32: names from Judges, David, Samuel and the prophets.
vv. 33–35a: faith that triumphs: kingdoms won, lions’ mouths shut, fire quenched, the dead given back.
vv. 35b–38: faith that suffers: torture, chains, stoning, the sword, the wilderness.
¶ The turning point is in the middle of v. 35. The second list is not a failure of faith. Both lists are “through faith”.
kw: A kind of torture by beating. The related word appears in the account of the old scribe Eleazar in 2 Maccabees 6:19, 28, which this passage seems to remember.
Better than the return to this life given to the widows’ sons (1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:18–37). The brothers in 2 Maccabees 7 refused release in the hope of being raised by God.
The word used in the Greek Old Testament for the mantle of Elijah. These are prophets’ clothes.
vv: who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions,
Lions recall Daniel (Daniel 6). The “raging fire” of the next verse recalls the three young men (Daniel 3).
Others were tortured, refusing to accept release, in order to obtain a better resurrection.
Faith here looks beyond death. Their courage rests on a promise that they did not see fulfilled.
They were stoned to death, they were sawn in two, they were killed by the sword;

Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the Temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). An old Jewish tradition says that Isaiah was sawn in two. A note on the text: some ancient manuscripts have one more verb here, “they were tested”, and the POC reflects a text of this kind (ചിലരെ വിചാരണ ചെയ്തു); the NRSV follows those without it.
of whom the world was not worthy.
A stunning reversal. The world judged them worthless and drove them out. God’s verdict is that the world did not deserve them.
ch: The Catechism calls Hebrews 11 a eulogy of the faith of the ancestors (CCC 147) and urges us to look to this “cloud of witnesses” (Hebrews 12:1; CCC 165). Martyrdom is “the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith” (CCC 2473). On this feast the reading lets the children of Bethlehem take their place in that long line.

r.h: A voice was heard in Ramah
set: Herod feared any rival. The Magi had asked him for the “king of the Jews” (2:2), a title that belonged to him by Roman grant. When they did not come back, he acted.

No other ancient writer records this event, and Bethlehem was small. Many scholars reckon the number of boys to have been modest, perhaps a score or so. Josephus does not mention it, but he describes a Herod who had his wife Mariamne and three of his own sons put to death, and the deed fits that picture.
str: vv. 13–15: the Child is taken to safety; Hosea 11:1 is fulfilled.
v. 16: Herod’s rage and the killing.
vv. 17–18: Jeremiah’s word is fulfilled.
¶ Matthew is telling a new story of Moses: a ruler kills Hebrew boys (Exodus 1:15–22), and one child escapes to save his people.
kw: The same verb is used when the soldiers mock Jesus as king (Matthew 27:29, 31). The powerful who cannot bear being mocked here will mock him there.
Burning anger, the same inner fire as Cain’s. Fear of losing power is enough to set it alight.
A masculine form, so the POC rightly says “boys” (ആൺകുട്ടികളെ). Two years is a wide margin: fear calculates generously.
vv: and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet, “Out of Egypt I have called my son.”
Hosea 11:1 speaks of Israel. Matthew sees Jesus as the true Son, who sums up his people’s whole story in himself.
he was infuriated, and he sent and killed all the children in and around Bethlehem who were two years old or under,
Matthew’s words are plain and restrained. He does not describe the scene; he states it.
Then was fulfilled what had been spoken through the prophet Jeremiah:
Compare the wording in 2:15, “This was to fulfill”. Here, as often noted, Matthew writes “Then was fulfilled”, avoiding any suggestion that God intended this evil.
“A voice was heard in Ramah, wailing and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be consoled, because they are no more.”
Tradition placed Rachel’s tomb on the way to Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19). The mothers of Bethlehem join the mother of Israel in her grief.
ch: The Catechism teaches that this event shows “the opposition of darkness to the light”, and that those who belong to Christ share his persecution (CCC 530). The Church honours these children as martyrs. St Irenaeus says that the Lord sent these children ahead of him into his kingdom (in substance). St Quodvultdeus of Carthage, in a sermon the Roman Office reads on this feast, says that these children die for Christ without knowing it, and that God’s grace gives them a crown (in substance). The feast is also a defence of the weakest: every human life is to be protected from its beginning (CCC 2270; Evangelium Vitae).

qa: How can babies be martyrs if they did not choose to die for Christ?

A martyr’s crown is above all God’s gift. These children died in place of Christ and because of him. The Church has long held that those who die for the sake of Christ without Baptism are baptized by their death for and with him (CCC 1258), and it has honoured the Innocents from early times.
Why did God warn Joseph and not the other families?

The Gospel gives no answer, and no honest reader should pretend that this is easy. Evil here comes from Herod, not from God. God does not explain suffering in the Bible by theory; he enters it. The Child saved today will not be saved from Calvary. The Catechism says that only the whole of the Christian faith answers the question of evil, and it points to the Cross and the Resurrection (CCC 309, 272).
What about children who die today without Baptism, or before they are born?
The Church entrusts them to the mercy of God, who desires that all be saved, and to Jesus’ tenderness toward children, which allows us to hope that there is a way of salvation for them (CCC 1261).
rite: In Kerala this day is known as Kunjippaithangal, and it is kept as Holy Childhood Day (Thirubalasakhyam). The Holy Childhood Association was founded in France in 1843 by Bishop Charles de Forbin-Janson so that children might pray and share for other children, and it is a Pontifical Mission Society. So the Syro-Malabar child who gives a small coin today stands against Herod in a real way.
