At the Holy Qurbana we may remember children who suffer now: the unborn, the abused, the trafficked, the hungry and those caught in war. We may also remember parents who have buried a child: the Bible gives them Rachel’s voice, and Rachel’s promise.
study: Before the crime God speaks to Cain: “you must master it”. What anger or envy is crouching at my door today?
Jeremiah 31 lets Rachel weep before God answers. How do we keep company with those who grieve, without hurrying them?
Hebrews says that the world was “not worthy” of those it despised. Who are the despised in my town, and how does the Church stand with them?
What can my parish or family do this year for children who suffer?

lead: Paul describes a community in which people carry one another’s burdens, and Luke shows the home where such love was learned. At twelve Jesus reveals who his Father is, and then goes down to Nazareth and is obedient. Both readings speak of patient, daily faithfulness that bears fruit in its own time.

r.h: Bear one another’s burdens
set: Paul has written to the Churches of Galatia with deep concern, because some were teaching that Gentile Christians must be circumcised and keep the Law. He has just contrasted the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit (5:16–26). Now, near the end, he shows what life in the Spirit looks like when someone in the community falls.
str: vv. 1–5: restoring the one who falls, carrying burdens, examining oneself.
v. 6: support for those who teach.
vv. 7–10: sowing and reaping: do not grow weary in doing good.
kw: The word used for mending nets (Mark 1:19) and, by medical writers, for setting a broken bone. Correction aims to heal, and it must be done gently.

Two different words. Barē in v. 2 are heavy weights that no one should carry alone. Phortion in v. 5 is a person’s own pack, the word used for a soldier’s kit. We help with the first; no one else can answer for the second.
Paul has just said that the whole Law is summed up in love of neighbour (5:14). Christ’s law is his own command of love, and his own life of carrying our burdens.
vv: if anyone is detected in a transgression, you who have received the Spirit should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.
The sign of having the Spirit is not spotless pride, but gentleness toward someone who has fallen. The warning follows: “Take care that you yourselves are not tempted.”
Bear one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.
So let us not grow weary in doing what is right, for we will reap at harvest time, if we do not give up.
The sower does not see the harvest on the day of sowing. Paul knows that good people get tired, and he gives them a promise.
ch: The Catechism calls the New Law a law of love (CCC 1972), and fraternal correction belongs to charity (CCC 1829). St Augustine devoted a whole reflection to this verse, teaching that nothing tests a friend so much as bearing the burden of another (in substance). The verse gives us a simple rule for parish and home: help first, then speak.

r.h: In my Father’s house
set: This is the only story in the Gospels from the years between Jesus’ infancy and his public ministry. The Law asked men to go up three times a year for the festivals (Deuteronomy 16:16), and Luke notes that Joseph and Mary went every year. Nazareth lay several days’ journey from Jerusalem. People travelled in groups of relatives and neighbours, which explains why they could walk a whole day without missing him.
str: vv. 41–45: the pilgrimage, and the boy missed.
vv. 46–47: found in the Temple among the teachers.
vv. 48–50: Mary’s question and Jesus’ first words in this Gospel.
vv. 51–52: the return to Nazareth; he is obedient and grows.
kw: A strong word: in pain, in anguish. Simeon’s sword (2:35) has already begun to pierce.
Literally “in the things of my Father”. It may mean his house, as the NRSV has it, or his affairs, as the POC has it. Both are true; the Greek allows both.
Luke’s verb says “he kept on being obedient”. It is the same word that Colossians 3:18 uses for ordering life under another. The eternal Son places himself under a carpenter and a village mother.
vv: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.
He listens first. “After three days” may also make the reader think of Easter (24:7, 46), when other seekers look for him and are told where he truly is.
Child, why have you treated us like this? Look, your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety.
A mother’s honest question. St Augustine notes that Mary, out of respect for her husband, names Joseph first, and that Joseph is rightly called father because of their true marriage (in substance).
Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?
Mary says “your father”, and Jesus answers “my Father”. His first words in Luke name the Father, as his last words on the Cross do (23:46). “Must” (dei) is the word Luke uses for God’s plan.
Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. His mother treasured all these things in her heart.
They did not understand (v. 50), yet Mary keeps what she does not understand. That is a model for all faith.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and in years, and in divine and human favor.
ch: The Catechism says that the finding in the Temple is the only event that breaks the silence of the Gospels about the hidden years, and that it lets us glimpse Jesus’ total consecration to the mission that flows from his divine sonship (CCC 534). His obedience to Mary and Joseph is an image in time of his obedience to the Father (CCC 532). Jesus truly grew in human knowledge, while his human mind also knew the Father in a unique way (CCC 472–473).

qa: Did the boy Jesus disobey his parents by staying behind?

The Gospel does not treat it as a fault. He acts out of a higher obedience to the Father, and at once afterward he goes home and is obedient to them. The episode shows that even the best family ties serve God’s call, and that a call may cost parents sorrow. Jesus was without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
study: Whose burden can I help to carry this week, and is there someone I should correct gently rather than criticize?
Mary kept in her heart what she did not understand. What am I being asked to keep, without yet understanding it?

lead: As the year runs out, both readings meet people who have reached the limit of their strength. Paul has pleaded three times for relief, and hears that grace is enough. The disciples row at night against the wind, and hear “It is I; do not be afraid.” The Child of Bethlehem is the Lord who comes to us in our weakness and in our dark.

r.h: My grace is sufficient for you
set: Rival preachers at Corinth, whom Paul calls “super-apostles” (11:5), were boasting of their gifts and looking down on him. Against his will he plays the “fool” and boasts in his turn (11:1–12:13): first of his sufferings, then of a vision in which he was taken up to the third heaven (12:1–5). He stops short at the point he most wants to make: what he has learned is weakness.
str: vv. 6–7a: why he holds back from boasting.
vv. 7b–8: the thorn, and three prayers.
v. 9a: the Lord’s answer.
vv. 9b–10: Paul’s new boast.
kw: A pointed stake or splinter, something that keeps on hurting. Paul never says what it was. Suggestions include a chronic illness (see Galatians 4:13) and persistent opposition, which is how St John Chrysostom took it (in substance). The silence helps: every reader can think of his own.
In the present tense: it is enough now. Paul asked for removal, and receives a promise of presence.
Literally “may pitch its tent over me”. It is related to the verb John uses of the Word who “lived among us” (John 1:14). The power of the Incarnate Lord makes its home in Paul’s weakness.
vv: a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me, to keep me from being too elated.
The same thing is both Satan’s attack and a gift within God’s plan. God can use even what he did not will as good.
Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me,
Paul prays as Jesus did in Gethsemane, three times (Matthew 26:44). Asking God for relief is not a lack of faith.
but he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.”
An answer that is not the answer he asked for. Yet it is an answer, and the Lord speaks to him in person.
for whenever I am weak, then I am strong.
ch: The Catechism teaches that even the most intense prayers do not always obtain healing, and that Paul had to learn from the Lord that grace is sufficient, and that suffering can mean “completing” what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (CCC 1508). It also says that faith “glories in its weaknesses in order to draw to itself Christ’s power” (CCC 273), as Mary did, the supreme model of such faith.

r.h: It is I; do not be afraid
set: John places this short story between the feeding of the five thousand (6:1–15) and the discourse on the Bread of Life (6:25–59), at the time of Passover (6:4). After the crowd tries to make him king, Jesus withdraws to the mountain alone, and the disciples leave without him. The Sea of Galilee is a lake set low among hills, and sudden strong winds are known there.
Matthew and Mark tell the same event (Matthew 14:22–33; Mark 6:45–52). John’s account is the shortest, and it has its own way of pointing to who Jesus is.
str: vv. 16–18: evening, darkness, wind.
vv. 19–21: Jesus comes on the water; “It is I”; the boat reaches land.
vv. 22–24: the crowd goes looking for him, which leads into the discourse on the Bread.
kw: In John, darkness is more than the time of day (1:5). Jesus “had not yet come to them” is said with some weight.
The Greek gives a measure in stadia, twenty-five or thirty, which the POC keeps. It comes to about five or six kilometres: well out on the water, and far from either shore.
Ordinary words for “It’s me”, and also the words “I AM”, which recall God’s self-revelation (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10). John often lets the phrase bear this weight (8:28, 58).
vv: The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.
they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were terrified.
In the Old Testament, God alone tramples the waves of the sea (Job 9:8) and makes a path through the great waters (Psalm 77:19). The disciples see divine power, and they are afraid.
But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”
He comes before they call. He does not first calm the sea: the first thing that is changed is their fear.
Then they wanted to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat reached the land toward which they were going.
The Psalm says that God “brought them to their desired haven” (107:30). Once he is welcome in the boat, the journey is completed.
ch: The Catechism says that by giving his life Jesus reveals that he himself bears the divine name “I AM” (CCC 211). The early Christian writer Tertullian saw the little ship as a figure of the Church, tossed by the waves of persecution and temptation, while the Lord patiently seems to sleep or stay away, and then comes to her (in substance; On Baptism 12). This reading is a good one to pray at the close of a year, while we look back over the storms it has held.

qa: Why does God not always answer prayers for healing?

We do not always know. Paul’s experience shows that a prayer may be answered by a gift other than the one requested. The Church continues to pray for the sick with confidence, and it knows that the Lord is present with us even where healing does not come (CCC 1508). His presence in suffering is itself grace.
study: What weakness have I been ashamed of this year, and how might Christ’s power be at work in it?
When has the Lord come to me “in the dark” before I called? How do I welcome him into my boat?

lead: On the last day of the civil year, the four readings work like an examination of conscience. Leviticus says that a wrong done to a neighbour must be repaired. Wisdom shows how quickly everything passes, except the reward of the righteous. First Timothy teaches contentment and sets our eyes on eternal life. Luke’s fig tree gives the whole day its tone: “let it alone for one more year”. The new year is mercy, and it is meant to bear fruit.

r.h: Repay, then offer
set: Leviticus 1–7 sets out the sacrifices. This passage closes the section on the guilt offering (5:14–6:7). In the Hebrew Bible these verses are numbered 5:20–26. It treats sins against a neighbour in matters of property, where a false oath has been sworn in God’s name.
str: vv. 1–3: the wrongs: deception, robbery, fraud, keeping what was found, false oaths.
vv. 4–5: restitution in full, with one-fifth added.
vv. 6–7: then the ram; the priest makes atonement, and there is forgiveness.
kw: A breach of faith. The cheated person is a neighbour, yet the text calls it a trespass “against the Lord”. Wronging a neighbour is wronging God.
An offering of reparation. Isaiah 53:10 uses the same word of the Suffering Servant: “an offering for sin”.
vv: you shall repay the principal amount and shall add one-fifth to it. You shall pay it to its owner when you realize your guilt.

Restitution comes first, and the victim is repaid before anything is offered at the altar. Jesus says the same: “first be reconciled” (Matthew 5:24). Zacchaeus does far more than the law requires (Luke 19:8).
The priest shall make atonement on your behalf before the Lord, and you shall be forgiven for any of the things that one may do and incur guilt thereby.
The list of sins ends with a sure promise: there is a way back.
ch: The Catechism says that many sins wrong our neighbour and that simple justice requires us to repair the harm, returning stolen goods and restoring a good name, and that absolution does not remove this duty (CCC 1459, 2412). Under the New Covenant, the one offering of Christ brings the forgiveness the old sacrifices pointed to (Hebrews 10:10–14).

r.h: The righteous live forever
set: The Book of Wisdom was written in Greek, most likely among the Jews of Alexandria in the first century BC. In this scene the ungodly, who had mocked the righteous, now see them vindicated (5:1–5) and speak with regret. Verses 7–10 are their words. Verses 14–16 give the author’s reply.
str: vv. 7–8: the regretful questions: what has arrogance profited us?
vv. 9–10: all has vanished, like a shadow or a ship’s track.
v. 14: the hope of the ungodly is like chaff and smoke.
vv. 15–16: the righteous live forever.
kw: There and gone. Wealth and fame cast no lasting mark.
What the righteous have is not their own achievement stored up; it is “with the Lord”, kept by him.
vv: What has our arrogance profited us? And what good has our boasted wealth brought us?
Honest questions, but asked too late. The reader has the chance to ask them today.
like a ship that sails through the billowy water, and when it has passed no trace can be found,
A fine image for a year gone by. What remains is what was done in God.
But the righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord; the Most High takes care of them.
One of the clearest Old Testament words of hope beyond death, close to “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (3:1).
ch: The Catechism teaches that each person receives eternal retribution at death, in a particular judgment that refers the life to Christ (CCC 1021–1022). At the end of a year this passage is not meant to frighten. It helps us ask what lasts.

r.h: Fight the good fight of the faith
set: The letter is traditionally by Paul; some scholars think a later disciple wrote it. It is addressed to Timothy, left in charge at Ephesus (1:3). The author has just warned of teachers who treat godliness as “a means of gain” (6:5), and he answers by turning the phrase around: real gain is godliness with contentment.
str: vv. 6–8: enough is enough: food and clothing.
vv. 9–10: the trap of wanting to be rich.
vv. 11–12: the man of God: flee, pursue, fight, take hold.
kw: A word prized by the Stoics for self-sufficiency. For Paul it rests on God, not on oneself (see Philippians 4:11–13).
The text does not call money the root of evil. It says that the love of money is “a root of all kinds of evil”.
Athletic language, the struggle in the games. The present tense tells him to keep on with it.
vv: for we brought nothing into the world, so that we can take nothing out of it;
An old saying of the Bible (compare Job 1:21).
For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil,
Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of the eternal life, to which you were called and for which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
The good confession may well be Timothy’s baptism, or his ordination. Every Christian may look back to a day on which a promise was made.
ch: The Catechism warns against greed and urges detachment from riches, which is needed for entry into the Kingdom (CCC 2536, 2544). A year’s accounts look different when a Christian reads them in this light.

r.h: One more year
set: Only Luke has this parable. Just before it, people have told Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate, and he has spoken of eighteen who died when a tower fell. He refuses to treat them as worse sinners, and says twice, “unless you repent, you will all perish” (13:3, 5). The parable answers the question: how long will God wait?

Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. Isaiah had sung of God looking for fruit in his vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7). Jesus speaks to his hearers, and through them to every reader: the point is each person’s response, not any people’s guilt.
str: v. 6: the owner comes looking for fruit.
v. 7: three years, nothing: “Cut it down!”
vv. 8–9: the gardener pleads for one more year, and promises to dig and manure.
¶ The story has no ending. We are not told what the tree does.
kw: Using up the soil without return. An empty life also takes up space that could bear fruit.
The same verb is used for “forgive” (compare Luke 23:34). The gardener’s plea is a word of mercy.
Hardly a noble word. The gardener is willing to get his hands dirty for the tree.
vv: So he said to the gardener, ‘See here! For three years I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree, and still I find none. Cut it down! Why should it be wasting the soil?’
Justice is real: fruit is expected.
He replied, ‘Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it.
Christian readers see Christ in the gardener, who stands between us and judgment and works on us. The extra year is not idle time; it is full of his labour.
If it bears fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’”
Mercy gives time, but time does not last forever.
ch: St Augustine preached on this parable, seeing in the manure the humble sorrow of the repentant sinner (in substance). God’s patience is “not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9; CCC 1037). The Church reminds us of the urgency of conversion while there is time (CCC 1036).

qa: Is the parable a threat for the new year?

It is a warning wrapped in mercy. The owner’s word is true, and the gardener’s plea is stronger. A Christian ends the year not in fear, but in thanksgiving for the time given, and with the resolve to use it.
rite: Many Syro-Malabar parishes close the year with a service of thanksgiving. It is a good moment to do what the readings ask: to thank God for the year, to put right a wrong we have done, and to ask for the grace of one more year that bears fruit. The Holy Qurbana is the Church’s great thanksgiving.
study: Is there something I owe someone, in money or in good name, that I should put right before this year ends?
What fruit does the Lord look for in me in the year to come, and what “digging” may he have to do in me to bring it about?
